questions.stem: A researcher stains a dividing human somatic cell and captures it at prophase of mitosis, after DNA synthesis is complete. How many chromatids are present in this cell?

explanation.summary: After S phase each of the 46 chromosomes carries two sister chromatids, so a prophase mitotic cell has 92 chromatids.
explanation.whyCorrect: During S phase DNA synthesis produces an identical copy of each DNA molecule, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids. At prophase of mitosis the cell still has 46 chromosomes but now contains 92 chromatids, double the amount of genetic material, ready for segregation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 chromatids would be found in a haploid gamete, not a somatic cell in mitosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 46 chromatids describes a cell in G1, before S phase replicates the DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 69 does not correspond to any normal cell state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 184 is twice the correct value and is not found in a normal cell.

questions.stem: A germ cell has completed meiosis I and is now in prophase II. How many chromatids does this cell contain?

explanation.summary: After meiosis I the homologs have separated to give 23 chromosomes, but each still has two sister chromatids, for 46 chromatids.
explanation.whyCorrect: In meiosis I homologous chromosomes segregate, so the daughter cell is haploid with 23 chromosomes. However, the sister chromatids do not separate until meiosis II, so each of the 23 chromosomes still consists of two identical chromatids, giving 46 total chromatids in prophase II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 chromatids is the count only after meiosis II is complete, when sister chromatids have separated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 69 does not correspond to any normal cell state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 92 chromatids is the count in a diploid cell at prophase of mitosis, before meiosis I reduces the number.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 184 is not found in a normal cell.

questions.stem: You are asked to relay a cytogenetics report for a healthy 34-year-old man being evaluated for infertility. His peripheral blood karyotype reads 46,XY,t(9;22)(p22;q13). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has a balanced translocation involving 9p and 22q

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has a balanced translocation involving 9q and 22p

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has a Robertsonian translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22

choices.label: D
choices.text: He has an interstitial deletion of chromosome 22

choices.label: E
choices.text: He has an unbalanced translocation involving 9p and 22q

explanation.summary: The 't' with a total of 46 chromosomes denotes a balanced reciprocal translocation, and the bands map in order to 9p and 22q.
explanation.whyCorrect: The abbreviation 't' indicates a translocation, and a total count of 46 chromosomes with no plus or minus sign indicates it is balanced, with no net gain or loss of material. The band coordinates in the second parentheses correspond in order to the chromosomes listed, so p22 belongs to chromosome 9 and q13 belongs to chromosome 22.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The band order matches the chromosome order, so the segments are 9p and 22q, not 9q and 22p.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Robertsonian translocation is denoted 'rob', involves only acrocentric chromosomes, and yields 45 chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A deletion would be denoted 'del', and this karyotype shows an exchange between two chromosomes, not a loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An unbalanced translocation implies unequal exchange with extra or missing material; the balanced 46-chromosome notation here excludes that.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia is found to have a balanced translocation in which no chromosomal material is gained or lost. Her physician explains that despite the balanced exchange, the rearrangement still causes disease. Which mechanism best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A breakpoint joins two genes to create an abnormal fusion gene such as BCR-ABL

choices.label: B
choices.text: The exchange produces a monosomy of the involved chromosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rearrangement converts all euchromatin to heterochromatin across the genome

choices.label: D
choices.text: The translocation adds a third copy of every gene on both chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: The translocation deletes an entire acrocentric chromosome

explanation.summary: Even a balanced translocation can be pathogenic when a breakpoint disrupts a gene or fuses two genes into an abnormal product.
explanation.whyCorrect: A balanced translocation has no net gain or loss of material, but the translocation breakpoints can still disrupt gene function. If the breakpoint falls within or between genes it can create a fusion gene, such as BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, leading to abnormal function and disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A balanced translocation does not remove a whole chromosome, so no monosomy results.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Position effects can locally alter expression, but a translocation does not convert the entire genome to heterochromatin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A balanced exchange does not triplicate genes; that would be a gain of material, making it unbalanced.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deletion of an entire chromosome is not a feature of a balanced reciprocal translocation.

questions.stem: A chromosomal rearrangement occurs in which the short arms of two acrocentric chromosomes are lost and their long arms fuse to form a single large chromosome with two long arms. This describes which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced reciprocal translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interstitial deletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pericentric inversion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Robertsonian translocation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tandem segmental duplication

explanation.summary: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of the short arms defines a Robertsonian translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Robertsonian translocation specifically refers to the fusion of the q (long) arms of two acrocentric chromosomes, with subsequent loss of the p (short) arms. Because the lost short arms carry only satellite DNA and redundant ribosomal RNA genes, the rearrangement is still considered balanced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A reciprocal translocation is an exchange of segments between two chromosomes, not a whole-arm fusion with arm loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A deletion is simply the loss of a chromosome segment, not a fusion of two chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An inversion flips a segment end to end within a single chromosome and does not fuse two chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A duplication is an extra copy of a portion of a chromosome, causing partial trisomy.

questions.stem: A couple with recurrent pregnancy loss undergoes karyotyping, and the woman is found to be a balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation reported as 45,XX,rob(13;14)(q10;q10). What is her total chromosome number?

explanation.summary: Balanced Robertsonian carriers have only 45 chromosomes because two acrocentric chromosomes fuse into one.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a Robertsonian translocation the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse into a single derivative chromosome and the short arms are lost. This reduces the total count by one, so balanced carriers have 45 chromosomes, exactly as the leading number in the karyotype indicates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 is the haploid number found in a gamete, not a somatic carrier cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 44 would imply loss of two whole chromosomes; only one derivative chromosome is lost in the count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 46 is the normal diploid number; the fusion reduces this by one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47 indicates an extra chromosome (aneuploidy), which is the opposite of this fusion.

questions.stem: A cytogeneticist is teaching which chromosomes can participate in a Robertsonian translocation, noting that only acrocentric chromosomes are involved. Which group correctly lists the human acrocentric autosomes?

explanation.summary: The acrocentric autosomes are 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22, and only these participate in Robertsonian translocations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acrocentric chromosomes have a centromere almost at the end, leaving a tiny p arm; in humans these are chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22. Their short arms contain satellite DNA and redundant ribosomal RNA genes, which is why their fusion in a Robertsonian translocation is still balanced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1, 3, 16, 19, and 20 are metacentric chromosomes with roughly equal arms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 2, 4, 5, 17, and 18 are submetacentric chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 6 through 10 are submetacentric, not acrocentric.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 11, 12, and X are submetacentric; this group is not the acrocentric set.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman has an amniocentesis after ultrasound suggests symmetrical fetal growth restriction. The report returns as 46,XX,del(4)(p15.1p15.32). Which of the following best describes this chromosomal finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced translocation between chromosome 4 and another chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete trisomy of chromosome 4 in all cell lines

choices.label: C
choices.text: Duplication of the short arm of chromosome 4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 4

explanation.summary: The notation del(4)(p15.1p15.32) denotes an interstitial deletion of the short (p) arm of chromosome 4.
explanation.whyCorrect: The abbreviation 'del' indicates a deletion, and the first parentheses identify chromosome 4. The second parentheses give two band coordinates, p15.1 and p15.32, both on the p arm; two coordinates flanking a lost internal segment indicate an interstitial (not terminal) deletion of the short arm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A translocation would be abbreviated 't' and involve two chromosomes; only chromosome 4 is affected here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The total count is 46 with no plus sign, so there is no extra whole chromosome 4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A duplication would be abbreviated 'dup'; this is a 'del' indicating loss, not gain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both band coordinates are on the p (short) arm, and two coordinates indicate an interstitial rather than a terminal deletion.

questions.stem: The parents of the fetus with 46,XX,del(4)(p15.1p15.32) ask about the risk of recurrence in a future pregnancy. Chromosomal analysis of both parents is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The deletion guarantees an identical deletion in all future pregnancies regardless of parental karyotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: The deletion is inherited from a parental balanced carrier, so recurrence risk is high

choices.label: C
choices.text: The deletion most likely arose spontaneously during gamete formation, and recurrence risk is low

choices.label: D
choices.text: The finding indicates a maternal Robertsonian translocation that was missed on routine karyotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: The result reflects trisomy 4 and warrants testing for advanced maternal age

explanation.summary: With normal parental karyotypes, the deletion is a de novo event that occurred during gamete formation, so recurrence risk is low.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because chromosomal evaluation of both parents is normal, neither carries a rearrangement that could be transmitted. This indicates the deletion happened spontaneously (de novo) during gamete formation in this pregnancy, and the recurrence risk in future pregnancies is low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A de novo event does not guarantee recurrence; the risk is actually low.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high recurrence risk would apply if a parent were a balanced carrier, but both parental karyotypes are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no Robertsonian translocation; the finding is an interstitial 4p deletion and the parents are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is a deletion (loss), not trisomy 4, and the mother is 26 rather than of advanced age.

questions.stem: A karyotype is reported as 47,XY,+21. Which of the following best describes the abnormality indicated by this notation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced translocation between chromosomes 21 and Y

choices.label: B
choices.text: A duplication of the long arm of chromosome 21

choices.label: C
choices.text: An interstitial deletion of chromosome 21

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monosomy of chromosome 21

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy 21 due to an extra copy of chromosome 21

explanation.summary: A total of 47 chromosomes with '+21' denotes an extra whole chromosome 21, that is, trisomy 21.
explanation.whyCorrect: In aneuploidy notation the total chromosome number changes and a plus or minus sign designates the extra or missing chromosome. Here 47 chromosomes with +21 means there are three copies of chromosome 21, a trisomy, which is the most common clinically significant aneuploidy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A translocation is denoted 't', and the total here is 47 from a gained chromosome, not an exchange.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A duplication is denoted 'dup' and affects part of an arm; this notation shows an extra whole chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A deletion is denoted 'del' and would not raise the total chromosome number to 47.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monosomy is loss of a copy, which would lower the count and use a minus sign, not +21.

questions.stem: A karyotype is reported as 46,XY,dup(5)(q31q42). Which statement best describes the genetic consequence of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It causes a partial trisomy from an extra copy of the q31 to q42 segment

choices.label: B
choices.text: It fuses two acrocentric chromosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inverts the orientation of chromosome 5 with no change in copy number

choices.label: D
choices.text: It represents complete monosomy of chromosome 5

choices.label: E
choices.text: It results in a net loss of the q31 to q42 segment

explanation.summary: A duplication is an extra copy of a chromosome portion, producing a partial trisomy of that segment.
explanation.whyCorrect: The abbreviation 'dup' indicates a duplication, an abnormal extra copy of a portion of a chromosome. Here the segment q31 to q42 on the long arm of chromosome 5 is present in an extra copy, creating a situation of partial trisomy for that region.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fusion of acrocentric chromosomes is a Robertsonian translocation, not a duplication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An inversion flips a segment without changing copy number; a duplication adds a copy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monosomy is loss of a whole chromosome; a duplication adds material to one chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A net loss would be a deletion ('del'), the opposite of a duplication.

questions.stem: A histology instructor asks about the basic repeating unit that packages DNA into chromatin. Which of the following correctly describes the protein core of a nucleosome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A centromeric spindle-attachment protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cohesin ring complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single H1 linker histone

choices.label: D
choices.text: A supercoiled loop of ribosomal RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: An octamer of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4

explanation.summary: The nucleosome core is a histone octamer of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, around which DNA is wound.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each chromosome is a continuous DNA double helix wound around histones and packaged as chromatin. The nucleosome, the basic repeating unit, consists of DNA wrapped around a core of two copies each of the histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spindle attachment occurs at the centromere and is unrelated to the nucleosome core proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cohesins hold sister chromatids together and are not part of the nucleosome core.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 is the linker histone that sits between nucleosomes to compact chromatin further; it is not the core octamer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribosomal RNA genes reside on acrocentric short arms and do not form the nucleosome core.

questions.stem: A first-year student compares the maternal copy of chromosome 7 with the paternal copy of chromosome 7 in a somatic cell. Which of the following best describes the relationship between these two homologous chromosomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are both inherited from the same parent and are transmitted together as a pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: They carry different subsets of genes, since each chromosome holds a unique gene set

choices.label: C
choices.text: They carry identical DNA sequences, having been copied from one another during S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: They carry the same set of genes but may carry different alleles of those genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: They remain physically joined at a shared centromere until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition

explanation.summary: Homologous chromosomes contain the same set of genes but are not identical, because they can carry different alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humans have diploid genomes made of pairs of homologous chromosomes. The term homologous means the respective chromosomes contain the same set of genes, but they are not identical because they can contain different versions of a gene, called alleles. One homolog comes from the mother and the other from the father.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Each human inherits one set of 23 chromosomes from the mother and a homologous set from the father, so homologs come from different parents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Each chromosome does carry a different subset of genes, but the two homologs of a pair carry the same subset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Identical copies produced in S phase are sister chromatids, not homologous chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sister chromatids, not homologs, share a centromere until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.

questions.stem: A microbiology student compares the genome organization of Escherichia coli with that of a human cell. Which of the following correctly contrasts the chromosomes of these two organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteria have a single circular chromosome; humans have multiple linear chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacteria have many linear chromosomes; humans have a single circular chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacteria have paired homologous chromosomes; humans have a single unpaired set

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both have a single circular chromosome, but the human chromosome is much larger

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both have multiple linear chromosomes, but only humans carry them in homologous pairs

explanation.summary: Prokaryotes have a single circular chromosome, whereas eukaryotic species have various numbers of linear chromosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prokaryotes such as bacteria carry their genome on a single circular chromosome. Eukaryotic species, including humans, have various numbers of linear chromosomes; humans have 46 arranged as 23 homologous pairs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the arrangement; it is the bacterium that has the single circular chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Humans, not bacteria, have the diploid genome made of homologous pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Human chromosomes are linear, not circular.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacteria do not have multiple linear chromosomes; they have one circular chromosome.

questions.stem: A fibroblast has just completed mitosis and cytokinesis and is now in G1 phase of the cell cycle. Which of the following describes the chromosome and chromatid content of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 23 chromosomes, 23 chromatids

choices.label: B
choices.text: 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids

choices.label: D
choices.text: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids

choices.label: E
choices.text: 92 chromosomes, 92 chromatids

explanation.summary: In G1 each of the 46 chromosomes consists of a single chromatid, so the cell has 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitosis maintains the diploid state, so the daughter cell has 46 chromosomes. During G1 phase, before S phase, each chromosome consists of a single chromatid, a continuous piece of genomic DNA. Only after S phase does each chromosome consist of two identical sister chromatids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 chromosomes with 23 chromatids describes a haploid gamete after meiosis II, not a diploid somatic cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 23 chromosomes with 46 chromatids describes a cell after meiosis I, not a mitotic daughter cell in G1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 46 chromosomes with 92 chromatids describes a cell after S phase (G2 or prophase), not G1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal cell never contains 92 chromosomes.

questions.stem: During interphase, the chromatin of a hepatocyte is dispersed throughout the nucleus, but as the cell prepares to divide the chromatin condenses into discrete chromosomes. Which of the following is the primary purpose of this condensation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows homologous chromosomes to pair and exchange segments

choices.label: B
choices.text: It allows the chromosomes to be cleanly separated into daughter cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It converts euchromatin to heterochromatin so that transcription increases

choices.label: D
choices.text: It halves the chromosome number so that gametes can form

choices.label: E
choices.text: It permits DNA synthesis to produce identical sister chromatids

explanation.summary: Chromatin condenses into discrete metaphase chromosomes so that they can be cleanly separated into daughter cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: During interphase (G1, S, and G2) chromatin is dispersed throughout the nucleus. When a cell is ready to divide, the chromatin condenses and supercoils into highly condensed metaphase chromosomes, which form discrete structures that can be cleanly separated into the daughter cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pairing and crossing over of homologs is a feature of meiosis I, not the purpose of condensation in a dividing somatic cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Condensation is for segregation, not for increasing transcription; highly condensed chromatin is not the transcriptionally active form.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduction of chromosome number happens only in meiosis; a hepatocyte divides by mitosis and stays diploid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DNA synthesis occurs in S phase of interphase, when chromatin is dispersed, not condensed.

questions.stem: After S phase, a proliferating cell must keep each pair of newly synthesized sister chromatids attached to one another until they are distributed to the daughter cells. Which of the following holds the sister chromatids together prior to cell division?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cohesin proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA repair ligation proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linker histone H1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitotic spindle fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleosome core histones

explanation.summary: Newly synthesized sister chromatids remain attached to one another via cohesins until cell division.
explanation.whyCorrect: To keep chromosomes organized for efficient assortment into each daughter cell, newly synthesized chromosomes remain attached to one another via proteins called cohesins prior to cellular division. The sister chromatids are connected at the centromere and are pulled apart by the mitotic spindle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA repair proteins rejoin chromosomal breaks; they are not the proteins that link sister chromatids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 is the linker histone that helps package DNA into chromatin; it does not hold sister chromatids together.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mitotic spindle is the machinery that pulls the sister chromatids apart, the opposite of holding them together.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) form the nucleosome around which DNA is wound; they do not link sister chromatids.

questions.stem: A cytogenetics report refers to a lesion on the shorter of the two arms of chromosome 5. Which of the following is the conventional designation for this arm, and what does the letter stand for?

choices.label: A
choices.text: p arm, for petite

choices.label: B
choices.text: p arm, for proximal

choices.label: C
choices.text: q arm, for petite

choices.label: D
choices.text: q arm, for quantity

choices.label: E
choices.text: s arm, for short

explanation.summary: By convention the shorter chromosome arm is the p arm (p for petite) and the longer arm is the q arm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The centromere divides each sister chromatid into two arms. By convention the shorter chromosome arm is known as the p arm, with p standing for petite, and the longer arm is the q arm. These designations are used in cytogenetic nomenclature such as del(5)(p15).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The p does stand for petite, not proximal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: q designates the longer arm, not the shorter one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: q is the longer arm, and it is not derived from the word quantity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no s arm designation in chromosome nomenclature.

questions.stem: On a karyotype, chromosome 1 is observed to have its centromere near the midpoint, with arms of relatively equal length on either side. Which of the following terms describes this chromosome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acrocentric

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterochromatic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homologous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metacentric

choices.label: E
choices.text: Submetacentric

explanation.summary: Metacentric chromosomes have relatively equal length arms on either side of the centromere; chromosome 1 is metacentric.
explanation.whyCorrect: The relative length of the p and q arms is used to identify and describe chromosomes. Metacentric chromosomes have relatively equal length arms on either side of the centromere; in humans these are chromosomes 1, 3, 16, 19, and 20.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) have the centromere almost at the end, leaving a very small p arm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heterochromatin describes a highly condensed state of chromatin, not a centromere position.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homologous describes the relationship between the two members of a chromosome pair, not the arm lengths.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Submetacentric chromosomes have one arm that is detectably shorter than the other, not arms of equal length.

questions.stem: A geneticist classifies the human sex chromosomes according to the relative lengths of their p and q arms. Which of the following correctly classifies the X and Y chromosomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X acrocentric; Y acrocentric

choices.label: B
choices.text: X acrocentric; Y submetacentric

choices.label: C
choices.text: X metacentric; Y metacentric

choices.label: D
choices.text: X submetacentric; Y acrocentric

choices.label: E
choices.text: X submetacentric; Y submetacentric

explanation.summary: The X chromosome is submetacentric, while the Y chromosome is acrocentric.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromosomes are grouped by centromere position. The submetacentric group includes chromosomes 2, 4 through 12, 17, 18, and X, which have one arm detectably shorter than the other. The acrocentric group, with the centromere almost at the end, includes 13, 14, 15, 21, 22, and Y.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The X is not acrocentric; only the Y among the sex chromosomes is acrocentric.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the assignments; X is submetacentric and Y is acrocentric.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither sex chromosome is metacentric; the metacentric chromosomes are 1, 3, 16, 19, and 20.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The X is submetacentric, but the Y is acrocentric, not submetacentric.

questions.stem: A primary spermatocyte is found to contain chromosomes in which segments have been exchanged between the maternal and paternal homologs. During which of the following stages does this crossing over and recombination take place?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meiosis II, when sister chromatids separate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitotic anaphase, when chromatids are pulled apart

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitotic prophase, when chromatin condenses

choices.label: E
choices.text: S phase, when DNA is replicated

explanation.summary: Crossing over and recombination occur in meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes pair up.
explanation.whyCorrect: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair up, and during this time crossing over and recombination occur. Chromosomes have to break apart for recombination to happen, and DNA repair proteins then rejoin them. Afterward, one homolog is segregated to each daughter cell rather than the chromatids separating.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Meiosis II separates the two identical sister chromatids; pairing and crossing over have already occurred in meiosis I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In mitotic anaphase sister chromatids are pulled apart; no exchange between homologs occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitosis maintains the diploid status and does not involve pairing and exchange between homologs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S phase produces identical sister chromatids; it is not when homologs pair and exchange segments.

questions.stem: A germ cell is observed in anaphase II of meiosis. Which of the following is being pulled toward opposite poles of the cell at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes, each consisting of two chromatids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paired maternal and paternal chromosomes after crossing over

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sister chromatids of each chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole sets of 46 chromosomes, one set to each daughter cell

explanation.summary: Sister chromatids separate during mitosis and meiosis II, whereas homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis I.
explanation.whyCorrect: In meiosis I, instead of the chromatids separating, one chromosome homolog is segregated to each daughter cell, leaving haploid cells whose chromosomes still consist of two identical sister chromatids. The two identical chromatids then separate during meiosis II, when the cells undergo another round of division, producing gametes with a single copy of each chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: By meiosis II the homologs have already separated; the cell is haploid and does not contain homologous pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homologs with two chromatids each are what separate in anaphase I, not anaphase II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paired homologs are separated in meiosis I; there are no homologous pairs left in a meiosis II cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A meiosis II cell is already haploid with 23 chromosomes, and it does not distribute 46-chromosome sets.

questions.stem: A researcher compares the products of one round of mitosis in a skin cell with the products of complete meiosis in a germ cell. Which of the following correctly describes the daughter cells produced by each process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitosis: four genetically different haploid cells; meiosis: two genetically identical diploid cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mitosis: four genetically identical diploid cells; meiosis: two genetically different haploid cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitosis: two genetically different haploid cells; meiosis: four genetically identical diploid cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitosis: two genetically identical diploid cells; meiosis: four genetically different haploid cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mitosis: two genetically identical haploid cells; meiosis: four genetically identical haploid cells

explanation.summary: Mitosis produces two identical diploid daughter cells, whereas meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitosis is the normal process of cell division during growth and maintenance of somatic tissues; it happens in diploid cells and produces two identical diploid daughter cells. Meiosis starts with a diploid cell and, after crossing over and two rounds of division, produces four genetically different haploid gametes, each with 23 chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This assigns the meiotic products to mitosis and vice versa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitosis yields two cells, not four, and meiosis yields four cells, not two.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the ploidy and the number of cells; mitotic products stay diploid and meiotic products are haploid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitotic daughter cells are diploid, not haploid, and meiotic gametes are genetically different, not identical.

questions.stem: A student examining a normal Giemsa-stained karyotype notes that each numbered position shows two homologous chromosomes, but the two sister chromatids of each chromosome cannot be distinguished as separate entities. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Giemsa stain binds only one chromatid of each pair, masking the other

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes fuse at their centromeres during metaphase preparation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sister chromatids had not yet formed because the cells were harvested before S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sister chromatids remain held together until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sister chromatids were separated during isolation and only one was retained per position

explanation.summary: Karyotype chromosomes are isolated at metaphase, when sister chromatids are still held together and are not distinguishable as separate entities.
explanation.whyCorrect: A karyotype is an organized view of chromosomes isolated from a cell during metaphase and stained. Sister chromatids are held together throughout interphase all the way until the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, so in chromosomes isolated during metaphase the sister chromatids are not distinguishable as separate entities even though each homolog is present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Giemsa reveals the banding pattern of the whole chromosome; it does not selectively mask one chromatid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homologous chromosomes do not fuse; each position shows two separate homologs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotype chromosomes are isolated at metaphase, after S phase, so sister chromatids have formed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both sister chromatids are present in each metaphase chromosome; they are simply held together.

questions.stem: A cytogenetic report describes several bands on the long arm of chromosome 5. Based on the standardized system for numbering bands, which of the following bands lies closest to the centromere?

explanation.summary: Band numbering starts at the centromere and increases toward the terminal end of each arm, so the lowest-numbered band is nearest the centromere.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alternating light and dark bands revealed by Giemsa staining give a way to label locations along each chromosome. Numbering of the bands starts at the centromere and increases as you near the terminal ends of the arms, so 5q11 is the band closest to the centromere among those listed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 5q13 is close to the centromere but not as close as 5q11.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5q15 lies farther from the centromere than 5q11 and 5q13.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 5q31 is farther from the centromere than 5q11, 5q13, and 5q15.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 5q35 has the highest number listed and therefore lies nearest the terminal end of the long arm.

questions.stem: A cytogenetics laboratory prepares a report for a phenotypically normal woman whose karyotype shows no numerical or structural abnormalities. Which of the following is the complete karyotype description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 23,XX

choices.label: B
choices.text: 44,XX

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46,XX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 46,XY

choices.label: E
choices.text: XX,46

explanation.summary: A karyotype description leads with the total chromosome number followed by the sex chromosomes, so a normal female is 46,XX.
explanation.whyCorrect: A karyotype description always leads off with the total number of chromosomes, followed by a description of the sex chromosomes. For a normal karyotype this is all the description that is necessary; additional information is added only when there are chromosomal abnormalities. A genetic female has 46 chromosomes with two X chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 is the haploid number of a gamete, not the total in a somatic karyotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 44 is not the normal total; the 22 autosome pairs plus the sex chromosome pair make 46.
whyWrongByChoice.D: XY describes a genetic male, not a female.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The total chromosome number comes first, before the sex chromosomes.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman experiences a spontaneous pregnancy loss at 9 weeks of gestation. She asks how likely it is that a chromosomal abnormality was responsible. Approximately what proportion of spontaneous first-trimester pregnancy losses involve a cytogenetic abnormality?

explanation.summary: Cytogenetic abnormalities are present in half of all spontaneous first-trimester pregnancy losses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Specific chromosome disorders are responsible for hundreds of distinct syndromes that collectively are more common than all single-gene diseases together. Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in nearly 1% of live births, in about 2% of pregnancies in women older than 35 who undergo prenatal diagnosis, and in half of all spontaneous first-trimester pregnancy losses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 1% is the frequency of cytogenetic abnormalities among live births, not first-trimester losses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 2% is the frequency in prenatally diagnosed pregnancies of women older than 35 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 10% substantially underestimates the contribution of chromosomal abnormalities to early pregnancy loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 25% is still well below the roughly one-half of first-trimester losses that carry a cytogenetic abnormality.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman undergoing prenatal diagnostic testing asks how likely it is that a cytogenetic abnormality will be found in her pregnancy. Compared with the frequency of cytogenetic abnormalities among live births, which of the following best describes the expected frequency in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1%, roughly equal to the rate in live births

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 2%, roughly double the rate in live births

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 10%, roughly ten times the rate in live births

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 25%, roughly a quarter of tested pregnancies

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 50%, roughly the rate in first-trimester losses

explanation.summary: Cytogenetic abnormalities occur in about 2% of pregnancies in women older than 35 undergoing prenatal diagnosis, versus nearly 1% of live births.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytogenetic abnormalities are present in nearly 1% of live births and in about 2% of pregnancies in women older than 35 years who undergo prenatal diagnosis. For a 38-year-old woman having prenatal diagnostic testing, the expected frequency is therefore about 2%, roughly twice that seen in live births overall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rate in prenatally tested pregnancies of women over 35 is higher than the roughly 1% seen in live births.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 10% overstates the frequency; the figure is about 2%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 25% far exceeds the frequency in prenatally diagnosed pregnancies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 50% is the frequency among spontaneous first-trimester losses, not among ongoing pregnancies undergoing prenatal diagnosis.

questions.stem: During meiosis I, chromosomes break so that recombination can occur, and the breaks are normally repaired. A child is later found to carry a structural chromosomal rearrangement that neither parent has. Which of the following best explains how such rearrangements typically arise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of chromatin to condense before the metaphase-to-anaphase transition

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of cohesins to hold sister chromatids together during anaphase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gain of an entire extra chromosome during segregation of homologs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Imperfect rejoining of chromosomal breaks by DNA repair proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of histone packaging, leaving DNA unprotected during S phase

explanation.summary: Chromosomal rearrangements often arise when DNA repair proteins imperfectly rejoin the breaks made during meiotic recombination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromosomal rearrangements often arise from errors in meiosis or DNA repair. During meiosis I, chromosomes have to break apart for recombination to happen, and DNA repair proteins fix these breaks by rejoining (ligating) the chromosomes. When these repair processes are not perfect, entire gene segments can be moved (translocated), deleted, duplicated, or flipped (inverted).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A failure of condensation would impair clean separation of chromosomes; it does not move, delete, duplicate, or invert segments.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cohesins hold sister chromatids together; a failure there would affect segregation, not create a rearranged segment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gaining a whole extra chromosome is a numerical abnormality (aneuploidy), not a structural rearrangement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histone packaging into chromatin is not described as the source of structural rearrangements.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows that a segment of chromosome 8 has become attached to chromosome 14. Which of the following features defines this rearrangement as a translocation rather than an ordinary exchange during meiotic recombination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The exchange occurred between the two members of a homologous pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: The exchange occurred between the two sister chromatids of one chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The segment moved between two nonhomologous chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The segment was copied, producing an extra copy on the same chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The segment was flipped end to end within a single chromosome

explanation.summary: A translocation is a rearrangement in which a piece of one chromosome moves to another, nonhomologous chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromosomal translocations are rearrangements between segments of nonhomologous chromosomes. In a translocation (trans meaning across), a piece of one chromosome moves to another, nonhomologous chromosome. Chromosomes 8 and 14 are nonhomologous, so movement of material between them is a translocation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Exchange between homologs is crossing over and recombination, which normally occurs in meiosis I.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome; exchange between them is not a translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An extra copy of a segment on the same chromosome is a duplication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flipping a segment end to end within one chromosome is an inversion.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows that a segment from the long arm of chromosome 4 has been inserted into chromosome 20. Chromosome 4 now lacks that segment and has received no material from chromosome 20 in return. Which of the following best classifies this rearrangement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct duplication of chromosome 20

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interstitial deletion of chromosome 20

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonreciprocal translocation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reciprocal translocation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Robertsonian translocation

explanation.summary: A one-way transfer of a segment from one chromosome to another without an exchange in return is a nonreciprocal translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a reciprocal translocation, two chromosome segments exchange places. In a nonreciprocal translocation, a segment of one chromosome transfers or moves to another without reciprocation by a segment from the other chromosome. Here a piece of chromosome 4 moved to chromosome 20 with nothing moving back, which is the nonreciprocal pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The material added to chromosome 20 came from chromosome 4, not from an extra copy of chromosome 20's own sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromosome 20 gained material rather than losing an internal segment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A reciprocal translocation requires that the two chromosomes trade segments; here chromosome 20 gave nothing back.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A Robertsonian translocation is the fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes; 4 and 20 are not acrocentric and no arm fusion occurred.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with developmental delay is found to carry a balanced translocation. Molecular analysis shows that neither breakpoint lies within a gene and that no genetic material is missing, yet a gene adjacent to one breakpoint is no longer expressed. Which of the following best explains the loss of expression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The breakpoint falls within the gene, disrupting its coding sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gene has fused with a partner gene to create an abnormal fusion gene product

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gene is now present in three copies, producing a partial trisomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gene now sits in a region with different chromatin or methylation patterns

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gene's coding sequence was deleted during the exchange of segments

explanation.summary: A position effect occurs when a translocation relocates a gene to a region with different epigenetic characteristics, silencing or altering its expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Even though a balanced translocation involves no net gain or loss of genetic material, several factors can still disrupt gene function. One is the position effect: a gene might be relocated to a region of the genome with different epigenetic characteristics, such as chromatin structure or DNA methylation patterns, which can silence or alter its expression. Because the breakpoints here do not fall within a gene and nothing is lost, the position effect best explains the silencing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A breakpoint effect requires the break to fall within the gene, which the analysis excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A fusion gene requires a breakpoint that joins two genes; the stem states that neither breakpoint lies within a gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A balanced translocation does not add extra copies of a segment; partial trisomy results from a duplication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The translocation is balanced and no genetic material is missing, so the coding sequence has not been deleted.

questions.stem: A phenotypically normal man is found to have the karyotype 45,XY,rob(14;21)(q10;q10). Which of the following best describes the chromosome 14 and chromosome 21 material present in his cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One normal 14 and one normal 21, with the remaining copies lost entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: One normal 14, one normal 21, and one derivative (14;21) chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two normal 14s, one normal 21, and one 21 missing its short arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two normal 14s, two normal 21s, and one additional fused chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two normal 21s, one normal 14, and one 14 missing its short arm

explanation.summary: A balanced rob(14;21) carrier has one normal 14, one normal 21, and a derivative chromosome made from the long arms of 14 and 21.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a Robertsonian translocation the q arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse and the p arms are lost. The karyotype 45,XY,rob(14;21)(q10;q10) describes a person with one normal chromosome 14, one normal chromosome 21, and a derivative (14;21) chromosome involving the long arms of 14 and 21. The total is 45 because two chromosomes have become one.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The long arms of the second 14 and second 21 are not lost; they persist together as the derivative chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Robertsonian translocation fuses one 14 and one 21 into a single derivative; it does not leave two intact 14s plus an altered 21.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That would give 47 chromosomes with extra material, not the 45 of a balanced carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Likewise, there are not two intact 21s; one 21 and one 14 contribute their long arms to the derivative.

questions.stem: A woman with recurrent pregnancy loss is found to be a balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation. She asks how the loss of two chromosome short arms can still be considered balanced. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The long arms carry backup copies of every gene on the short arms

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lost short arm material is duplicated elsewhere on the derivative chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lost short arms hold only satellite DNA and redundant ribosomal RNA genes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lost short arms persist in the cell as a separate marker chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The short arms of acrocentric chromosomes contain no DNA at all

explanation.summary: Acrocentric p arms carry only satellite DNA and hundreds of copies of ribosomal RNA genes, none of which is critical, so their loss leaves the carrier balanced.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only the acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) participate in Robertsonian translocations. The p arms of these chromosomes contain satellite DNA and hundreds of copies of ribosomal RNA genes, none of which is critical genetic information. Therefore, even with loss of the p arms, Robertsonian translocations are still considered balanced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The long arms do not duplicate the short-arm content; the short arms are dispensable because their content is redundant elsewhere in the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The derivative chromosome is formed from the fused q arms; it does not carry duplicated p-arm material.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The p arms are lost, not retained as a separate chromosome; the carrier has 45 chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The short arms do contain DNA, specifically satellite DNA and ribosomal RNA genes.

questions.stem: A karyotype is reported as 46,XY,del(5)(p15). Which of the following best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duplication of band p15 on chromosome 5

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interstitial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5

choices.label: D
choices.text: Terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5

choices.label: E
choices.text: Terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5

explanation.summary: del(5)(p15) with a single band coordinate denotes a terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5.
explanation.whyCorrect: A deletion is loss of a chromosome segment, either at the end of an arm (terminal) or in the middle of an arm (interstitial). The notation uses 'del', then the chromosome affected, then the band location. A single band coordinate such as (p15) marks a terminal deletion from that band to the end of the short arm, whereas an interstitial deletion lists two coordinates for the start and end of the lost segment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A duplication would be abbreviated 'dup', not 'del'.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The coordinate is on the p (short) arm, and a single coordinate indicates a terminal, not interstitial, deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An interstitial deletion would be written with two band coordinates, such as del(20)(q11q13).
whyWrongByChoice.D: p15 is on the short arm, not the long arm.

questions.stem: A healthy 29-year-old woman undergoing karyotyping for family planning is found to carry a chromosomal inversion in which a segment of chromosome 9 has been flipped end to end. She asks what this means for her own health. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rearrangement adds an extra copy of the segment, causing partial trisomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rearrangement changes no gene content and usually causes no clinical problem

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rearrangement fuses two chromosomes, reducing her count to 45

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rearrangement joins two genes into a fusion gene product that causes disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rearrangement removes the genetic material within the flipped segment

explanation.summary: An inversion involves no gain or loss of genetic information, and carriers generally do not present with clinically significant abnormalities.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flipping a chromosomal segment end to end causes a chromosomal inversion. An inversion does not involve loss or gain of genetic information; it is simply a rearrangement of the DNA. Carriers of inversions generally do not present with any clinically significant abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An extra copy of a segment is a duplication, not an inversion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fusion of two chromosomes with a count of 45 describes a Robertsonian translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fusion genes such as BCR-ABL arise from translocation breakpoints; they are not a described consequence of inversions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of a segment is a deletion; an inversion keeps all the genetic material.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman delivers a newborn with flat facies, prominent epicanthal folds, a single transverse palmar crease, and a wide gap between the first and second toes. Karyotype shows 47,XX,+21. This trisomy most commonly results from nondisjunction occurring during which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maternal meiosis I

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal meiosis II

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitosis after fertilization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paternal meiosis I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paternal meiosis II

explanation.summary: Most trisomy 21 arises from meiotic nondisjunction, the great majority in maternal meiosis I.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 95% of Down syndrome results from meiotic nondisjunction, with roughly 88% of those events occurring in female (maternal) meiosis I. This relates to oogenesis, in which oogonia remain arrested in prophase I for many years, and the risk rises with advanced maternal age.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal errors more often occur in meiosis I than meiosis II; meiosis II is a less common source.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization produces mosaicism (46,XX/47,XX,+21), not the uniform 47,XX,+21 seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paternal nondisjunction accounts for only about 8% of cases, far fewer than maternal errors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paternal meiosis II is an even rarer contributor than paternal meiosis I.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn is noted to have a punched-out scalp lesion (cutis aplasia), microcephaly, midline cleft lip and palate, extra digits on both hands, and imaging shows a single fused cerebral ventricle. Which karyotype is most consistent with this presentation?

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XXY

explanation.summary: Cutis aplasia, holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, and polydactyly are hallmarks of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13).
explanation.whyCorrect: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13, 47,+13) is characterized by cutis aplasia, microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, umbilical hernia/omphalocele, and rocker-bottom feet, with congenital heart and renal defects. Cutis aplasia in particular is specific for Patau syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X (Turner) causes short stature and a webbed neck, not this constellation of midline and scalp defects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trisomy 18 (Edwards) features micrognathia, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet rather than cutis aplasia and polydactyly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trisomy 21 (Down) presents with flat facies, single palmar crease, and a toe gap, not holoprosencephaly and cutis aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,XXY (Klinefelter) is a sex-chromosome aneuploidy and does not produce these severe congenital malformations.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A neonate is born with micrognathia, a prominent occiput, low-set ears, clenched fists with the second and fifth fingers overlapping the third and fourth, and rocker-bottom feet. A ventricular septal defect is detected. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turner syndrome (45,X)

explanation.summary: Clenched hands with overlapping fingers plus micrognathia and rocker-bottom feet point to trisomy 18.
explanation.whyCorrect: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) classically presents with micrognathia, prominent occiput, low-set ears, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and limited hip adduction, along with congenital heart and renal defects. Prognosis is poor, with 50% dying by 2 months and 90-95% by 1 year.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Down syndrome shows flat facies, single palmar crease, and a toe gap, not overlapping fingers and micrognathia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome aneuploidy without these congenital anomalies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Patau syndrome features cutis aplasia, holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, and polydactyly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature and webbed neck, not this pattern of malformations.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn with flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a single palmar crease develops bilious vomiting on the first day of life. An abdominal radiograph shows a 'double bubble' sign. Which of the following gastrointestinal anomalies is most strongly associated with this infant's underlying chromosomal disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biliary atresia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duodenal atresia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Meckel diverticulum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyloric stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tracheoesophageal fistula

explanation.summary: Down syndrome is associated with duodenal atresia, which produces the double-bubble sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dysmorphic features indicate Down syndrome (trisomy 21). The brick lists duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease among its gastrointestinal associations; duodenal atresia classically causes bilious vomiting and a double-bubble sign on radiograph.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary atresia presents with progressive neonatal jaundice, not a double-bubble sign.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meckel diverticulum typically presents with painless lower GI bleeding, not neonatal bilious vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting and is not a Down syndrome association here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tracheoesophageal fistula is not among the associations emphasized for trisomy 21 and does not produce a double-bubble sign.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A phenotypically normal woman has the karyotype 45,XX,rob(21;21), a balanced Robertsonian translocation in which both copies of chromosome 21 are fused into a single chromosome. Regarding her potential offspring, which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About one half of her liveborn children will be chromosomally normal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every liveborn child she has will have Down syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her children are at increased risk for Patau syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: One sixth of her liveborn children will be balanced translocation carriers

choices.label: E
choices.text: She cannot achieve any viable pregnancy

explanation.summary: In a rob(21;21) carrier, viable gametes yield only trisomy 21, so every surviving child has Down syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the long arms of both chromosome 21s are physically attached, they cannot segregate away from each other during meiosis. Half of the gametes carry the fused 21q21q chromosome (leading to trisomy 21 on fertilization) and half carry no chromosome 21 (leading to nonviable monosomy 21). Thus, every liveborn child will have Down syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No gamete can carry exactly one normal chromosome 21, so a chromosomally normal child is not possible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This translocation involves chromosome 21, producing trisomy 21 (Down), not trisomy 13 (Patau).
whyWrongByChoice.D: A balanced carrier outcome is impossible because the single fused chromosome cannot recreate a normal balanced complement in offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viable pregnancy is possible; the trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) conceptions are viable.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A healthy 34-year-old woman has had four miscarriages, and two of her fetuses had translocation trisomy 14. Her karyotype is 45,XX,rob(13;14). Which of the following best explains why she is a healthy carrier yet has difficulty carrying a pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her advanced maternal age causes meiosis II nondisjunction in most oocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: She carries a point mutation that is lethal in the homozygous state

choices.label: C
choices.text: She has mosaic trisomy 14 confined to her ovaries and absent from blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is a balanced carrier, but abnormal segregation produces unbalanced gametes

choices.label: E
choices.text: She lost critical genetic material from both 13q and 14q when the translocation formed

explanation.summary: A balanced Robertsonian carrier is healthy but produces unbalanced gametes during meiotic segregation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Balanced translocation carriers are phenotypically normal because there is no net loss or gain of critical genetic material. However, the rearrangement causes problems during gamete production: the fused chromosome cannot pair and segregate normally, so a large fraction of gametes are unbalanced, leading to nonviable fetuses or trisomic offspring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Her losses are driven by unbalanced segregation of the translocation, not by age-related meiosis II nondisjunction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem is a chromosomal rearrangement affecting dosage, not a single-gene point mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Her karyotype reflects a constitutional balanced translocation, not confined ovarian mosaicism for trisomy 14.
whyWrongByChoice.E: By definition a balanced translocation involves no loss or gain of critical genetic information, which is why she is healthy.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has milder-than-expected features of Down syndrome. Karyotype analysis of a blood sample reports 46,XX/47,XX,+21. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nondisjunction in paternal meiosis II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniparental disomy of chromosome 21

explanation.summary: Two cell lines (46 and 47,+21) indicate mosaicism from a postfertilization mitotic error.
explanation.whyCorrect: The notation 46,XX/47,XX,+21 denotes two genetically distinct cell lineages derived from a single zygote (mosaicism). This does not occur during gamete production but is a postfertilization error in mitosis; mitotic nondisjunction creates a clonal population of aneuploid cells so that only some cells carry the extra chromosome 21.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal meiosis I nondisjunction produces a uniform 47,XX,+21 in every cell, not two cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paternal meiosis II nondisjunction likewise affects every cell of the zygote, not a mosaic subset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An unbalanced Robertsonian translocation would appear as a rob(...) karyotype with +21, not two separate cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uniparental disomy does not change chromosome number and would not produce a 46/47 mosaic pattern.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with Down syndrome is brought in with a two-year history of progressive memory loss and functional decline consistent with early-onset Alzheimer disease. Increased dosage of a gene on which chromosome best explains his elevated risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosome 13

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromosome 14

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chromosome 18

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chromosome 21

choices.label: E
choices.text: The X chromosome

explanation.summary: Chromosome 21 carries APP, so trisomy 21 gives three copies and raises Alzheimer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromosome 21 carries the gene coding for amyloid precursor protein (APP), which is involved in the pathophysiology of Alzheimer disease. Three copies of APP in Down syndrome are thought to increase Alzheimer risk, with disease onset typically beginning around age 40.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromosome 13 is implicated in Patau syndrome and does not carry APP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromosome 14 is commonly involved in Robertsonian translocations but does not explain the APP dosage effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chromosome 18 is implicated in Edwards syndrome, not the APP-driven Alzheimer association.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The APP gene relevant to this association is on chromosome 21, not the X chromosome.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 44-year-old pregnant woman is counseled that her risk of having a fetus with trisomy 21 has risen to roughly 1 in 25, compared with about 1 in 1500 in women younger than 20. Which feature of female gametogenesis best accounts for this age-related increase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitotic nondisjunction increases in the endometrium with age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oocytes complete meiosis before birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for decades

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sister chromatids are duplicated during fertilization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spermatogonia divide continuously throughout adult life

explanation.summary: Prolonged meiotic arrest of oocytes underlies the maternal-age effect on nondisjunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: In oogenesis, oogonia remain arrested in prophase I for many years. This prolonged arrest predisposes to nondisjunction, and the risk increases with advanced maternal age (from about 1:1500 in women under 20 to about 1:25 in women over 45). Most Down syndrome nondisjunction occurs in maternal meiosis I.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The relevant error is meiotic nondisjunction in the oocyte, not endometrial mitotic nondisjunction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oocytes do not complete meiosis before birth; they are held in prolonged arrest, which is the point of vulnerability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sister chromatids are not duplicated at fertilization; DNA replication precedes meiosis in the oocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Continuous spermatogonial division relates to paternal factors and does not explain the maternal-age effect on trisomy 21.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with Down syndrome develops fatigue, easy bruising, and pancytopenia, and a marrow examination confirms an acute leukemia. Which type of leukemia is most characteristically associated with his chromosomal disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adult T-cell leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hairy cell leukemia

explanation.summary: Down syndrome carries an increased risk of leukemia, usually acute myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists an increased risk of leukemia (usually AML) among the associations of trisomy 21, and notes this is thought to be due to silencing of PRC2. Acute myeloid leukemia is therefore the characteristic association in a young child with Down syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Adult T-cell leukemia is linked to HTLV-1 infection, not to Down syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a disease of older adults and is not the Down syndrome association.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic myeloid leukemia is associated with the BCR-ABL translocation, not specifically with Down syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hairy cell leukemia is a rare B-cell malignancy of adults, unrelated to trisomy 21.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A first-trimester miscarriage is evaluated, and cytogenetic analysis of the products of conception reveals 69,XXY. Which of the following terms best describes this chromosome complement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aneuploid due to a single extra chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diploid with a balanced translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monosomic for an autosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mosaic for two cell lines

choices.label: E
choices.text: Triploid, and therefore euploid

explanation.summary: 69 chromosomes is an exact multiple of the haploid number (3n), making it triploid and euploid.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the chromosome number is an exact multiple of the haploid number (n = 23), it is euploid. 69 chromosomes equals 3n (triploid), which is euploid but not viable; triploid and tetraploid complements are occasionally seen in fetuses but do not survive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aneuploidy refers to a number that is NOT an exact multiple of the haploid number; 69 is exactly 3n.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The count is 69 chromosomes (triploid), not a diploid 46 with a translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monosomy means one missing chromosome (2n - 1); triploidy is a gain of an entire haploid set.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single 69,XXY result reflects one triploid cell line, not a mosaic of two distinct lineages.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and primary amenorrhea and is found to have a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Her karyotype shows a single sex chromosome. This condition is notable as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A euploid condition with a normal chromosome count

choices.label: B
choices.text: A result of an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The most common viable autosomal trisomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: The most commonly occurring trisomy overall

choices.label: E
choices.text: The only monosomy compatible with life

explanation.summary: Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) is the only monosomy compatible with life.
explanation.whyCorrect: The findings describe Turner syndrome (45,X). Autosomal monosomies are always incompatible with life; the only monosomy compatible with life is monosomy of the sex chromosome X, which causes Turner syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X is aneuploid (2n - 1), not euploid with a normal chromosome count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Turner syndrome results from loss of an X chromosome, not from an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The most common viable autosomal trisomy is Down syndrome (trisomy 21), not a monosomy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trisomy 16 is the most commonly occurring trisomy overall, but it is always fatal in utero and is not this patient.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A geneticist explains to a medical student why a fetus with an extra copy of an entire chromosome has severe developmental consequences even though the DNA sequence of every gene on that chromosome is entirely normal. Which of the following concepts best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of homologous recombination in meiosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Imbalance of gene dosage in the affected region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of heterozygosity at tumor suppressor loci

choices.label: D
choices.text: Point mutations within coding sequences

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silencing of one parental copy by imprinting

explanation.summary: Chromosome disorders cause disease through abnormal gene dosage, not abnormal gene sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The central concept for chromosome and genomic disorders is gene dosage and its balance or imbalance. For chromosome abnormalities, the concern is the dosage of genes within the relevant chromosomal region rather than the normal or abnormal sequence of those genes; one or three doses of genetic information instead of two is generally not conducive to normal function for genes typically expressed from two copies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recombination failure is not the explanation for the phenotype; the extra chromosome alters dosage regardless of recombination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of heterozygosity describes loss of one allele, not the gain of a whole extra chromosome producing three doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem specifies that every gene sequence is normal; the problem is copy number, not sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imprinting silences a parental copy of specific genes and does not explain the global effect of an extra chromosome.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A diagram of normal gametogenesis shows homologous chromosome pairs associating, undergoing homologous recombination, and separating to opposite poles. Which of the following events characterizes the second meiotic division that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosomes are duplicated to produce sister chromatids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes pair and undergo recombination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes separate as whole chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sister chromatids separate to produce haploid gametes

choices.label: E
choices.text: The diploid chromosome number is restored by fusion

explanation.summary: Meiosis I separates homologs as whole chromosomes; meiosis II separates sister chromatids to yield haploid gametes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally, chromosomes associate as homologous pairs, undergo homologous recombination, and separate to opposite poles, still as whole chromosomes, during meiosis I. Then, during meiosis II, sister chromatids separate, generating haploid gametes with a single set of unpaired chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sister chromatids are produced by DNA replication before meiosis begins, not during meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pairing and recombination of homologs occur in meiosis I, before the first separation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Whole homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis I, not meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restoration of the diploid number occurs at fertilization when two haploid gametes fuse, not during meiosis II.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A cytogenetics laboratory reviews one year of abnormal karyotypes from patients with clinically significant chromosome disorders. Which of the following abnormalities is expected to be the most frequent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monosomy of a sex chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monosomy of an autosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tetraploidy (four haploid sets, 4n)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Triploidy (three haploid sets, 3n)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy of a single chromosome

explanation.summary: Aneuploidy is the most common human chromosome disorder, and among aneuploid patients trisomy is more frequent than monosomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aneuploidy is the most common and clinically significant type of human chromosome disorder. Most aneuploid patients have either trisomy (three instead of the normal pair of a particular chromosome) or, less often, monosomy (only one representative of a particular chromosome).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Monosomy X is the only viable monosomy, but monosomy overall is less frequent than trisomy among aneuploid patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal monosomies are always incompatible with life, so they are not seen among living patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tetraploid complements are occasionally seen in fetuses but are not viable and are uncommon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Triploid complements are seen occasionally in fetuses but are not viable and are far less common than trisomy.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A girl has 47,XX,+21 in every cell examined. Polymorphic DNA markers located close to the centromere of chromosome 21 are analyzed: her mother is heterozygous at these markers, and the child carries one paternal allele plus two copies of the same maternal allele. Which of the following errors most likely produced the extra chromosome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nondisjunction in maternal meiosis II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nondisjunction in paternal meiosis I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nondisjunction in paternal meiosis II

explanation.summary: Meiosis II nondisjunction yields two identical sister chromatids from a single homolog; meiosis I nondisjunction yields both homologs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondisjunction during meiosis II results in two copies of a particular chromosome that are identical sister chromatids, representative of only one of the homologous pair.
