Two copies of the same maternal allele, in a heterozygous mother, therefore indicate the extra chromosome 21 arose in maternal meiosis II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A postfertilization mitotic error produces mosaicism, but the trisomy here is present in every cell examined.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Meiosis I nondisjunction causes both maternal homologs to segregate together, so the child would carry two different maternal alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A paternal error would give the child two paternal alleles and only one maternal allele, the opposite of what is observed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paternal meiosis II nondisjunction would produce two identical paternal alleles, not two maternal ones.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: During spermatogenesis in a healthy man, meiosis I of a primary spermatocyte proceeds normally, but in one of the two resulting secondary spermatocytes the sister chromatids of chromosome 21 fail to separate during meiosis II. Of the four sperm ultimately derived from the original primary spermatocyte, how many have a normal haploid chromosome complement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four

choices.label: B
choices.text: None

choices.label: C
choices.text: One

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two

explanation.summary: Meiosis II nondisjunction affects only one of the two secondary cells, leaving two normal gametes, one n+1, and one n-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: When meiosis I is normal, both secondary spermatocytes receive a single homolog. Nondisjunction in meiosis II of one secondary spermatocyte produces one n+1 and one n-1 gamete, while the other secondary spermatocyte divides normally into two n gametes. The outcome is two normal gametes, one trisomic-producing gamete, and one monosomic-producing gamete.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Four normal gametes would require entirely normal meiosis I and meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No normal gametes would result from nondisjunction in meiosis I, where all four products are either n+1 or n-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only one normal gamete is not a possible outcome; the unaffected secondary spermatocyte contributes two normal sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Three normal gametes is impossible because the affected division must yield one n+1 and one n-1 product.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has several features suggestive of Down syndrome. A karyotype of peripheral blood lymphocytes shows 46,XX in all 30 cells counted, but a karyotype of cultured skin fibroblasts shows 47,XX,+21 in 40% of cells. Which of the following best explains the discrepancy between the two tissues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitotic nondisjunction occurred in a skin precursor cell lineage

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood and skin cells were derived from two separate zygotes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The blood sample was contaminated with maternal lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The trisomic line arose from nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy 21 cells are unable to survive within the bone marrow

explanation.summary: The tissues affected by mosaicism depend on the developmental stage and cell lineage in which mitotic nondisjunction occurred.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondisjunction during mitosis creates two distinct populations of cells that go on to clonally reproduce, producing mosaicism. The number and identity of the cells affected by mitotic nondisjunction depends on the developmental stage and cell lineage where the nondisjunction occurs, so one tissue can carry the trisomic clone while another does not.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mosaicism by definition involves genetically different cell lineages derived from a single zygote.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal cell contamination would not create a normal karyotype in 30 of 30 cells from a child who is truly trisomic in all tissues; the tissue-specific pattern reflects mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A meiotic error would affect every cell in the body, so the blood karyotype would also be trisomic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 21 cells clearly survive in blood in nonmosaic Down syndrome; the absence here reflects lineage, not lethality.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn boy has micrognathia, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet, although the findings are milder than typical. Chromosome analysis shows that some cells contain 46 chromosomes and others contain an extra chromosome 18. Which of the following is the correct karyotype designation?

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46,XY,dup(18q)

explanation.summary: Mosaicism is written with a slash separating the two cell lineages.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a karyotype description, mosaicism is denoted with a '/' representing the two different cell lineages. A male with some normal cells and some cells carrying an extra chromosome 18 is written 46,XY/47,XY,+18, analogous to the 46,XX/47,XX,+21 example for mosaic trisomy 21.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This notation describes a monosomy 18 line, which is an autosomal monosomy incompatible with life, alongside a trisomic line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A count of 46 with an added chromosome 18 is internally inconsistent; an extra whole chromosome brings the total to 47.
whyWrongByChoice.C: dup(18q) denotes a partial trisomy from a duplicated segment within one chromosome, not two cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,XY,+18 indicates nonmosaic trisomy 18 present in every cell.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A healthy 29-year-old man and his wife have had three first-trimester miscarriages. His karyotype reveals a balanced reciprocal translocation between two nonacrocentric autosomes. Which of the following best explains why he produces chromosomally unbalanced gametes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each rearranged chromosome carries two centromeres and is lost at anaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recombination is blocked throughout his entire genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rearranged chromosomes pair with difficulty with their homologs during meiosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The translocated segments are silenced, producing functional monosomy in every sperm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The translocation deleted genes required for normal spermatogenesis

explanation.summary: Balanced translocation carriers make unbalanced gametes because rearranged chromosomes pair poorly with their homologs in meiosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carriers of balanced reciprocal translocations and Robertsonian translocations are at high risk of producing unbalanced gametes because of the difficulty in pairing the affected chromosomes with their homologs during meiosis. The carrier is phenotypically normal because no critical genetic information was lost or gained, but the rearrangement causes gene dosage problems in the germ cells produced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A reciprocal translocation exchanges segments between chromosomes; it does not create dicentric chromosomes lost at anaphase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recombination is not globally blocked; the problem is specific to pairing and segregation of the rearranged chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The translocated segments remain functional in the carrier; unbalanced gametes arise from segregation, not silencing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: By definition a balanced translocation involves no loss of critical genetic material, and he is healthy.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A karyotype report for a phenotypically normal 26-year-old woman reads 45,XX,rob(14;21)(q10;q10). Which of the following structural events produced her abnormal chromosome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duplication of the entire long arm of chromosome 21 within one chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exchange of terminal segments between two nonhomologous chromosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of the short arms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fusion of the short arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of the long arms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of an entire chromosome 21 during maternal meiosis I

explanation.summary: A Robertsonian translocation is the fusion of the q arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of their p arms.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Robertsonian translocation is formed from the fusion of the q arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of the p arms. The single fused chromosome carries 14q and 21q, which is why the carrier has 45 chromosomes yet is phenotypically normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A duplication of 21q would be written dup(21q) with 46 chromosomes and would add, not remove, genetic material.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exchange of segments between nonhomologous chromosomes describes a reciprocal translocation, which preserves the count of 46.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The short (p) arms are the parts lost in a Robertsonian translocation; the long (q) arms are the parts joined.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of a whole chromosome 21 would be a monosomy, which is incompatible with life, not a balanced rearrangement.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A geneticist reviewing a karyotype identifies a single abnormal chromosome formed by the joining of the long arms of two different acrocentric chromosomes. Which of the following pairs of chromosomes could have participated in this rearrangement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 and 3

choices.label: B
choices.text: 7 and 11

choices.label: C
choices.text: 13 and 14

choices.label: D
choices.text: 16 and 18

choices.label: E
choices.text: 18 and 21

explanation.summary: Robertsonian translocations involve only the acrocentric chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acrocentric chromosomes (chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22) are the ones commonly involved in Robertsonian translocations, which form by fusion of the q arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of the p arms. Chromosomes 13 and 14 are both acrocentric, as in the 13;14 translocation carried by TE in the brick's case.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromosomes 1 and 3 are not acrocentric and do not form Robertsonian translocations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromosomes 7 and 11 are not among the acrocentric chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither chromosome 16 nor chromosome 18 is acrocentric.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chromosome 21 is acrocentric, but chromosome 18 is not, so this pair cannot fuse in a Robertsonian translocation.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A healthy 31-year-old man is karyotyped after his newborn daughter is diagnosed with Down syndrome. His chromosome count is 45 in every cell examined. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his karyotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He carries a balanced Robertsonian translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: He carries an unbalanced reciprocal translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has a mosaic cell line that lacks a sex chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: He has a triploid cell line in his peripheral blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: He has monosomy of chromosome 21 in all of his cells

explanation.summary: A phenotypically normal person with 45 chromosomes is a balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Robertsonian translocation fuses the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes into a single chromosome, so a balanced carrier such as 45,XY,rob(14;21) has 45 chromosomes with no loss or gain of critical genetic information and is phenotypically normal. Such a carrier can transmit the fused chromosome plus a normal 21, producing translocation Down syndrome in offspring.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An unbalanced translocation causes loss or gain of genetic material and a phenotypically abnormal individual; reciprocal translocations also preserve the count of 46.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mosaicism is reported as two cell lines separated by a slash and was found in every cell here; it also would not explain his daughter's trisomy 21.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A triploid line would contain 69 chromosomes, not 45, and triploidy is not viable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autosomal monosomies are always incompatible with life, so a healthy adult cannot have monosomy 21 in all cells.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman gives birth to an infant with flat facies, prominent epicanthal folds, and a single transverse palmar crease. Chromosome analysis of the infant shows 46 chromosomes, including one chromosome composed of the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21, together with two normal chromosome 21s. Which of the following statements about this etiology of Down syndrome is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accounts for roughly 4% of cases of Down syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: It accounts for the large majority of cases of Down syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: It produces a mixture of trisomic and normal cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It results from a postfertilization error in mitosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its risk rises steeply with advancing maternal age

explanation.summary: Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation, most commonly 14;21, causes about 4% of Down syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the 5% of Down syndrome cases not caused by meiotic nondisjunction, 4% result from an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation, most commonly between chromosomes 14 and 21. The infant's karyotype, 46,XX,rob(14;21),+21, shows the translocation chromosome plus two free chromosome 21s, giving three doses of 21q with a normal count of 46.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The large majority of cases (95%) result from meiotic nondisjunction, producing 47,+21.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mixture of trisomic and normal cells is mosaicism; a translocation trisomy affects every cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A postfertilization mitotic error describes mosaicism, which accounts for only about 1% to 2% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The maternal-age effect described applies to nondisjunction in oogenesis; this infant's trisomy arose from a translocation chromosome, and the mother is young.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman with the karyotype 45,XX,rob(13;14)(q10;q10) has had several miscarriages and asks whether she could ever have a healthy child. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No; all of her gametes carry an unbalanced chromosome complement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes; about 1/3 of her gametes could yield a phenotypically healthy child

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes; about 1/6 of her gametes could yield a phenotypically healthy child

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes; about 2/3 of her gametes could yield a phenotypically healthy child

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yes; but only gametes carrying the balanced translocation yield healthy children

explanation.summary: A rob(13;14) carrier has two routes to a healthy child: 1/6 of gametes are normal and 1/6 are balanced carriers, about 1/3 in total.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 2/3 of a 13;14 Robertsonian carrier's gametes have an abnormal number of chromosomes, leading either to a nonviable fetus or a child with trisomy 13. However, two possibilities lead to a healthy child: 1/6 of her gametes have no chromosome alteration, and another 1/6 are balanced carriers of the same 13;14 translocation. Together, about 1/3 of her gametes can produce a phenotypically healthy child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unlike a rob(21;21) carrier, a rob(13;14) carrier produces some normal and some balanced gametes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One sixth is the fraction that are chromosomally normal; it omits the additional 1/6 that are healthy balanced carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 2/3 of her gametes are the abnormal ones, not the healthy ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gametes with a completely normal chromosome complement also yield healthy children, not only the balanced carriers.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who carries a balanced Robertsonian translocation, 45,XX,rob(13;14)(q10;q10), delivers a liveborn infant girl with multiple congenital anomalies. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely in the infant?

explanation.summary: A rob(13;14) carrier's viable abnormal offspring have translocation trisomy 13 with a chromosome count of 46.
explanation.whyCorrect: A gamete carrying the fused 13;14 chromosome plus a normal chromosome 13, fertilized by a normal gamete, yields an individual with the translocation chromosome and two free chromosome 13s: three doses of 13q with a total count of 46. Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is survivable until birth, so this is the viable abnormal outcome, whereas translocation trisomy 14 is nonviable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced carrier is phenotypically normal, not an infant with multiple congenital anomalies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Translocation trisomy 14 is not compatible with live birth; TE's two such fetuses were miscarried.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free trisomy 13 with 47 chromosomes arises from meiotic nondisjunction, not from transmission of the fused translocation chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The count is wrong: the fused chromosome plus two free chromosome 13s totals 46 chromosomes, not 47.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn has micrognathia, a prominent occiput, low-set ears, and clenched hands with overlapping fingers. Chromosome analysis shows 46 chromosomes, and further study reveals that one chromosome 18 contains a duplicated segment of its long arm. Which of the following best describes the genetic basis of this infant's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete trisomy 18 from meiotic nondisjunction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mosaicism for a trisomy 18 cell line

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partial monosomy for the distal region of 18q

choices.label: D
choices.text: Partial trisomy for a critical region of 18q

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation of chromosome 18

explanation.summary: Edwards syndrome can result from partial trisomy when a duplication gives three copies of a critical 18q region.
explanation.whyCorrect: Edwards syndrome is most often caused by meiotic nondisjunction, but some cases are due to mosaicism or partial trisomy involving only a segment of the chromosome. In partial trisomy, one chromosome 18 contains a duplication of a critical region, so the individual has three total copies of that region of 18q, with two of those copies contained within a single chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete trisomy 18 from nondisjunction produces 47 chromosomes with a whole extra chromosome 18.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mosaicism would show two distinct cell lines (46/47), not a duplicated segment within one chromosome in a 46-chromosome karyotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A duplication adds material, producing extra dosage (trisomy), not a loss (monosomy).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chromosome 18 is not acrocentric and does not participate in Robertsonian translocations.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has a spontaneous abortion at 9 weeks of gestation. Cytogenetic analysis of the products of conception shows 47,XY,+16. Which of the following statements about this finding is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a euploid complement and is unrelated to the pregnancy loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is survivable until birth but rarely beyond infancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the most common trisomy among live births

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the most commonly occurring trisomy but is always fatal in utero

choices.label: E
choices.text: It most often arises from an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation

explanation.summary: Trisomy 16 is the most commonly occurring trisomy overall, but it is always fatal in utero.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trisomy 16 is the most commonly occurring trisomy, but it is always fatal in utero, which is why it is seen in products of conception rather than in liveborn infants. Most trisomies are embryonic lethal abnormalities; only trisomies 21, 18, and 13 are survivable until birth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 47 chromosomes is aneuploid, not an exact multiple of the haploid number, and trisomy 16 explains the loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Survival until birth but rarely beyond infancy describes trisomies 18 and 13, not trisomy 16.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common trisomy among live births; trisomy 16 never reaches live birth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chromosome 16 is not acrocentric, so it does not form Robertsonian translocations; trisomy 16 arises by nondisjunction.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A neonatologist counseling a resident notes that Down syndrome occurs in roughly 1 of every 700 live births. Which of the following is the approximate incidence of Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) among live births?

explanation.summary: Live-birth incidence falls from 1:700 for trisomy 21 to 1:5000 for trisomy 18 and 1:15000 for trisomy 13.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incidence in live births is 1:700 for Down syndrome, 1:5000 for Edwards syndrome, and 1:15000 for Patau syndrome. Among the three viable autosomal trisomies, Down syndrome is the most common among live births.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1:1500 is the risk of trisomy 21 in women younger than 20 years, not an Edwards syndrome incidence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1:15000 is the live-birth incidence of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13).
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1:25 is the risk of trisomy 21 in women older than 45 years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1:700 is the live-birth incidence of Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn with cutis aplasia, microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, and polydactyly is confirmed to have 47,XY,+13. The parents ask about their son's expected survival. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 50% die by 1 month of age and 90% by 1 year

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 50% die by 2 months of age and 90%-95% by 1 year

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most deaths occur after age 40 years from early-onset Alzheimer disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Survival to school age is typical once cardiac defects are repaired

choices.label: E
choices.text: Survival well into adulthood with mild intellectual disability is expected

explanation.summary: Patau syndrome carries death within 1 year of birth for most: 50% by 1 month and 90% by 1 year.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prognosis for Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is death within 1 year of birth, with 50% dying by 1 month and 90% by 1 year. Those with Edwards and Patau syndromes rarely live past a few years old, in contrast to people with Down syndrome, who live well into adulthood.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 50% by 2 months and 90%-95% by 1 year are the figures for Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alzheimer disease risk beginning at age 40 is a Down syndrome prognosis point; infants with trisomy 13 rarely survive infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Survival to school age is not typical in Patau syndrome regardless of cardiac repair; most die within the first year.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Survival into adulthood with mild to moderate intellectual disability describes Down syndrome, not Patau syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl with Down syndrome is evaluated for poor feeding and tachypnea, and echocardiography shows an atrial septal defect. Her parents ask which problem poses the greatest risk of death for children with Down syndrome in early life. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital heart disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Duodenal atresia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Early-onset Alzheimer disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hirschsprung disease

explanation.summary: Congenital heart disease is the most common cause of death early in life in Down syndrome; Alzheimer disease is the most common cause later.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Down syndrome, congenital heart disease (for example, atrial septal defect) is the most common cause of death in early life. Alzheimer disease risk is increased starting at age 40 years and is the most common cause of death later in life.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukemia risk is increased in Down syndrome, but it is not listed as the leading cause of early death; congenital heart disease is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Duodenal atresia is an association of Down syndrome but not its most common cause of early death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of death later in life, with risk increasing from about age 40, not in infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hirschsprung disease is an association of Down syndrome but not the leading cause of death in early life.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A pediatrician tells a group of students that a single chromosomal condition is the number one known cause of intellectual disability, and that the disability it causes is typically mild to moderate rather than severe. Which of the following conditions is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monosomy X

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trisomy 13

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trisomy 16

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trisomy 18

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy 21

explanation.summary: Down syndrome is the number one known cause of intellectual disability, which is mild to moderate in severity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) causes mild to moderate intellectual disability and is the number one known cause of intellectual disability. All three viable autosomal trisomies involve some degree of intellectual disability, but in Edwards and Patau syndromes it is severe.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) is the only viable monosomy but is not described as the leading known cause of intellectual disability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Patau syndrome causes severe intellectual disability and occurs in only 1:15000 live births.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trisomy 16 is always fatal in utero and therefore causes no living cases of intellectual disability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Edwards syndrome causes severe intellectual disability and is far less common (1:5000 live births).

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 3-day-old boy with flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a wide gap between the first and second toes has not passed meconium and has progressive abdominal distention without bilious vomiting on the first day of life. Which of the following associated conditions most likely explains his gastrointestinal findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biliary atresia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duodenal atresia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hirschsprung disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Omphalocele (abdominal wall defect)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease is a Down syndrome association that presents with failure to pass meconium and distention.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dysmorphic features indicate Down syndrome, whose gastrointestinal associations are duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease. Failure to pass meconium with abdominal distention in a newborn points to Hirschsprung disease rather than a proximal obstruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary atresia is not a listed Down syndrome association and presents with jaundice rather than obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duodenal atresia is also a Down syndrome association, but it presents with bilious vomiting on the first day of life, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Umbilical hernia/omphalocele is listed as a feature of Patau syndrome, not Down syndrome, and is an abdominal wall defect, not a cause of failure to pass meconium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyloric stenosis is not among the associations listed for Down syndrome and does not cause failure to pass meconium.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn has rocker-bottom feet, a ventricular septal defect, and a renal anomaly on ultrasound, findings that occur in both trisomy 18 and trisomy 13. The presence of which of the following additional findings would most strongly favor trisomy 18 over trisomy 13?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cutis aplasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microphthalmia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Omphalocele

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polydactyly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prominent occiput

explanation.summary: Rocker-bottom feet, heart defects, and renal defects overlap; a prominent occiput is an Edwards feature, whereas cutis aplasia, polydactyly, omphalocele, and microphthalmia are Patau features.
explanation.whyCorrect: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is characterized by micrognathia, prominent occiput, low-set ears, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and limited hip adduction, with congenital heart and renal defects. Because rocker-bottom feet and cardiac and renal defects are shared with Patau syndrome, the prominent occiput is the discriminating finding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cutis aplasia is specific for Patau syndrome (trisomy 13).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microphthalmia is listed among the features of Patau syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Umbilical hernia/omphalocele is a feature of Patau syndrome, not Edwards syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polydactyly is a Patau syndrome feature; Edwards syndrome hands show overlapping fingers.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with trisomy 21 develops pallor, fever, and bruising, and bone marrow examination confirms acute myeloid leukemia. Silencing of which of the following is thought to underlie the increased leukemia risk in his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: APP

choices.label: B
choices.text: BCR-ABL

choices.label: C
choices.text: PRC2

choices.label: D
choices.text: RB1

choices.label: E
choices.text: TP53

explanation.summary: The leukemia (especially AML) association of Down syndrome is thought to result from silencing of PRC2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Down syndrome is associated with leukemia, especially acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and this is thought to be due to silencing of PRC2. This is distinct from the Alzheimer association, which relates to three copies of the APP gene on chromosome 21.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APP on chromosome 21 is linked to the early-onset Alzheimer disease risk in Down syndrome, not to leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCR-ABL is a fusion gene of chronic myeloid leukemia and is not the mechanism of AML risk in trisomy 21.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 is not the factor implicated in the Down syndrome leukemia association.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 is not the factor implicated in the Down syndrome leukemia association.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A newborn boy has micrognathia, low-set ears, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and limited hip adduction. Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect. In addition to the cardiac evaluation, which of the following organ systems should be specifically imaged for structural defects associated with his chromosomal condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematologic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatobiliary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pulmonary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal

explanation.summary: Edwards and Patau syndromes are both associated with congenital heart defects and renal defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The findings indicate Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18). Its listed associations are congenital heart defects and renal defects, the same pair of associations listed for Patau syndrome, so renal imaging is warranted alongside the cardiac evaluation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endocrine defects are not among the associations listed for trisomy 18.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematologic malignancy (leukemia) is an association of Down syndrome, not of Edwards syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatobiliary defects are not among the associations listed for trisomy 18.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary structural defects are not among the listed associations of Edwards syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical & Structural Chromosomal Alterations (1/3) - Variants in Chromosome Number

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl presents for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. She is embarrassed that she has not started menstruating like her friends. On examination her height is at the fifth percentile for age, and you note extra skin folds on the neck, a broad chest, and a systolic murmur in the aortic region. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XY

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: Short stature, webbed neck, broad chest, and primary amenorrhea in a phenotypic female indicate Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanation.whyCorrect: Turner syndrome results from a single X chromosome (45,X, also written 45,XO). It is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea because the ovaries are replaced by nonfunctional fibrous tissue, and it classically produces short stature, a short webbed neck, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and cardiac defects such as a bicuspid aortic valve.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A 46,XY karyotype is a normal male and would not present as a phenotypic female with primary amenorrhea and these somatic features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Triple X (47,XXX) females typically have normal sexual development, normal fertility, and are often taller than average, not short with amenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) occurs in males, who present with tall stature, small testes, and gynecomastia rather than these findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XYY (47,XYY) occurs in males with normal genitalia and tall stature, not in a phenotypic female with amenorrhea.

questions.stem: You are counseling the parents of a newborn girl whose karyotype is reported as 45,X. They ask what cardiac problem she is most at risk for. Which of the following congenital heart defects is most strongly associated with her diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrial septal defect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bicuspid aortic valve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tetralogy of Fallot

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tricuspid valve atresia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ventricular septal defect

explanation.summary: Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common cardiac malformation in Turner syndrome (45,X).
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiovascular disease is the most serious health problem in Turner syndrome. Aortic valve abnormalities, primarily a bicuspid aortic valve, along with aortic coarctation, are the most common cardiac malformations and contribute to reduced life expectancy through aortic dilation and dissection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrial septal defect is characteristically associated with Down syndrome, not Turner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tetralogy of Fallot is classically linked to DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tricuspid valve atresia is associated with lithium exposure during pregnancy, not with monosomy X.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ventricular septal defect is characteristically associated with Down syndrome rather than Turner syndrome.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He is tall with disproportionately long arms and legs, and examination reveals gynecomastia, sparse facial hair, and small, firm testes. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XY

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: Tall stature, gynecomastia, small firm testes, and infertility in a male indicate Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).
explanation.whyCorrect: Klinefelter syndrome results from an extra X chromosome (47,XXY). The Y chromosome drives male differentiation while the extra X imparts some feminizing features; patients characteristically have a tall body with long limbs, gynecomastia, small fibrotic testes, reduced testosterone, and infertility from germ cell degeneration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Turner syndrome (45,X) occurs in phenotypic females and presents with short stature and ovarian failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal 46,XY male would not have gynecomastia, small fibrotic testes, and azoospermia as a syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Triple X (47,XXX) occurs in females, not males.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XYY (47,XYY) males have normal genitalia, normal testosterone, and normal fertility, not gynecomastia and azoospermia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a 47,XXY karyotype is being counseled about hormone therapy. His small, fibrotic testes show germ cell degeneration on biopsy. Which of the following hormonal findings is most consistent with his diagnosis, and best explains why testosterone supplementation is often prescribed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent estrogen production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased testosterone production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated progesterone production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased testosterone production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal gonadal hormone balance

explanation.summary: Klinefelter syndrome causes reduced testosterone from testicular dysfunction, so testosterone supplementation is commonly given.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Klinefelter syndrome the testes are small and fibrotic with germ cell degeneration, leading to reduced testosterone production and a testosterone-to-estrogen imbalance. Because of this deficiency, testosterone supplementation is often prescribed to address the hypogonadal state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estrogen is not absent; in fact a relative testosterone-to-estrogen imbalance contributes to features such as gynecomastia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated progesterone is not a described feature of Klinefelter syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testosterone production is reduced, not increased, in Klinefelter syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gonadal hormone balance is abnormal, which is precisely why supplementation is needed.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy is referred for behavioral concerns including impulsivity and difficulty focusing. He is notably tall for his family, has severe acne, and is noted to have flat feet and mild tremor. Genital examination is normal, and serum testosterone is within the normal range. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XY

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: Tall stature, severe acne, flat feet, normal genitalia, and behavioral impulsivity with normal testosterone indicate XYY (Jacobs) syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: XYY syndrome (47,XYY) occurs in males who have normal male external genitalia and normal testosterone levels. Associated findings include tall stature, hypotonia with flat feet (pes planus) and tremor, severe acne in adolescence, and behavioral features such as impulsivity, ADHD, and autism spectrum disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Turner syndrome (45,X) occurs in short-statured females, not tall males with normal genitalia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal 46,XY male would not constitute the described cluster of tall stature with behavioral and skeletal findings as a syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Triple X (47,XXX) occurs in females.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with small testes, gynecomastia, and low testosterone, not normal genitalia and normal testosterone.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman is found to have a sex chromosome aneuploidy after genetic testing during a learning-disability evaluation. She is taller than average, has normal external genitalia and normal pubertal development, and is expected to have normal fertility. Which of the following karyotypes best fits this presentation?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XX

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: A taller-than-average female with normal genitalia, normal fertility, and learning-disability risk fits triple X syndrome (47,XXX).
explanation.whyCorrect: Triple X syndrome (47,XXX) affects females and may cause minimal or no noticeable effects. External genitalia and sexual development are normal, affected individuals are often taller than average and can have children, and the main associated finding is an increased risk of learning disabilities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature, ovarian failure, and infertility, the opposite of this picture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 46,XX karyotype is a normal female and is not a sex chromosome aneuploidy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) occurs in males with small testes and infertility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XYY (47,XYY) occurs in males, not females.

questions.stem: During early embryonic development, a transcription factor encoded by a single gene commits the bipotential gonad toward testis formation; embryos lacking this gene tend to develop female sexual organs. On which chromosome is this gene normally located, and what is its product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An autosome; it encodes a structural collagen protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mitochondrial genome; it encodes an oxidative enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pseudoautosomal region; it encodes a recombination enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: The X chromosome; it encodes an X-inactivation transcript

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Y chromosome; it encodes the testis-determining factor

explanation.summary: The SRY gene on the Y chromosome encodes testis-determining factor, a transcription factor that directs male sex determination.
explanation.whyCorrect: SRY is normally found on the Y chromosome and encodes testis-determining factor (TDF), a transcription factor critical for sex determination. Embryos with a copy of SRY tend to develop male sexual organs, and those without it tend to develop female sexual organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SRY is not autosomal and does not encode a structural collagen protein; it encodes a transcription factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SRY is a nuclear sex-chromosome gene, not a mitochondrial gene, and its product is a transcription factor, not an oxidative enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pseudoautosomal region allows X-Y pairing and recombination but does not itself contain the SRY gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SRY is not on the X chromosome and does not encode an X-inactivation transcript; X-inactivation is a separate dosage-compensation process.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying how paternal meiotic errors generate abnormal sex chromosome complements. If nondisjunction occurs during male meiosis II and the resulting abnormal sperm fertilizes a normal X-bearing egg, which of the following karyotypes is most characteristically produced?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XYY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,YYY

explanation.summary: Paternal meiosis II nondisjunction can create a YY sperm that, with a normal X egg, yields 47,XYY.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondisjunction during male meiosis II fails to separate sister chromatids and can generate XX or YY sperm. A YY sperm fertilizing a normal X egg produces a 47,XYY zygote. In contrast, meiosis I nondisjunction is what generates XY sperm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X arises when a nullisomic gamete lacking any sex chromosome combines with an X gamete, not specifically from a meiosis II YY sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 47,XXX requires an XX egg fertilized by an X sperm; it is a maternal, not this paternal meiosis II, outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 47,XXY arises from an XY sperm (a meiosis I error) plus an X egg, or an XX egg plus a Y sperm, not from a meiosis II YY sperm and an X egg.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,YYY would require multiple abnormal events and complete absence of an X, which cannot result from a single YY sperm fertilizing a normal X egg.

questions.stem: In a pregnancy, a nondisjunction event occurs during maternal meiosis while paternal spermatogenesis is entirely normal. Which of the following offspring karyotypes is LEAST likely to result from this pregnancy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XX

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: Because the mother is XX, maternal nondisjunction can only make XX or nullisomic eggs, so a 47,XYY child is essentially impossible without a paternal error.
explanation.whyCorrect: The maternal genotype is XX, so nondisjunction during maternal meiosis can produce only XX eggs or eggs lacking any sex chromosome. Generating 47,XYY requires two Y chromosomes, which the mother cannot supply; with normal paternal sperm, XYY is essentially not achievable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X can occur if a maternal egg lacking a sex chromosome is fertilized by a normal X sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 46,XX is a normal outcome when a normal maternal X egg meets a normal X sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 47,XXX can occur if a maternal XX egg is fertilized by a normal X sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 47,XXY can occur if a maternal XX egg is fertilized by a normal Y sperm.

questions.stem: Although the X and Y chromosomes are structurally very different, they must pair and can undergo limited homologous recombination during male meiosis. Which feature of the sex chromosomes makes this pairing possible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The centromeric heterochromatin of the Y chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: The large number of unique genes on the X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pseudoautosomal region shared by X and Y

choices.label: D
choices.text: The SRY gene on the Y chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-inactivation of one X chromosome

explanation.summary: The pseudoautosomal region, essentially identical on X and Y, allows the two to pair and recombine like autosomes during male meiosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genes in the pseudoautosomal region are found on both the X and Y chromosomes, and these stretches are essentially identical. This homology lets the X and Y pair and undergo homologous recombination during male meiosis, similar to how autosomes behave.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Centromeric heterochromatin of the Y is not the homologous region that permits X-Y pairing and recombination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The many unique X genes are precisely the non-homologous portion and do not enable X-Y pairing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SRY drives male sex determination but does not mediate the physical pairing of X and Y during meiosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-inactivation is a dosage-compensation mechanism in cells with extra X chromosomes and is unrelated to meiotic pairing.

questions.stem: A geneticist explains why individuals with two or more X chromosomes do not express X-linked genes at proportionally higher levels than 46,XY males. Which of the following processes accounts for this normalization of X-gene dosage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deletion of the extra X chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expression of the SRY gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inactivation of extra X chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nondisjunction during meiosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombination in the pseudoautosomal region

explanation.summary: X-inactivation silences extra X chromosomes so that X-linked gene dosage is balanced between the sexes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In individuals with two or more X chromosomes, inactivation of the extra X chromosomes is a normal physiological process. It ensures that X-chromosomal genes are not expressed at proportionally higher levels compared with XY males, providing dosage compensation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The extra X chromosome is not physically deleted; it is transcriptionally inactivated while remaining present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SRY expression governs male sex determination and does not regulate X-gene dosage compensation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nondisjunction is a cause of aneuploidy, not a mechanism for balancing gene dosage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pseudoautosomal recombination allows X-Y pairing in meiosis but does not silence extra X genes.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with Turner syndrome (45,X) has never menstruated. Her mother asks why she has not begun having periods. Which of the following best explains the underlying cause of her primary amenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An imperforate hymen obstructing menstrual outflow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess testosterone from functioning testicular tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ovarian dysgenesis with premature ovarian failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pituitary overproduction of estrogen and progesterone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uterine agenesis with normally functioning ovaries

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome causes ovarian dysgenesis and premature ovarian failure with insufficient estrogen, making it the most common cause of primary amenorrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Turner syndrome the ovaries are replaced by nonfunctional fibrous tissue and stop functioning at a young age (premature ovarian failure). The resulting lack of estrogen means menstruation and pubertal development do not occur normally, and this ovarian dysgenesis makes Turner syndrome the most common cause of primary amenorrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An imperforate hymen causes outflow obstruction, not the ovarian failure and low estrogen characteristic of Turner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Turner patients do not have functioning testicular tissue or excess testosterone; the problem is estrogen deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hormonal picture is estrogen deficiency, not pituitary overproduction of estrogen and progesterone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The defect is ovarian (dysgenesis), not uterine agenesis with normal ovaries.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the structure of the human sex chromosomes. Which of the following best contrasts the gene content of the X and Y chromosomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The X and Y each contain fewer than 100 genes, none shared

choices.label: B
choices.text: The X and Y each contain roughly 900 genes, most of them shared

choices.label: C
choices.text: The X contains about 900 genes, all of which are also on the Y

choices.label: D
choices.text: The X contains about 900 genes; the Y contains fewer than 100

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Y contains about 900 genes; the X contains fewer than 100

explanation.summary: The X chromosome carries about 900 genes, whereas the structurally distinct Y chromosome carries fewer than 100.
explanation.whyCorrect: The X chromosome contains approximately 900 genes, most of which are unique to the X. The Y chromosome is structurally distinct and contains less than 100 genes. Only the genes in the pseudoautosomal region are shared between the two chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The X carries about 900 genes, and the two chromosomes do share the genes of the pseudoautosomal region.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Y is far smaller in gene content than the X, and most X genes are unique to the X rather than shared.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most X genes are unique to the X; only the pseudoautosomal region is also present on the Y.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the relationship; it is the X, not the Y, that carries about 900 genes.

questions.stem: During spermatogenesis, homologous chromosomes pair before being segregated in meiosis I. Which of the following correctly describes how the X and Y chromosomes behave during this stage in a 46,XY male?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are inactivated and excluded from the meiotic spindle

choices.label: B
choices.text: They fuse into a single chromosome before segregating

choices.label: C
choices.text: They pair with chromosome 22 rather than with each other

choices.label: D
choices.text: They pair with each other and behave as a homologous pair

choices.label: E
choices.text: They remain unpaired and segregate randomly to either pole

explanation.summary: In male meiosis the X and Y act as homologs, pairing before segregation despite their structural differences.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homologous chromosomes pair up during meiosis I before being segregated into the daughter cells. During meiosis, the two sex chromosomes act as homologs even when they are an X and a Y, a pairing made possible by the shared pseudoautosomal region.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither sex chromosome is inactivated or excluded from meiosis in males; they pair and segregate normally.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The X and Y pair and then separate as homologs; they do not fuse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sex chromosomes pair with each other as the 23rd pair, not with an autosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The X and Y do pair with each other in male meiosis; they do not segregate as unpaired chromosomes.

questions.stem: A sex chromosome nondisjunction error occurs during meiosis I of spermatogenesis in an otherwise normal 46,XY man. Which sex chromosome contents are expected in the sperm that result from this division?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sperm carrying a single X and sperm carrying a single Y

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sperm carrying both X and Y, and sperm carrying no sex chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sperm carrying XX and sperm carrying a single Y

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sperm carrying XX, sperm carrying YY, and sperm carrying no sex chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sperm carrying YY and sperm carrying a single X

explanation.summary: Meiosis I nondisjunction in a male produces XY sperm and sperm lacking any sex chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: In meiosis I the X and Y homologs normally separate. If they fail to disjoin, one daughter cell receives both X and Y and the other receives neither; after meiosis II this yields sperm containing both an X and a Y and sperm with no sex chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Single-X and single-Y sperm are the products of normal meiosis, not of a nondisjunction error.
whyWrongByChoice.C: XX sperm arise from meiosis II errors, and a normal Y sperm would not be the paired abnormal product of a meiosis I error.
whyWrongByChoice.D: XX and YY sperm are products of meiosis II nondisjunction, when sister chromatids fail to separate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: YY sperm arise from meiosis II nondisjunction, not from a meiosis I error.

questions.stem: Two primary spermatocytes each undergo a single sex chromosome nondisjunction event: in one it occurs during meiosis I, in the other during meiosis II. Which of the following correctly compares the four sperm produced from each spermatocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both errors yield four abnormal sperm out of four

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both errors yield two abnormal sperm out of four

choices.label: C
choices.text: The meiosis I error yields four abnormal sperm; the meiosis II error yields two

choices.label: D
choices.text: The meiosis I error yields one abnormal sperm; the meiosis II error yields three

choices.label: E
choices.text: The meiosis I error yields two abnormal sperm; the meiosis II error yields four

explanation.summary: Nondisjunction in meiosis I affects more gametes than nondisjunction in meiosis II.
explanation.whyCorrect: When nondisjunction occurs during meiosis I, both daughter cells are abnormal (one XY, one empty), so all four resulting sperm are abnormal. When the error occurs in meiosis II, only one of the two secondary spermatocytes is affected, producing two abnormal sperm (XX or YY plus an empty one) and two normal sperm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A meiosis II error leaves the unaffected secondary spermatocyte to produce two normal sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A meiosis I error propagates through both daughter cells, so all four sperm are abnormal, not two.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nondisjunction produces abnormal gametes in pairs; it cannot yield one or three abnormal sperm out of four.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the relationship; the earlier (meiosis I) error is the one that affects all four gametes.

questions.stem: A sperm formed after a nondisjunction error in paternal meiosis II carries two X chromosomes and no Y chromosome. It fertilizes a normal egg. Which of the following best describes the resulting child?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A female with triple X syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: A female with Turner syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: A male with Jacobs syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: A male with Klinefelter syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: A phenotypically normal female

explanation.summary: An XX sperm combining with a normal X egg produces a 47,XXX zygote, a female with triple X syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondisjunction in male meiosis II can produce XX sperm. When an XX sperm fertilizes an egg carrying a single X, the zygote is XXX, which develops as a female with triple X syndrome. Thus triple X can originate from a paternal as well as a maternal error.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Turner syndrome (X) results when a sperm lacking any sex chromosome fertilizes an X egg.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Jacobs syndrome (XYY) requires a YY sperm, not an XX sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) requires a Y chromosome, which an XX sperm does not carry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal female (XX) results from a normal single-X sperm, not a sperm carrying two X chromosomes.

questions.stem: A karyotype report for a girl with short stature reads 45,X. Which of the following alternative notations describes the same karyotype?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 45,XO

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46,XO

choices.label: D
choices.text: 46,XX

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XXX

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome is written 45,X or equivalently 45,XO; the total count is 45 because one X is missing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The notation for monosomy X is 45,X, and it may also be denoted 45,XO. The usual chromosome total is 46, but since one X chromosome is missing the total count is 45, with pairs for chromosomes 1-22 and a single chromosome for the 23rd pair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only one chromosome is missing, so the total is 45, not 44.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A total of 46 is incorrect; with one sex chromosome missing the count is 45.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 46,XX is the normal female karyotype, not monosomy X.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,XXX is triple X syndrome, with an extra rather than a missing X.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with a confirmed 45,X karyotype is examined. When she fully extends her arms at her sides, her forearms angle outward, away from her body. Which of the following terms describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cubitus valgus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypertelorism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphedema

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macroskelia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pes planus

explanation.summary: Cubitus valgus, the forearm angled away from the body when the arm is fully extended, is a characteristic feature of Turner syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Commonly described physical characteristics of Turner syndrome include a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a short webbed neck, and cubitus valgus, defined as the forearm being angled out away from the body when the arm is fully extended.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypertelorism means widely spaced eyes, described in XYY and triple X syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphedema is swelling of the hands and feet seen in Turner neonates, not an elbow carrying angle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macroskelia refers to the long legs and arms of Klinefelter syndrome, not an angulation of the forearm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pes planus (flat feet) is a feature of XYY syndrome related to hypotonia, not an elbow finding.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a short, webbed neck and puffy swelling over the dorsum of both hands and both feet. Karyotype analysis confirms monosomy X. Which of the following best describes the swelling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central adiposity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital lymphedema

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cubitus valgus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generalized hypotonia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Macroskelia (long limbs)

explanation.summary: Neonates with Turner syndrome may present with congenital lymphedema of the hands and feet together with a webbed neck.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although short stature is the most consistent feature of Turner syndrome, neonates may have notable congenital lymphedema of the hands and feet and a webbed neck, which can prompt early recognition of monosomy X.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central adiposity is a feature pictured in boys with XYY (Jacobs) syndrome, not swelling of the hands and feet.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cubitus valgus is an outward angulation of the forearm, not swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypotonia is decreased muscle tone, described in XYY syndrome, and does not cause puffy hands and feet.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macroskelia describes the long limbs of Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stem: An embryo with a 46,XY karyotype and an intact, normally located SRY gene nevertheless develops female sexual organs. Which of the following best accounts for this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other genes besides SRY are also required in the sex determination pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: SRY is only expressed when two X chromosomes are present

choices.label: C
choices.text: The SRY gene lies in the pseudoautosomal region and was exchanged onto the X

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Y chromosome cannot direct testis formation without a second Y

choices.label: E
choices.text: X inactivation silenced the SRY gene on the Y chromosome

explanation.summary: SRY is critical but not the only determinant of male development; other genes also participate in the sex determination pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Embryos with a copy of SRY tend to develop male sexual organs and those without it tend to develop female organs, but SRY is not the sole determinant. Other genes are also involved in the sex determination pathway, so an embryo with a normal SRY can still fail to develop male organs if those additional components are defective.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SRY is a Y-linked gene that acts in XY embryos; its expression does not depend on two X chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SRY is not in the pseudoautosomal region, and the stem states the gene is intact and normally located on the Y.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single Y carrying SRY is sufficient for normal male development in a 46,XY male; a second Y is not needed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X inactivation silences extra X chromosomes for dosage compensation; it does not silence the Y chromosome or SRY.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with a 45,X karyotype undergoes routine cardiac screening. Echocardiography shows a discrete narrowing of the aorta. Which of the following cardiac malformations does this finding represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortic coarctation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atrial septal defect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bicuspid aortic valve

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tetralogy of Fallot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tricuspid valve atresia

explanation.summary: Aortic coarctation, a narrowing of the aorta, is one of the common cardiac malformations of Turner syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiovascular disease is the most serious health problem in Turner syndrome. Along with aortic valve abnormalities (primarily bicuspid aortic valve), the common cardiac malformations include aortic coarctation, defined as narrowing of the aorta, as well as vasculopathy and conduction abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Atrial septal defect is a septal opening, not a narrowing of the aorta, and is associated with Down syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A bicuspid aortic valve is a valve leaflet abnormality, not a narrowing of the aorta itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetralogy of Fallot is associated with DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome and is not a narrowing of the aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tricuspid valve atresia is associated with lithium exposure in pregnancy and involves the tricuspid valve, not the aorta.

questions.stem: The parents of a 6-year-old girl with Turner syndrome ask about her long-term prognosis. Which of the following complications most accounts for the roughly 10-year reduction in life expectancy associated with her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortic dilation and dissection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital lymphedema of the hands and feet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cubitus valgus of both elbows

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonverbal learning disabilities

choices.label: E
choices.text: Premature ovarian failure

explanation.summary: Cardiovascular complications, including bicuspid aortic valve, aortic dilation, and dissection, shorten life expectancy in Turner syndrome by about 10 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individuals with Turner syndrome have a life expectancy shortened by approximately 10 years because of the syndrome's association with cardiovascular complications such as bicuspid aortic valve, aortic dilation, and aortic dissection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Congenital lymphedema of the hands and feet is a neonatal physical finding, not a life-limiting complication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cubitus valgus is a skeletal feature of Turner syndrome and has no effect on life expectancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Learning disabilities are associated with triple X and other aneuploidies but do not shorten survival.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Premature ovarian failure causes amenorrhea and infertility but is not the cause of reduced life expectancy.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with Turner syndrome and premature ovarian failure wishes to become pregnant. Which of the following approaches is described as making pregnancy possible in some cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expectant management, since fertility is usually preserved

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth hormone therapy to reactivate the failing ovaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: In vitro fertilization with estradiol-17B and progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical excision of the fibrous ovarian tissue with follow-up

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone supplementation to induce regular ovulation

explanation.summary: In some Turner patients, pregnancy is possible with in vitro fertilization plus administered estradiol-17B and progesterone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individuals with Turner syndrome often have fertility problems due to ovarian dysgenesis and premature ovarian failure. In some cases, pregnancy is possible with in vitro fertilization (IVF) combined with treatment using administered estradiol-17B and progesterone to replace the hormones the fibrous ovaries cannot produce.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fertility is not preserved; ovarian dysgenesis and premature ovarian failure commonly cause infertility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Growth hormone is not described as restoring ovarian function in Turner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing the fibrous ovarian tissue would not restore egg production or hormone output.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone supplementation is the therapy prescribed for Klinefelter syndrome, not a fertility treatment in Turner syndrome.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea, short stature, and a webbed neck is diagnosed with a 45,X karyotype. Which of the following hormonal patterns is expected in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated estrogen and elevated progesterone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated testosterone with normal estrogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low estrogen and low progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low testosterone with elevated estrogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal estrogen with elevated progesterone

explanation.summary: Defective ovaries in Turner syndrome produce insufficient estrogen and progesterone, so estrogen therapy is needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Turner syndrome the ovaries are defective or nonfunctional, replaced by fibrous tissue, so estrogen and progesterone levels are low. As a consequence menstruation and pubertal development do not occur normally; treatment with estrogen therapy is necessary, and the patient is referred to an endocrinologist to begin a treatment plan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nonfunctional ovaries cannot produce elevated levels of either hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Turner syndrome is not characterized by excess testosterone; the defect is deficient ovarian estrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen is deficient in Turner syndrome; a low-testosterone, high-estrogen imbalance describes Klinefelter syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogen is low, not normal, and progesterone is low rather than elevated.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor discusses the origin of a 45,X karyotype with the parents of an affected infant. Which of the following statements about how the missing sex chromosome arose is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It arises from either meiotic division in either parent, most often maternal

choices.label: B
choices.text: It arises from either meiotic division in either parent, most often paternal

choices.label: C
choices.text: It arises only from nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I

choices.label: D
choices.text: It arises only from nondisjunction in maternal meiosis II

choices.label: E
choices.text: It arises only from nondisjunction in paternal meiosis II

explanation.summary: Monosomy X can result from nondisjunction at either meiotic division in either parent, but about 80% of cases are paternal in origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes during meiosis I or II can produce a gamete with no sex chromosome; combining this empty gamete with a normal X-bearing gamete yields 45,X. This can occur in either spermatogenesis or oogenesis, but about 80% of cases result from paternal nondisjunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The parent-of-origin distribution is reversed; most 45,X cases are paternal, not maternal, in origin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The error is not restricted to the mother or to meiosis I; either parent and either division can be responsible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal meiosis II is only one of several possible sources, and it is not the most common.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although paternal errors predominate, they are not limited to meiosis II, and maternal errors also occur.

questions.stem: A newborn boy is noted to have a micropenis, hypospadias, and bilateral cryptorchidism. Karyotyping reveals a sex chromosome aneuploidy. Which of the following results is most likely?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XX

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: Micropenis, hypospadias, and cryptorchidism are the Klinefelter (47,XXY) phenotypes that may be detectable at birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many cases of Klinefelter syndrome are not diagnosed until adulthood, but phenotypes that may be detectable at birth include micropenis, hypospadias, or cryptorchidism. Later findings such as gynecomastia and female hair distribution do not appear until puberty.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X produces a phenotypic female with short stature and webbed neck, not a boy with genital anomalies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 46,XX is a normal female karyotype and is not an aneuploidy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 47,XXX affects females and features normal external genitalia development.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,XYY males have normal male external genitalia development, not micropenis or cryptorchidism.

questions.stem: The parents of an 8-year-old boy with a 47,XXY karyotype ask what to expect regarding his learning and development. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Development is typically normal, with no link to learning disabilities

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impulsivity and autism spectrum disorders predominate; intelligence is unaffected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intelligence is usually above average, without added learning problems

choices.label: D
choices.text: Learning disabilities and anxiety are common; intelligence is average or low-average

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe intellectual disability is present in nearly every affected boy

explanation.summary: Klinefelter syndrome is associated with developmental delay, learning disabilities, and anxiety disorders, with average or low-average intelligence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Affected males are likely to have developmental delay. Learning disabilities and anxiety disorders are common in Klinefelter syndrome, and patients typically have average or low-average intelligence, with considerable variability in phenotype severity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Developmental delay and learning disabilities are expected associations, not absent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Impulsivity, ADHD, and autism spectrum disorders are the behavioral features described for XYY syndrome, not XXY.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Above-average intelligence is not characteristic, and learning disabilities are common.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intelligence is typically average or low-average, not severely impaired.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a 47,XXY karyotype is examined. Which of the following combinations of physical findings is most consistent with his karyotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broad shoulders, narrow hips, and heavy beard growth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Frontal baldness, dense chest hair, and a male pubic pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: Narrow shoulders, wide hips, and poor beard growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Short limbs, a broad chest, and widely spaced nipples

choices.label: E
choices.text: Webbed neck, cubitus valgus, and lymphedema of the feet

explanation.summary: Klinefelter syndrome produces a feminized habitus: narrow shoulders, wide hips, poor beard growth, absent frontal baldness, and female-type pubic hair.
explanation.whyCorrect: The extra X-chromosome genes impart female features to a male differentiated by his Y chromosome. Common physical characteristics include absent frontal baldness, poor beard growth, a tendency to grow fewer chest hairs, breast development, narrow shoulders, wide hips, a female-type pubic hair pattern, small testes, and long legs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Broad shoulders, narrow hips, and heavy beard growth are typical male features that are diminished in Klinefelter syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Frontal baldness is absent, chest hair is sparse, and the pubic hair pattern is female-type in Klinefelter syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Short limbs, broad chest, and widely spaced nipples describe Turner syndrome; Klinefelter patients have long limbs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Webbed neck, cubitus valgus, and lymphedema are features of Turner syndrome, not Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with a 47,XXY karyotype has azoospermia attributed to germ cell degeneration in small, fibrotic testes. This testicular process is described as analogous to which of the following findings in Turner syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortic coarctation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital lymphedema

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cubitus valgus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inactivation of the extra X chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Premature ovarian failure

explanation.summary: Germ cell degeneration in Klinefelter syndrome parallels premature ovarian failure in Turner syndrome; both cause infertility through gonadal failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Those with Klinefelter syndrome often have germ cell degeneration analogous to premature ovarian failure in Turner syndrome. Because germ cells produce sperm, affected men have abnormal sperm production and are often infertile owing to the inability to make functioning sperm cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aortic coarctation is a cardiovascular malformation of Turner syndrome and has no counterpart in testicular germ cell loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Congenital lymphedema is a neonatal swelling of the hands and feet, unrelated to gonadal failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cubitus valgus is a skeletal angulation of the forearm, not a gonadal finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X inactivation is a normal dosage-compensation process, not a degenerative gonadal process.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with a 47,XXY karyotype is described as having a tall, slim body with disproportionately long legs and long arms. Which of the following terms refers to this limb finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cubitus valgus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypertelorism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypotonia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macroskelia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pes planus

explanation.summary: Macroskelia is the term for the long legs and long arms that characterize the tall, slim Klinefelter body shape.
explanation.whyCorrect: Males with Klinefelter syndrome characteristically present with a tall, slim body shape with macroskelia, meaning long legs and long arms, contributing to the eunuchoid body shape described for trisomy XXY.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cubitus valgus is the outward angulation of the forearm seen in Turner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypertelorism means widely spaced eyes, described in XYY and triple X syndromes.
