whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypotonia means decreased muscle tone, a feature of XYY syndrome rather than a limb-length term.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pes planus means flat feet, a finding associated with hypotonia in XYY syndrome.

questions.stem: Tall stature is a shared feature of several sex chromosome aneuploidies. Which of the following karyotypes is instead characteristically associated with short stature?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XY

choices.label: C
choices.text: 47,XXX

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XYY

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome (45,X) is the sex chromosome aneuploidy with short stature; XXY, XYY, and XXX individuals tend to be tall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Short stature is the most consistent physical feature of Turner syndrome. In contrast, Klinefelter males have a tall, slim body with long limbs, triple X females are often taller than average, and XYY males can be very tall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 46,XY is a normal male karyotype and is not associated with a stature abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Triple X (47,XXX) females are often taller than average.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klinefelter (47,XXY) males have a tall, slim body shape with macroskelia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XYY (47,XYY) males can be very tall.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with a 47,XXX karyotype has epicanthal folds and hypertelorism. Her parents ask whether all girls with this karyotype share these facial features. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Facial features are variable, and some affected girls have no dysmorphic features

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypertelorism is present in every affected girl and is required for diagnosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: These features indicate an associated cardiac malformation requiring echocardiography

choices.label: D
choices.text: These features indicate that her karyotype is more likely 45,X than 47,XXX

choices.label: E
choices.text: These features predict infertility and abnormal genital development

explanation.summary: Facial features in trisomy X are variable; some girls have epicanthal folds and hypertelorism while others lack dysmorphic features entirely.
explanation.whyCorrect: Triple X syndrome may cause no noticeable effects or only minimal ones. Facial features are variable: epicanthal folds and hypertelorism can be seen in some young girls, while other affected individuals, such as a 19-year-old shown for comparison, have no dysmorphic features at all.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypertelorism is not universal and is not a diagnostic requirement; the karyotype defines the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cardiac malformations are the hallmark of Turner syndrome, not triple X, and these facial features do not indicate one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epicanthal folds and hypertelorism are described in girls with trisomy X; they do not point toward monosomy X.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most females with triple X have normal external genitalia, normal sexual development, and can have children.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with a 47,XYY karyotype is evaluated. In addition to hypertelorism and pes planus, which of the following physical findings is characteristic of his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enlarged front teeth and central adiposity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epicanthal folds and short stature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gynecomastia and micropenis with sparse body hair

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypospadias and bilateral cryptorchidism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Webbed neck and a broad, shield-like chest

explanation.summary: Physical features of boys with XYY (Jacobs) syndrome include hypertelorism, enlarged front teeth, pes planus, and central adiposity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Boys with XYY syndrome can have hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes), enlarged front teeth, pes planus (flat feet) related to hypotonia, and central adiposity, in addition to tall stature and, during adolescence, severe acne.

whyWrongByChoice.B: XYY males are tall rather than short; epicanthal folds are described in trisomy X girls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gynecomastia and micropenis are features of Klinefelter syndrome; XYY males have normal male genitalia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypospadias and cryptorchidism are neonatal findings of Klinefelter syndrome, not XYY.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Webbed neck and broad chest are features of Turner syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of sex chromosome aneuploidies is characteristically associated with infertility because of abnormal functioning of the gonadal endocrine hormone pathways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klinefelter syndrome and XYY syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Triple X syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Triple X syndrome and XYY syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turner syndrome and triple X syndrome

explanation.summary: Turner and Klinefelter syndromes cause infertility through abnormal gonadal hormone pathways, whereas triple X and XYY individuals typically retain normal fertility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Turner and Klinefelter syndromes often cause infertility because of the abnormal functioning of the female and male endocrine hormone pathways: nonfunctional fibrous ovaries with low estrogen in Turner syndrome, and small fibrotic testes with low testosterone in Klinefelter syndrome. In contrast, triple X females have normal sexual development and can have children, and XYY males have normal testosterone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: XYY males have normal testosterone and normal male genitalia; infertility is not characteristic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Triple X syndrome is not associated with infertility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both triple X and XYY individuals have normal genital development and are generally fertile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triple X females usually have normal sexual development and can have children.

questions.stem: A student is asked to define the process that gives rise to embryos with missing or extra sex chromosomes. Which of the following best defines nondisjunction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exchange of segments between two nonhomologous chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of chromosomes to separate correctly during cell division

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of a segment from one arm of a chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pairing of the X and Y chromosomes in the pseudoautosomal region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcriptional silencing of an extra X chromosome

explanation.summary: Nondisjunction is the sticking together of chromosomes during cell division so that they fail to separate correctly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondisjunction is the lack of normal separation of chromosomes, the sticking together of chromosomes during cell division. When it occurs in meiosis I or meiosis II, chromosomes separate incorrectly, producing gametes and thus embryos with missing or extra sex chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Exchange of segments between nonhomologous chromosomes is a structural rearrangement, not a failure of separation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of a chromosome segment is a structural deletion, not a numerical error of separation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudoautosomal pairing is the normal mechanism that allows X and Y to behave as homologs, not an error.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Silencing of an extra X describes X inactivation, a normal dosage-compensation process.

questions.stem: A 1-month-old girl is evaluated for microcephaly and low birth weight noted at birth. Over the first few weeks of life she has had difficulty feeding because of trouble swallowing. Her mother reports a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry that was very different from that of her older sibling. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cri du chat syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Down syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turner syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Williams syndrome

explanation.summary: Microcephaly, intellectual disability, and a high-pitched cat-like cry in an infant indicate cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion).
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat syndrome results from a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). The name means 'cry of the cat' in French and refers to the characteristic high-pitched cry; other features include microcephaly, intellectual disability, and cardiac abnormalities such as ventricular septal defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome features conotruncal cardiac defects, immunodeficiency, and hypocalcemia rather than a high-pitched cry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is associated with flat epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease, not the described cry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Turner syndrome (45,X) affects females with short stature and gonadal dysgenesis and is not characterized by a cat-like cry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) presents with elfin facies, overfriendliness, and supravalvular aortic stenosis, not a cat-like cry.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A geneticist confirms cri du chat syndrome in a female infant. Which of the following karyotype descriptions is most consistent with this diagnosis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46,XX,del(5p)

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XXY

explanation.summary: Cri du chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, written as 46,XX,del(5p) in a female.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat syndrome is caused by a deletion on chromosome 5p. Because the breakpoints and extent of the deleted segment are variable, the notation is often written simply as del(5p), with a band location added only when known.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X indicates a female with Turner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 46,XX,del(22q11.2) describes a female with 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 46,XX,del(7q11.23) describes a female with Williams syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,XXY indicates a male with Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A newborn boy has a truncus arteriosus detected on echocardiography, a cleft palate, and an unusual facial appearance. On the second day of life he develops jitteriness and a seizure; laboratory studies reveal a low serum calcium concentration. Deletion of which of the following chromosomal regions is the most likely cause?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5p

explanation.summary: Conotruncal cardiac defects with hypocalcemia and craniofacial anomalies point to a 22q11.2 deletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome) results from a ~3 Mb deletion on chromosome 22 and is characterized by craniofacial anomalies, conotruncal cardiac defects, immunodeficiency, and hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia and immunodeficiency reflect underdevelopment of the parathyroid glands and thymus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 4p16 deletion is associated with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome and is not the cause of this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5p deletion causes cri du chat syndrome, characterized by a high-pitched cry and microcephaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 7q11.23 deletion causes Williams syndrome, which features supravalvular aortic stenosis and hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 15q11 abnormalities are linked to Prader-Willi/Angelman syndromes, not the conotruncal-defect/hypocalcemia phenotype described.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is described by his parents as strikingly friendly with strangers. On examination he has a broad forehead, puffiness around the eyes, a flat nasal bridge, full cheeks, and a small chin. A systolic murmur is heard, and echocardiography reveals supravalvular aortic stenosis. Deletion of which chromosomal region best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5p

choices.label: E
choices.text: Xp22

explanation.summary: Elfin facies, overfriendliness, and supravalvular aortic stenosis indicate Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion).
explanation.whyCorrect: Williams syndrome results from a deletion at 7q11.23 affecting 25-27 genes. It is characterized by mild to moderate intellectual disability, distinctive 'elf-like' facial features, overfriendliness with a lack of social inhibition, hypercalcemia, and cardiovascular disease, most commonly supravalvular aortic stenosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5p deletion causes cri du chat syndrome, with microcephaly and a cat-like cry rather than these features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 17p11.2 abnormalities relate to other genomic syndromes and do not explain supravalvular aortic stenosis with overfriendliness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 22q11.2 deletion is associated with conotruncal cardiac defects and hypocalcemia, not supravalvular aortic stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Xp22 deletions are not the cause of the described Williams-syndrome phenotype.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Two unrelated patients are found to have deletions of nearly identical size and genomic location. This kind of recurrent structural variant is best explained by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single point mutation in a coding exon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nonallelic homologous recombination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining after a double-stranded break

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniparental disomy

explanation.summary: Recurrent structural variants arise from nonallelic homologous recombination, producing consistent size and location across unrelated people.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent structural variants are caused by nonallelic homologous recombination, unequal crossing over between misaligned chromatids or chromosomes that contain highly homologous sequences. Because these homologous stretches sit at consistent genomic sites, the resulting rearrangements have similar size and location in unrelated individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A point mutation alters a single base and does not delete a multi-gene chromosomal segment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining produces nonrecurrent variants with highly variable breakpoints, not recurrent ones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trinucleotide repeat expansion causes disorders like Huntington disease, not recurrent segmental deletions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uniparental disomy involves inheriting both homologs from one parent and does not create these recurrent deletions.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A structural variant is described as nonrecurrent, with breakpoints and deleted-segment size that differ from patient to patient and appear to occur at random. Which repair pathway is most likely responsible for this type of variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonallelic homologous recombination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair

explanation.summary: Nonrecurrent variants result from nonhomologous end joining, an error-prone repair of double-stranded breaks with variable breakpoints.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonrecurrent structural variants are caused by nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), the pathway that repairs double-stranded DNA breaks. Because NHEJ does not use a homologous template, it is inherently error-prone and can occur at random, giving rise to highly variable breakpoints.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair removes damaged single bases and is unrelated to double-strand-break rejoining.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair corrects base-pairing errors from replication and does not generate large deletions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonallelic homologous recombination produces recurrent variants of consistent size and location, the opposite of what is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions such as pyrimidine dimers, not chromosomal breakpoints.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is seen in the outpatient pediatrics clinic for follow-up, and the geneticist reports a 7q11.23 chromosomal microdeletion. Which of the following findings would you most expect to observe on examination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elf-like facial features and overfriendliness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flat epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequent infections and malformed thumbs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many bruises, low-grade fever, and weight loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microcephaly and a high-pitched cry

explanation.summary: A 7q11.23 microdeletion causes Williams syndrome, with elfin facies and an overfriendly personality.
explanation.whyCorrect: Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 7 (7q11.23). Its features include distinctive 'elf-like' facial features, mild to moderate intellectual disability, and a personality notable for overfriendliness and lack of social inhibition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Flat epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease are characteristic of Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Frequent infections and malformed thumbs are seen in Fanconi anemia, a defect in nonhomologous end joining DNA repair.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bruising, fever, and weight loss are nonspecific features of leukemia, which can arise from a chromosomal translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microcephaly and a high-pitched cry occur in cri du chat syndrome from a 5p deletion, not a 7q11.23 deletion.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A neonate with a 22q11.2 deletion is admitted with hypocalcemic tetany and is found to have severely reduced T-lymphocyte numbers. Underdevelopment of which structure best accounts for the immunodeficiency in this syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal cortex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bursa-equivalent lymphoid tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymus

explanation.summary: In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, thymic aplasia leads to T-cell immunodeficiency, and parathyroid hypoplasia causes hypocalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge) is remembered by the features of cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia. Failure of thymic development impairs T-lymphocyte maturation, producing the immunodeficiency, while parathyroid hypoplasia produces hypocalcemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal cortical dysfunction is not a feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow produces lymphoid precursors but is not the structure that fails in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome; the T-cell defect stems from thymic aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A bursa-equivalent controls B-cell development in birds; the T-cell immunodeficiency here is due to thymic, not B-cell, failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen contributes to immune function but its underdevelopment does not explain the T-cell deficiency of this syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A pediatrician is considering both Williams syndrome and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome in a young child with dysmorphic features and a heart murmur. Which feature would most specifically favor Williams syndrome over 22q11.2 deletion syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A conotruncal cardiac malformation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleft palate with velopharyngeal insufficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypocalcemia due to parathyroid hypoplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recurrent infections from thymic aplasia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supravalvular aortic stenosis

explanation.summary: Supravalvular aortic stenosis plus an overfriendly personality distinguishes Williams syndrome from 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although the two syndromes share overlapping features and are both on the differential, the most common congenital heart lesion differs: supravalvular aortic stenosis is characteristic of Williams syndrome, whereas conotruncal malformations are associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Overfriendliness and excessive empathy are also unique to Williams syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conotruncal malformations are associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, not Williams syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleft palate is part of the 22q11.2 deletion (velocardiofacial) phenotype rather than Williams syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypocalcemia is a feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome; Williams syndrome is associated with hypercalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunodeficiency from thymic aplasia is a hallmark of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, not Williams syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes why some subchromosomal variants are classified as recurrent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They always involve the same single nucleotide substitution in every patient

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion in every affected family studied

choices.label: C
choices.text: They arise only during mitosis in somatic cells after fertilization

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have highly variable breakpoints that differ between patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: They tend to occur at nearly the same location and size in unrelated patients

explanation.summary: Recurrent variants occur at nearly the same genomic location and size in unrelated individuals because they arise from consistently placed homologous sequences.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent variants occur in nearly the same location and size in unrelated patients. This consistency reflects nonallelic homologous recombination between highly similar stretches of DNA that lie at fixed genomic positions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recurrent structural variants involve segments of DNA, not a single nucleotide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recurrence refers to consistent genomic location across unrelated people, not a particular inheritance pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The recurrent mechanism relates to meiotic nonallelic homologous recombination, not exclusively somatic mitosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Highly variable breakpoints describe nonrecurrent variants caused by nonhomologous end joining.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Among the deletion syndromes discussed, which is best described as a nonrecurrent structural variant in which most cases are sporadic and the breakpoints and extent of the deletion are highly variable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cri du chat syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Klinefelter syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turner syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Williams syndrome

explanation.summary: Cri du chat is a nonrecurrent variant with sporadic cases and variable breakpoints, though a critical 5p region is deleted in all patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat syndrome is an example of a nonrecurrent chromosomal variant: most cases are sporadic and the breakpoints and extent of the deleted segment of 5p are highly variable. Research has nonetheless identified a critical region missing in all patients with the phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is a recurrent structural variant with a consistent ~3 Mb deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klinefelter syndrome is a numerical alteration (47,XXY), not a variable subchromosomal deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Turner syndrome is a numerical alteration (45,X), not a nonrecurrent deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Williams syndrome is also a recurrent variant, with a consistent 7q11.23 deletion.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A child with a confirmed chromosomal microdeletion syndrome is found to have an elevated serum calcium concentration. This laboratory finding is most consistent with which of the following syndromes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cri du chat syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Klinefelter syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turner syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Williams syndrome

explanation.summary: Hypercalcemia is characteristic of Williams syndrome, in contrast to the hypocalcemia of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) can have increased calcium levels in the blood. This helps distinguish it from 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, which is instead associated with hypocalcemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cri du chat syndrome is characterized by microcephaly and a high-pitched cry, not a distinctive calcium abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klinefelter syndrome is a numerical sex-chromosome disorder and is not defined by hypercalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Turner syndrome is a numerical sex-chromosome disorder and is not defined by hypercalcemia.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A cytogenetics report on a 4-year-old boy with developmental delay describes a segment of one chromosome that has been broken out and reinserted into the same chromosome in reversed orientation, with no net loss of genetic material. Which of the following terms best describes this subchromosomal structural variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deletion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duplication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insertion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inversion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Translocation

explanation.summary: A chromosomal segment that is flipped within its own chromosome is an inversion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromosomal rearrangements result in segments of chromosomes being misplaced: moved to another chromosome (translocation), deleted (deletion), or flipped (inversion). A flipped segment reinserted in reverse orientation in the same chromosome is an inversion. Because only part of a chromosome is affected, it is a subchromosomal variant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A deletion removes a segment, producing a net loss of genetic material, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A duplication produces an extra copy of a segment, a net gain of material.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An insertion adds a segment into a chromosome; it does not describe reversal of orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A translocation moves a segment to another chromosome rather than flipping it in place.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with developmental delay and dysmorphic features is found to carry a balanced translocation between two chromosomes. Genomic analysis shows no net gain or loss of DNA. Which of the following best explains how this balanced rearrangement can still produce a clinical phenotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duplication of the genes adjacent to each breakpoint

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halving of the dosage of every gene in the exchanged segments

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interaction between two gene regions that are normally separate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of an entire chromosome in subsequent cell divisions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of several hundred kilobases of DNA at a breakpoint

explanation.summary: Even a balanced translocation can cause disease by bringing together gene regions that are normally distinct in genomic location and function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shifting chromosomal material changes the way genes are expressed. A balanced translocation has the potential to cause problems if, for example, it causes interaction between two gene regions that would normally be distinct in genomic location and function, even though no material is gained or lost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced translocation does not duplicate genes; there is no net gain of material.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gene dosage is unchanged in a balanced exchange; the segments are moved, not lost.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Whole-chromosome loss is a numerical alteration and is not the mechanism by which a balanced translocation causes disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: By definition the rearrangement is balanced, with no net loss of DNA at the breakpoints.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA break in a germ cell is repaired by nonhomologous end joining. Given how this pathway operates, which of the following is the most likely consequence at the repair site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A deletion of fixed, predictable size is generated

choices.label: B
choices.text: A portion of DNA is lost or translocated

choices.label: C
choices.text: A rearrangement identical to that in unrelated patients forms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Missing sequence is copied from the homologous chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The break is restored precisely using the sister chromatid

explanation.summary: Nonhomologous end joining repairs double-stranded breaks without a template, so portions of DNA may be translocated or lost.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) is the pathway that repairs DNA damage caused by double-stranded breaks. Because a homologous template is not used, NHEJ is inherently error-prone, and portions of the DNA may be translocated or lost, producing nonrecurrent structural variants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NHEJ occurs at random and produces highly variable breakpoints, not deletions of fixed size.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rearrangements that recur identically in unrelated patients arise from nonallelic homologous recombination, not NHEJ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copying from the homologous chromosome describes template-based repair, not NHEJ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NHEJ does not use a sister chromatid or any homologous template, which is exactly why it is error-prone.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes line up and exchange pieces with one another. Which of the following best explains why this normal crossing over usually does not produce a genomic disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crossing over occurs only between identical sister chromatids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recombined chromosomes are eliminated before gametes form

choices.label: C
choices.text: The exchange occurs only in somatic cells and is not transmitted

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exchanged segments are immediately repaired by end joining

choices.label: E
choices.text: The swapped regions contain the same genes, so no material is gained or lost

explanation.summary: Normal homologous recombination swaps regions that carry the same genes, so there is usually no net gain or loss of genetic material.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crossing over, or homologous recombination, is a normal process in meiosis I. Because the regions of the homologous chromosomes that line up and switch places have the same genes, there is usually no net gain or loss of genetic material, and the process simply introduces genetic variability in the gametes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crossing over occurs between homologous chromosomes, not exclusively between sister chromatids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recombined chromosomes are not eliminated; they are the normal products of meiosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crossing over occurs during meiosis in germ cells and its products are transmitted in gametes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonhomologous end joining is a repair pathway for double-stranded breaks, not a step in normal crossing over.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A geneticist counsels the parents of a newborn recently diagnosed with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. The parents ask how common the condition is. Which of the following is the approximate frequency of this syndrome in live births?

explanation.summary: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is a fairly common recurrent structural variant, affecting around 1 in 3400 live births.
explanation.whyCorrect: 22q11.2 deletion is an example of a recurrent structural variant that is fairly common, affecting around 1 in 3400 live births. Its recurrent nature reflects nonallelic homologous recombination at a consistent genomic location.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1 in 10,000 understates how common this syndrome is.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1 in 1000 is more frequent than the stated prevalence of the syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1 in 2500 does not match the frequency given for 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1 in 700 overstates the frequency of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Genomic testing confirms 22q11.2 deletion syndrome in an infant with a conotruncal cardiac defect. Which of the following best characterizes the genomic alteration responsible for this syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ~3 kb deletion removing a single coding exon

choices.label: B
choices.text: A ~3 Mb deletion spanning several dozen genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: A ~30 Mb deletion removing most of the long arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: A ~300 bp deletion within a single gene promoter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of one entire copy of chromosome 22

explanation.summary: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome results from a ~3 Mb deletion that includes several dozen genes on one copy of chromosome 22.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deletion of approximately 3 Mb, a region that includes several dozen genes, on one copy of chromosome 22 causes 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. This multigene loss explains why the syndrome has many possible signs and symptoms affecting almost any part of the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 3 kb single-exon deletion is a single-gene event, far smaller than the multigene 22q11.2 deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 30 Mb deletion removing most of the long arm is ten times larger than the actual ~3 Mb deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 300 bp promoter deletion affects one gene and would not account for a several-dozen-gene syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of a whole chromosome is a numerical alteration; 22q11.2 deletion is a subchromosomal variant.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A medical student reviewing old records notes that one patient was labeled with "velocardiofacial syndrome" and another with "conotruncal anomaly face syndrome," whereas both are now diagnosed with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Which of the following best explains the change in terminology?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conditions were found to arise from deletions of different sizes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conditions were found to share the same genetic basis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conditions were reclassified as nonrecurrent variants

choices.label: D
choices.text: The older names described only the cardiac manifestations

choices.label: E
choices.text: The older names referred to numerical rather than structural alterations

explanation.summary: DiGeorge, velocardiofacial, and conotruncal anomaly face syndromes were unified as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome once they were recognized to share the same genetic basis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of the large variation in signs and symptoms, different groupings of features were originally described as different conditions, including DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome, and conotruncal anomaly face syndrome. Once it was recognized that they all share the same genetic basis, the terminology changed to 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The conditions were unified precisely because they share a common deletion, not because their deletions differ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 22q11.2 deletion is a recurrent structural variant; it was not reclassified as nonrecurrent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The older names captured various feature groupings such as palate and facial anomalies, not cardiac findings alone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The older names described the same subchromosomal deletion, not whole-chromosome numerical alterations.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with a conotruncal cardiac defect repaired in infancy, a cleft palate, and a history of recurrent infections is found to have a 22q11.2 deletion. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypercalcemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperkalemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypocalcemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypoglycemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hyponatremia

explanation.summary: Hypocalcemia is one of the most common features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and is the H in the CATCH-22 mnemonic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome include characteristic craniofacial anomalies, intellectual disability, immunodeficiency, heart defects (most often conotruncal), and hypocalcemia (low calcium levels). The CATCH-22 mnemonic captures cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia, and chromosome 22 deletion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypercalcemia is a feature of Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion), not 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperkalemia is not a characteristic finding of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypoglycemia is not among the features associated with this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyponatremia is not a recognized feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Molecular testing in a 5-year-old girl with supravalvular aortic stenosis confirms a deletion at 7q11.23. Approximately how many genes are affected by the deletion that causes this syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 to 3 genes

choices.label: B
choices.text: 25 to 27 genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Approximately 250 genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 1000 genes

explanation.summary: The Williams syndrome deletion at 7q11.23 affects 25-27 genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Williams syndrome, a deletion at a specific region on the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q11.23) affects 25-27 genes. Loss of this multigene segment underlies the intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, and cardiovascular problems of the syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The deletion involves far more than 2 to 3 genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Williams syndrome is a contiguous multigene deletion, not a single-gene disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Approximately 250 genes overstates the size of the 7q11.23 deletion by about tenfold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: More than 1000 genes would approach the gene content of an entire chromosome arm, far larger than the Williams deletion.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with Williams syndrome is starting elementary school. His parents ask what to expect regarding his cognitive abilities. Which of the following best describes the typical cognitive profile of this syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mild to moderate intellectual disability or learning problems

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal intelligence with no learning difficulties

choices.label: C
choices.text: Profound intellectual disability requiring total care

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive cognitive decline beginning in adolescence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe intellectual disability with absent language

explanation.summary: Williams syndrome is characterized by mild to moderate intellectual disability or learning problems.
explanation.whyCorrect: The phenotype of Williams syndrome is characterized by mild to moderate intellectual disability or learning problems, distinctive facial features, and increased risk of cardiovascular problems, especially supravalvular aortic stenosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Intellectual disability or learning problems are a core part of the Williams phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Profound intellectual disability requiring total care overstates the typical degree of impairment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Williams syndrome is a static developmental condition, not a progressive cognitive decline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The intellectual disability of Williams syndrome is mild to moderate, not severe with absent language.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Two unrelated children in different cities are each diagnosed with Williams syndrome. If the deletions in these two children were compared by genomic analysis, which of the following would most likely be found?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A deletion in one child and a duplication of the region in the other

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletions located on different chromosomes in the two children

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deletions nearly identical in size and location at 7q11.23

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deletions that differ widely in size and location on chromosome 7

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deletions with random breakpoints produced by end joining

explanation.summary: Williams syndrome is a recurrent variant, so the 7q11.23 deletion occurs at the same specific region in all patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Williams syndrome is a recurrent structural variant caused by a deletion at a specific region on the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q11.23). Recurrent variants arise from nonallelic homologous recombination at consistent genomic sites, so they have the same size and occur in the same genomic location in unrelated individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both children have Williams syndrome, which is caused by a deletion, not a duplication, of 7q11.23.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Williams syndrome always involves chromosome 7 at 7q11.23.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Widely varying size and location describe a nonrecurrent variant such as cri du chat, not Williams syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random breakpoints from nonhomologous end joining characterize nonrecurrent variants, not the recurrent Williams deletion.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy with microcephaly and a high-pitched cry is confirmed to have a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5. A murmur is noted on examination. Which of the following cardiac abnormalities is most characteristically associated with his syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bicuspid aortic valve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coarctation of the aorta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conotruncal malformation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supravalvular aortic stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ventricular septal defect

explanation.summary: Cri du chat syndrome (5p-) is associated with cardiac abnormalities such as ventricular septal defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cri du chat syndrome, a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 causes microcephaly, intellectual disability, a high-pitched cry, and an association with cardiac abnormalities such as ventricular septal defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bicuspid aortic valve is not the cardiac abnormality associated with cri du chat syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coarctation of the aorta is not the cardiac lesion linked to 5p deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conotruncal malformations are associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Supravalvular aortic stenosis is the characteristic cardiac lesion of Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion).

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: Genomic analysis of several unrelated patients with cri du chat syndrome shows that the breakpoints and the extent of the deleted segment on chromosome 5p differ substantially between patients, yet all share the characteristic phenotype. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A critical region of 5p is missing in every patient with the phenotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: All patients have lost the entire short arm of chromosome 5

choices.label: C
choices.text: The deleted segments are identical in size in every patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: The deletions are all generated by recombination at one fixed site

choices.label: E
choices.text: The phenotype is produced by the remaining intact chromosome 5

explanation.summary: Although cri du chat deletions are variable, research has identified a critical region of 5p that is missing in all patients with the phenotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat is a nonrecurrent chromosomal variant: most cases are sporadic and the breakpoints and extent of the deleted segment of chromosome 5p are highly variable. However, research has identified a critical region that is missing in all patients with the phenotype, which explains the shared clinical features despite variable deletions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The extent of the deletion varies; patients do not uniformly lose the entire short arm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem states that deletion size differs between patients; identical sizes describe recurrent variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombination at one fixed site would produce a recurrent variant with consistent breakpoints, the opposite of what is observed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The phenotype results from the missing material, not from the intact homolog.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A newborn girl with microcephaly and a high-pitched, cat-like cry undergoes genetic testing. The deletion responsible for her syndrome most often involves which of the following parts of chromosome 5?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The centromere itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: The entire chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pericentromeric region of the long arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: The terminal portion of the long arm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The terminal portion of the short arm

explanation.summary: Cri du chat syndrome results from deletion of the terminal portion of the p (short) arm of chromosome 5.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat (5p-) syndrome is caused by a nonrecurrent variant consisting of deletion of the terminal portion of the p arm of chromosome 5. It is associated with microcephaly, intellectual disability, a high-pitched cry, and cardiac abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The centromere is not the deleted segment in cri du chat syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of an entire chromosome is a numerical alteration; cri du chat is a subchromosomal deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The deletion is on the short (p) arm, not near the centromere on the long arm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The long arm is the q arm; cri du chat is a 5p, not 5q, deletion.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: The parents of an infant newly diagnosed with cri du chat syndrome ask whether the condition was passed down from one of them. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It arises from a recurrent deletion carried by one of the parents

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 5 in a parental gamete

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is inherited through mitochondrial DNA from the mother

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern from an affected parent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most cases are sporadic rather than inherited

explanation.summary: Cri du chat is a nonrecurrent variant in which most cases are sporadic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat is an example of a nonrecurrent chromosomal variant. Most cases are sporadic, and the breakpoints and extent of the deleted segment of chromosome 5p are highly variable, consistent with random double-stranded breaks repaired by nonhomologous end joining rather than a transmitted familial variant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cri du chat is a nonrecurrent variant; it is not a recurrent deletion carried by a parent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The syndrome results from a deletion of 5p, not an extra copy of chromosome 5.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cri du chat is a nuclear chromosomal deletion, not a mitochondrial disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Most cases are sporadic, not transmitted from an affected parent in a dominant pattern.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: After genetic testing returns 46,XX,5p- in a 1-month-old girl, her mother asks what the diagnosis means and whether it can be cured. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chromosome segment is flipped, and surgery restores normal development

choices.label: B
choices.text: A piece of genetic material is missing from one chromosome, and there is no cure

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single DNA base has changed, and enzyme replacement corrects it

choices.label: D
choices.text: An extra chromosome is present, and it can be removed with gene therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two genes have swapped chromosomes, and the symptoms resolve with age

explanation.summary: Cri du chat is a rare genetic condition in which a missing piece of chromosome 5 causes the syndrome; there is no cure, but ongoing supportive care is provided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cri du chat syndrome is explained to families as a rare genetic condition in which a genetic error leads to a missing piece of genetic material on one of the child's chromosomes (the short arm of chromosome 5). Although there is no cure, the physician commits to caring for the child and answering the family's questions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The segment is deleted, not inverted, and no surgery corrects the underlying genetic loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The alteration is a subchromosomal deletion of many genes, not a single base change treatable with enzyme replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cri du chat is a deletion, not an extra chromosome, and no gene therapy cure exists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The syndrome is a deletion, not a translocation, and its features do not resolve with age.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for frequent infections. On examination he has malformed thumbs. Fanconi anemia is diagnosed. The underlying defect in this condition impairs which of the following processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision of deaminated bases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair of replication errors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonallelic homologous recombination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining of DNA breaks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision of bulky adducts

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia, which presents with frequent infections and malformed thumbs, is a defect in nonhomologous end joining DNA repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frequent infections and malformed thumbs are physical findings in Fanconi anemia, a defect in nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) DNA repair. NHEJ is the pathway that repairs DNA damage caused by double-stranded breaks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair removes damaged single bases and is not the pathway affected in Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair corrects base-pairing errors and is not the pathway implicated in Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonallelic homologous recombination is a mechanism generating recurrent structural variants, not the repair defect of Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair handles bulky lesions and is not the defect in this condition.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with many bruises, a low-grade fever, and weight loss over several weeks. Evaluation leads to a diagnosis of leukemia. Which of the following categories of chromosomal alteration is a recognized cause of this malignancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aneuploidy from meiotic nondisjunction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromosomal translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Terminal deletion of a short arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniparental disomy

explanation.summary: Bruising, fever, and weight loss are nonspecific features of leukemia, which can be caused by a chromosomal translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased bruisability, fever, and weight loss are nonspecific features associated with leukemia, which can be caused by a chromosomal translocation. Translocations move a segment of one chromosome to another and can alter gene expression, including by bringing together gene regions that are normally distinct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Meiotic nondisjunction produces constitutional aneuploidy such as trisomy 21, which is not the alteration described for this leukemia presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Terminal short-arm deletion is the mechanism of cri du chat syndrome, not the described cause of leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trinucleotide repeat expansion is not a chromosomal rearrangement and is not the mechanism cited for leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uniparental disomy is not the chromosomal alteration associated with leukemia in this context.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A newborn boy has flat epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease. The chromosomal alteration responsible for his condition is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A numerical alteration (trisomy)

choices.label: C
choices.text: A subchromosomal deletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: A subchromosomal duplication

choices.label: E
choices.text: A subchromosomal inversion

explanation.summary: Flat epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease indicate Down syndrome, a numerical alteration (trisomy 21) rather than a subchromosomal variant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flat epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease are characteristic of Down syndrome caused by trisomy 21, an extra whole chromosome. Subchromosomal variants, by contrast, affect only a segment of a chromosome, as in the 22q11.2, 7q11.23, and 5p deletion syndromes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced translocation moves a segment without net gain or loss and is not the alteration described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Subchromosomal deletions cause syndromes such as 22q11.2 deletion, Williams, and cri du chat, not Down syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A duplication adds a copy of a segment, whereas Down syndrome involves an entire extra chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An inversion flips a chromosomal segment and does not produce trisomy 21.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A pediatric geneticist explains to residents that many genomic disorders caused by subchromosomal structural variants arise from a net gain or loss of DNA. On which of the following scales does the gained or lost DNA typically fall in these disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Entire chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hundreds of kilobases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hundreds of megabases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single nucleotides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tens of base pairs

explanation.summary: Many genomic disorders result from gain or loss of hundreds of kilobases of DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shifting or losing chromosomal material changes the way genes are expressed, and many genomic disorders result from gain or loss of hundreds of kilobases of DNA. This scale is large enough to include multiple genes (for example, the ~3 Mb, several-dozen-gene 22q11.2 deletion) yet affects only part of a chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gain or loss of an entire chromosome is a numerical alteration, not a subchromosomal variant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hundreds of megabases would exceed the size of most chromosomes, not a subchromosomal segment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Single-nucleotide changes are point mutations, not subchromosomal structural variants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tens of base pairs is far too small to constitute a structural variant that removes multiple genes.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A first-year medical student asks why homologous chromosomes exchange segments during meiosis I if the process carries a risk of producing structural variants. Which of the following best describes the normal biological benefit of this crossing over?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It ensures each gamete receives a full diploid set

choices.label: B
choices.text: It introduces genetic variability into the gametes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It prevents misalignment of homologous chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes mutated genes from the germline

choices.label: E
choices.text: It repairs double-stranded breaks without a template

explanation.summary: Crossing over in meiosis I is a normal process that increases offspring diversity by introducing genetic variability in the gametes.
explanation.whyCorrect: During meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes line up, pieces of the homologous chromosomes swap places and cross over. This homologous recombination is a normal process in meiosis that helps increase the diversity of offspring by introducing genetic variability in the gametes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gametes are haploid; crossing over does not provide a diploid set.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crossing over does not prevent misalignment; misaligned crossing over is in fact the cause of recurrent variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombination shuffles alleles but does not selectively remove mutated genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Template-free repair of double-stranded breaks describes nonhomologous end joining, not crossing over.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A recurrent 22q11.2 deletion arises during gametogenesis through nonallelic homologous recombination. In this process, unequal crossing over occurs between which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broken DNA ends rejoined without any homologous template

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous chromosomes correctly aligned at the same locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Misaligned chromatids that carry highly similar nonallelic sequences

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous chromosomes sharing no sequence similarity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sister chromatids paired at the identical allelic position

explanation.summary: Nonallelic homologous recombination is unequal crossing over between misaligned chromatids or chromosomes that contain highly homologous sequences that are not true homologs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Problems arise when crossing over happens between chromatids or chromosomes that have very similar stretches of sequence but are not actually homologs. Recurrent structural variants are caused by nonallelic homologous recombination, which is unequal crossing over between misaligned chromatids or chromosomes that contain highly homologous sequences. Because these similar stretches sit at consistent genomic positions, the resulting deletions have the same size and location in unrelated individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rejoining broken ends without a template describes nonhomologous end joining, the mechanism of nonrecurrent variants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correctly aligned homologous recombination is the normal, balanced crossing over of meiosis I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonallelic homologous recombination requires highly similar sequences; chromosomes with no sequence similarity would not recombine this way.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exchange between sister chromatids at the identical position is equal and produces no net gain or loss.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, and a heart murmur is being evaluated. Both Williams syndrome and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome are on the differential diagnosis. Which of the following findings is a feature of both syndromes and therefore does not help distinguish between them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Congenital heart defects

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypercalcemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overfriendliness with lack of social inhibition

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supravalvular aortic stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymic aplasia with immunodeficiency

explanation.summary: Both Williams and 22q11.2 deletion syndromes feature congenital heart disease; it is the specific lesion type, not the presence of heart disease, that discriminates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Due to overlapping phenotype features such as intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, and heart defects, 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and Williams syndrome may both be considered in a differential diagnosis. Heart disease is present in both; the differentiating point is the most common type: supravalvular aortic stenosis in Williams syndrome versus conotruncal malformations in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased blood calcium is specific to Williams syndrome; 22q11.2 deletion syndrome causes hypocalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Overfriendliness, excessive empathy, and lack of social inhibition are unique features of Williams syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Supravalvular aortic stenosis is the characteristic lesion of Williams syndrome and helps distinguish it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymic aplasia with immunodeficiency is a feature of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, not Williams syndrome.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: An infant is found to have a ~3 Mb deletion on one copy of chromosome 22 at band q11.2. Which of the following best describes the state of the genes within the deleted interval and the resulting basis for the clinical syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both copies of each gene are lost, so their products are absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both copies remain but are silenced by the rearrangement

choices.label: C
choices.text: One copy of each gene remains, causing altered gene dosage

choices.label: D
choices.text: The genes are duplicated, causing overexpression

choices.label: E
choices.text: The genes are inverted, disrupting their promoters

explanation.summary: The 22q11.2 deletion removes one copy of several dozen genes, and the syndrome reflects altered gene dosage for genes within the region.
explanation.whyCorrect: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is caused by deletion of ~3 Mb on one copy of chromosome 22, leaving a single copy of the genes in that interval. Subchromosomal abnormalities affect only a segment of a chromosome and cause genomic disorders related to altered gene dosage for one or more genes encoded within the region.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The deletion is on one copy of chromosome 22; the other homolog retains its copy of each gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The genes on the deleted homolog are physically lost, not merely silenced, and the remaining copy is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is caused by loss, not duplication, of the region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The variant is a deletion, not an inversion, so promoter disruption by flipping is not the mechanism.

questions.topicName: Numerical and Structural Chromosomal Alterations (2/3) - Subchromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A geneticist describes a patient whose body contains two cell populations that differ in genetic sequence but can both be traced back to the same fertilized egg. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aneuploidy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chimerism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mosaicism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nondisjunction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polyploidy

explanation.summary: Mosaicism is the presence in an individual of at least two genetically distinct cell lineages derived from a single zygote.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines mosaicism as the presence in an individual or tissue of at least two cell lineages that differ genetically but are derived from a single zygote. It arises from a post-conception genetic event during mitotic cell division, producing a clonal population of genetically distinct cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome number and is a type of mutation, not a description of two distinct lineages from one zygote.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chimerism describes cell populations that arise from two different zygotes, not a single one, so it fails the single-zygote criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nondisjunction is a mechanism that can cause mosaicism, but it names the event, not the coexistence of two lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polyploidy is having complete extra sets of chromosomes and does not describe coexisting genetically distinct lineages.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for delayed onset of puberty. Karyotype testing reveals 46,XX in approximately half of the cells examined and 45,X in the other half. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the two karyotypes observed in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Germline mosaicism was present in one of the parents

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meiotic nondisjunction in the oocyte produced a uniformly 45,X conceptus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mosaicism was present at fertilization and became generalized

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nondisjunction occurred in a single cell early in development

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nondisjunction occurred simultaneously in half the cells during early development

explanation.summary: Mosaicism (here, mosaic Turner syndrome) arises when a post-zygotic event in a single cell establishes a clonal lineage that coexists with the original line.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosaicism occurs when a genetic event, such as mitotic nondisjunction, happens in one cell that then continues to divide, giving rise to a clonal lineage. A single early nondisjunction event losing an X establishes a 45,X line that coexists with the 46,XX line, producing mosaic Turner syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Germline mosaicism in a parent transmits a mutation that would make the child fully (uniformly) affected, not mosaic with two karyotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Meiotic nondisjunction would yield a uniform 45,X karyotype in all cells, not a two-line mosaic pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mosaicism always arises after fertilization within the affected individual; it cannot be present at the moment of fertilization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simultaneous nondisjunction in many separate cells is far less likely than a single event that clonally expands to produce a large fraction of cells.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman reports muscle fatigue and weakness climbing stairs, with elevated serum creatine kinase. Neither parent nor her siblings are affected, but genetic testing shows she and her mother are both carriers of a pathogenic variant in the DMD gene (X-linked recessive Duchenne muscular dystrophy). Which of the following most likely explains the appearance of symptoms in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She has a de novo mutation in the second copy of the DMD gene on her other X

choices.label: B
choices.text: She has monosomy X (Turner syndrome), leaving only the mutant X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutation is imprinted and therefore always expressed from the maternal X

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pathogenic variant blocks X inactivation, so both X chromosomes express extra dystrophin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The X chromosome carrying the mutation is active in a high proportion of her muscle cells

explanation.summary: A manifesting heterozygote results when skewed X inactivation leaves the mutation-bearing X active in a large fraction of the relevant tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: By chance, X inactivation can be skewed so that the normal X is silenced in most muscle cells, leaving the mutant DMD X active in a high proportion of cells. Such a female carrier expresses the phenotype and is called a manifesting heterozygote.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A second-hit mutation would be detected on testing and would cause the full Duchenne phenotype rather than mild, carrier-level symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Turner syndrome would show a single X and additional systemic features; her karyotype and family testing point to a heterozygous carrier state.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DMD is not an imprinted gene; the partial expression is explained by the X-inactivation pattern, not imprinting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mutations in X-linked protein-coding genes do not prevent X inactivation, and reduced (not extra) dystrophin causes disease.

questions.stem: A couple with no signs of disease has two children who both carry the identical transition mutation in the FBN1 gene causing Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder. Detailed examination and blood-based genetic testing of both parents are negative for the mutation. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confined placental mosaicism affected both pregnancies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germline mosaicism is present in one of the parents

choices.label: C
choices.text: One parent carries the mutation but has non-penetrant disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: The condition is actually autosomal recessive in this family

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two independent de novo mutations coincidentally occurred in the children

explanation.summary: Unaffected parents with more than one child sharing the same dominant mutation suggest germline (gonadal) mosaicism in a parent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Germline mosaicism should be considered when unaffected parents have multiple affected offspring with the same mutation. A parent whose mutation is confined to the germline is phenotypically normal and tests negative in blood, yet transmits the FBN1 variant, so future offspring have an increased recurrence risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Confined placental mosaicism involves only extraembryonic tissue and would not transmit a mutation to the children themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both parents tested negative on genetic testing, so an unexpressed but present constitutional mutation is not supported.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant; a single mutant FBN1 allele is sufficient to cause disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two independent identical de novo mutations at the same site in siblings is exceedingly improbable and does not fit the shared identical variant.

questions.stem: An individual is found to have pure somatic mosaicism for a pathogenic mutation. Which of the following cell types would NOT be expected to carry the mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidney cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skeletal muscle cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skin cells

explanation.summary: In pure somatic mosaicism, only non-germline tissues can be affected; gametes are spared.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pure somatic mosaicism indicates that the mutation is present in some somatic tissues but not in the gametes. Oocytes are part of the germline and therefore would not carry the mutation, so the phenotype is not transmitted to offspring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood is a somatic tissue and can harbor the mutation in somatic mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kidney is a somatic tissue and may be affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skeletal muscle is a somatic tissue and may be affected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin is a somatic tissue and may be affected.

questions.stem: A couple's first child is diagnosed with segmental neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), with pigmentation changes and benign tumors restricted to only some tissues, indicating mosaicism for an NF1 mutation. NF1 is autosomal dominant with nearly complete penetrance, and neither parent has any phenotype. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding risk assessment for this family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All subsequent offspring of the parents will be affected with segmental NF1

choices.label: B
choices.text: The child's future offspring are at increased risk of having full (nonsegmental) NF1

choices.label: C
choices.text: The child's future offspring are at increased risk of having segmental NF1

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parents are at increased risk of having another child with full (nonsegmental) NF1

choices.label: E
choices.text: The parents are at increased risk of having another child with segmental NF1

explanation.summary: Segmental disease reflects a post-zygotic mutation; if the germline is involved, offspring inherit a constitutional mutation and develop the full disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: Segmental NF1 results from a post-zygotic mutation, so the parents are not at increased recurrence risk. Because germline involvement in the child cannot be excluded, the child may transmit the mutant allele; since NF1 is autosomal dominant, such offspring would have full (nonsegmental) NF1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mosaicism arose post-fertilization in the child; subsequent siblings are not obligately affected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Segmental disease requires a post-zygotic event in that individual; an inherited constitutional mutation produces full, not segmental, disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The parents did not transmit the mutation and are not at increased risk for either segmental or full NF1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutation arose after fertilization in the child, so the parents' recurrence risk is not increased.

questions.stem: During prenatal evaluation, chorionic villus sampling reveals a trisomic cell line, but follow-up amniocentesis and the newborn's karyotype are normal. The pregnancy was complicated by intrauterine growth restriction. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confined placental mosaicism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Constitutional trisomy of the fetus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal cell contamination of the sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pure germline mosaicism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic mosaicism in the fetus

explanation.summary: Confined placental mosaicism is an abnormal cell line limited to extraembryonic tissue, sometimes causing delayed fetal growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: In confined placental mosaicism, the mutation or aneuploidy is found only in extraembryonic tissue and not in the embryo proper. It can result in a normal outcome or, with trisomy mosaicism, delayed fetal growth, matching the trisomic villi with a normal fetus and growth restriction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Constitutional trisomy would be present in fetal cells and the neonate, whose karyotypes were normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal contamination would typically produce a normal maternal karyotype, not a trisomic line, and does not explain growth restriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pure germline mosaicism is restricted to gametes and would not appear in placental villi or cause fetal growth restriction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic mosaicism in the fetus would be detectable in fetal-derived cells such as amniocytes, which were normal here.

questions.stem: The X inactivation center contains an unusual non-coding RNA gene that acts as a master regulator of X inactivation. It is expressed from the allele on the inactive X and produces a long RNA that remains in the nucleus coating that chromosome. Which of the following genes is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DMD

choices.label: B
choices.text: FBN1

choices.label: C
choices.text: FMR1

choices.label: D
choices.text: SRY

choices.label: E
choices.text: XIST

explanation.summary: XIST is the non-coding RNA master regulator that silences the inactive X.
explanation.whyCorrect: The X inactivation center contains XIST, an unusual non-coding RNA gene expressed from the inactive X. Its long ncRNA stays in the nucleus in close association with the inactive X and drives epigenetic silencing of most of its genes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DMD encodes dystrophin and is an X-linked disease gene, not the master regulator of inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1 and is associated with Marfan syndrome, unrelated to X inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FMR1 is the fragile X gene, an X-linked protein-coding gene, not the inactivation regulator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SRY is the Y-linked testis-determining gene and has no role in X inactivation.

questions.stem: A buccal smear from a phenotypic female shows a single condensed heterochromatic mass at the periphery of the nucleus in interphase cells. This structure most directly represents which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A condensed Y chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clumped autosomal heterochromatin

choices.label: C
