choices.text: The inactive X chromosome (Barr body)

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nucleolus (rRNA synthesis site)

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transcriptionally active X chromosome

explanation.summary: The Barr body is the cytologically visible inactive X in interphase cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytologically, the inactive X chromosome is visible as a heterochromatic mass called the Barr body in interphase cells. It reflects the epigenetically silenced, condensed inactive X.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single Barr body indicates one inactivated X in a female; it is not a Y chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mass specifically corresponds to the inactivated X, not generic autosomal heterochromatin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleolus is a distinct organelle associated with ribosomal RNA synthesis, not the inactivated X.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The active X remains euchromatic and is not seen as a condensed peripheral mass.

questions.stem: A patient has 46 chromosomes with one structurally abnormal X (an isochromosome). Studies show that in nearly all of her cells the same (abnormal) X chromosome is inactivated, rather than a random pattern. Which of the following best explains this nonrandom inactivation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genomic imprinting silences all structurally abnormal chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Random inactivation always preferentially silences the paternal X

choices.label: C
choices.text: Selection against genetically unbalanced cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The abnormal X lacks a functional centromere

choices.label: E
choices.text: The XIST gene is present only on the normal X chromosome

explanation.summary: Skewed inactivation of a structurally abnormal X reflects postnatal selection against genetically unbalanced cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The initial inactivation event early in development is random, but in nearly all patients with unbalanced structural X abnormalities the abnormal chromosome is the inactive X. The observed skew reflects selection against genetically unbalanced cells that have reduced viability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imprinting affects a small subset of specific genes and does not silence whole abnormal chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Random X inactivation does not systematically favor the paternal X; typical distributions are roughly balanced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The chromosome is described as an X with a structural abnormality that persists in cells; a missing centromere is not the mechanism given.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pattern is driven by cell selection, not by absence of XIST from the abnormal X.

questions.stem: A child has somatic mosaicism for an autosomal dominant disorder, with some tissues affected and others normal. Regarding this child's own future reproductive risk, which of the following is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All of the child's offspring will be mosaic like the child

choices.label: B
choices.text: Risk exists only if the child's future partner is also a carrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Risk is zero because the mutation arose after fertilization

choices.label: D
choices.text: The child is at increased risk of having fully affected offspring

choices.label: E
choices.text: There is no reproductive risk because mosaicism is never heritable

explanation.summary: A mosaic individual is at increased risk of fully affected offspring because their germ cells may also carry the mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Somatic mosaicism confirms the mutation is present in some tissues, but it does not tell us whether the germline is involved. Because germ cells may carry the mutation, the child is at increased risk of transmitting the mutant allele, and for an autosomal dominant disorder such offspring would be fully affected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Offspring inheriting a constitutional mutation would be fully affected, not mosaic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: For an autosomal dominant disorder, a single transmitted mutant allele is sufficient; a carrier partner is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A post-fertilization event can still affect germ cells, so the risk is not zero.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mosaicism can involve the germline, so it is not universally non-heritable.

questions.stem: A child has features of Down syndrome that are subtler than typically expected. Karyotype analysis shows two cell lines: some cells with trisomy 21 and some with normal disomy 21. Compared with a child with full (nonmosaic) trisomy 21, this child is most likely to have which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A consistently more severe phenotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: A phenotype only if the germline is involved

choices.label: C
choices.text: A typically less severe phenotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: An identical phenotype in all cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: No phenotype whatsoever

explanation.summary: Mosaic Down syndrome, a mixture of disomic and trisomic cells, typically produces a less severe phenotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosaic Down syndrome is a mixture of cells that are disomic and trisomic for chromosome 21, seen in about 1-3% of trisomy 21 live births. These individuals typically have a less severe phenotype because a proportion of cells have the normal chromosome complement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The presence of normal disomic cells generally lessens, rather than worsens, the phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The somatic trisomic cell line drives the phenotype; germline involvement is not required for features to appear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phenotype is variable and usually milder, not identical to full trisomy 21.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomic cells are present, so an affected phenotype is still expected, just typically milder.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is found to have a clonal population of skin cells carrying a single-nucleotide substitution that is absent from her blood. Her sister has a clonal population of cells carrying an extra copy of an entire chromosome that is likewise absent from her other tissues. A medical student asks whether both findings qualify as mosaicism. Which of the following best describes the range of post-conception genetic events that can give rise to mosaicism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anything from a nondisjunction event to a single-gene mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only events that occur in a parental gamete before fertilization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only nondisjunction events that change whole-chromosome number

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only single-nucleotide substitutions within protein-coding genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only structural rearrangements such as deletions and duplications

explanation.summary: The post-conception event that produces mosaicism can lie anywhere on the mutation size spectrum, from nondisjunction to a single-gene mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosaicism can affect any cells or tissue within a developing embryo or at any point after conception. The genetic event that gives rise to it can happen anywhere along the mutation size spectrum, from a nondisjunction event that alters chromosome number all the way down to a single-gene mutation, so both sisters' findings are forms of mosaicism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mosaicism is defined by an event after conception in a single zygote's descendants, not by an event in a parental gamete.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nondisjunction is only one end of the spectrum; single-gene mutations also produce mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Point mutations are only the small end of the spectrum; whole-chromosome changes also produce mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Structural rearrangements are not the only possibility; the spectrum includes aneuploidy and single-gene mutations.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes genetic testing on multiple tissues as part of a research study. A clonal population of blood cells carries a point mutation that is absent from his skin fibroblasts, oral mucosa, and skeletal muscle. He asks whether such a genetic difference between his tissues must have originated during embryonic development. Which of the following best describes when a post-conception genetic event giving rise to mosaicism can occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At any point after conception, prenatally or postnatally

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after birth, once tissues are fully differentiated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only before the germline separates from somatic lineages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only during meiosis in the parental germline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only during the first few cleavage divisions of the zygote

explanation.summary: Mosaicism-producing events can happen prenatally or postnatally, at any point from conception to adulthood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genetic events that occur after conception in a single cell go on to give rise to daughter cells that are genetically different from the original zygote, and these events can happen prenatally or postnatally. Mosaicism can affect any cells or tissue within a developing embryo or at any point after conception to adulthood, which is why adults are in reality genetic mosaics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prenatal events are a common source of mosaicism; postnatal timing is not a requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Events after lineage separation still produce mosaicism, such as pure somatic or pure germline mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A meiotic event in a parent produces a uniformly affected conceptus, not mosaicism, which requires a post-conception event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Early cleavage divisions are one possible time, but mosaicism can arise much later, including after birth.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has mild hypotonia and a few subtle dysmorphic features. Karyotype analysis of peripheral blood reveals that some cells have trisomy 21 and others have a normal chromosome complement. Her parents ask how often Down syndrome takes this mosaic form. Approximately what proportion of trisomy 21 live births are mosaic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 0.1%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 0.5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 1-3%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 10-15%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 25%

explanation.summary: Mosaic Down syndrome is seen in about 1-3% of trisomy 21 live births.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosaic Down syndrome is a mixture of cells that are disomic and trisomic for chromosome 21. It is seen in 1-3% of trisomy 21 live births, and these individuals typically have a less severe phenotype than those with full trisomy 21.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mosaicism is not this rare among trisomy 21 live births; the stated figure is 1-3%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This underestimates the frequency; the stated figure is 1-3%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overestimates the frequency; the stated figure is 1-3%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The large majority of trisomy 21 live births are nonmosaic; mosaicism accounts for only 1-3%.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with mild developmental delay and subtle facial features of Down syndrome has a karyotype showing two cell lines: 47,XY,+21 in 30% of cells and 46,XY in 70% of cells. During which of the following processes did the nondisjunction event responsible for this pattern most likely occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mitotic division in the early embryo

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal meiosis I in the developing oocyte

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal meiosis II at the time of ovulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Meiosis in the child's own germline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paternal meiosis I during spermatogenesis

explanation.summary: Mosaic Down syndrome arises from nondisjunction of chromosome 21 during mitotic divisions in the early embryo.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosaic Down syndrome is a mixture of disomic and trisomic cells for chromosome 21. It arises due to nondisjunction events involving chromosome 21 during mitotic divisions in the early embryo, which establishes a trisomic clonal lineage alongside the normal line.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A meiotic error in the mother would make every cell of the conceptus trisomic, producing nonmosaic Down syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal meiosis II nondisjunction likewise yields a uniformly trisomic zygote, not two cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The child's own germline meiosis affects his gametes, not the karyotype of his somatic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A paternal meiotic error would produce a uniformly trisomic conceptus rather than a mosaic one.

questions.stem: A genetics textbook divides mosaicism into confined placental mosaicism, pure somatic mosaicism, pure germline mosaicism, and combined somatic-plus-germline mosaicism. Which of the following is the basis for this classification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The severity of the resulting clinical phenotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: The size of the mutation, from aneuploidy to point mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tissues in which the mutant cell lineage is present

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether an autosome or a sex chromosome is involved

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the event occurred before or after birth

explanation.summary: Types of genetic mosaicism are classified according to the tissues affected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Different types of genetic mosaicism are classified depending on the tissues affected: confined placental (extraembryonic tissue only), pure somatic (some embryonic tissues but not gametes), pure germline (gamete lineage only), and combinations (somatic lineages plus germline).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenotype severity varies within each category and is a consequence, not the basis, of the classification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mutation size ranges from nondisjunction to single-gene mutation within any type; it does not define the categories.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The chromosome involved is not the basis; any of the types can involve any chromosome or gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prenatal versus postnatal timing does not define these categories; all four are defined by tissue distribution.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation undergoes chorionic villus sampling because of advanced maternal age. Analysis of the villus stroma shows a mosaic trisomic cell line. Follow-up amniocentesis at 16 weeks shows a normal fetal karyotype in all cells examined. In which of the following cell populations did the abnormal lineage most likely originate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A maternal decidual cell contaminating the villus specimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: A primordial germ cell of the developing fetal gonad

choices.label: C
choices.text: A somatic cell of the embryo proper shortly after gastrulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A trophoblast cell or a non-fetal cell of the inner cell mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: The single-cell zygote, before its first mitotic division

explanation.summary: Confined placental mosaicism arises from a mutation in a trophoblastic cell or in non-fetal cells of the inner cell mass, often confined to the chorionic villus stroma.
explanation.whyCorrect: In confined placental mosaicism the mutation is found only in extraembryonic tissue and not in the embryo proper. Such mutations might arise in a trophoblastic cell or in non-fetal cells of the inner cell mass, where they are often confined to the chorionic villus stroma, which fits a trisomic line in villi with a normal fetal karyotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Maternal cells would show a normal maternal karyotype and would not account for a trisomic cell line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A primordial germ cell mutation produces germline mosaicism in the fetus and would not appear in placental villi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mutation in the embryo proper would produce fetal somatic mosaicism and be detectable in amniocytes, which were normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A zygote-level event would make the entire conceptus, including the fetus, trisomic rather than confined to the placenta.

questions.stem: Two pregnancies are each found on chorionic villus sampling to have confined placental mosaicism, with normal fetal karyotypes confirmed on amniocentesis. In pregnancy 1, the placental cell line is trisomic for an autosome. In pregnancy 2, the placental cell line carries a single-gene point mutation. Which of the following outcomes is most likely to differ between the two pregnancies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal outcome is possible only in pregnancy 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delayed fetal growth is more likely in pregnancy 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delayed fetal growth is more likely in pregnancy 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Germline of fetus 2 will carry the point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic tissues of fetus 1 will carry the trisomic line

explanation.summary: Delayed fetal growth with confined placental mosaicism is most likely related to trisomy mosaicism, not a single-gene mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Confined placental mosaicism can result in a normal pregnancy outcome or is sometimes associated with delayed growth of the fetus. Delayed growth would most likely be related to trisomy mosaicism rather than a single-gene mutation, so the trisomic placental line in pregnancy 1 carries the greater risk of growth delay.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A normal pregnancy outcome is possible with either form of confined placental mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single-gene mutation confined to the placenta is the scenario least likely to impair fetal growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mutation is confined to extraembryonic tissue and is not present in the fetus or its germline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: By definition, confined placental mosaicism spares the embryo proper; the fetal karyotype was normal.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor explains to a couple why a mutation can be present in a parent's gametes but nowhere else in that parent's body. She notes that the germline undergoes many mitotic divisions before meiosis, providing ample opportunity for mutation after germ cells separate from somatic cells. Which of the following best describes the approximate number of mitotic divisions in the germline before meiosis in females and males, respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 3 in females and about 30 in males

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 30 in both females and males

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 30 in females and several hundred in males

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several hundred in females and about 30 in males

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several thousand in both females and males

explanation.summary: Roughly 30 germline mitotic divisions precede meiosis in females and several hundred in males, allowing pure gonadal mosaicism to arise.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are approximately 30 mitotic divisions in the cells of the germline before meiosis in the female and several hundred in the male. This gives ample opportunity for mutations to occur in germline cells after their separation from somatic cells, resulting in pure gonadal mosaicism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates both sexes; the female figure is about 30 and the male figure is several hundred.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The male germline undergoes several hundred divisions, many more than the female germline.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the sexes; the male germline undergoes far more divisions than the female germline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This overstates the number of divisions in both sexes.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with no clinical features of an autosomal dominant disorder has fathered two children with the same pathogenic variant; the variant is not detectable in his blood, skin, or buccal cells. Pure germline (gonadal) mosaicism is diagnosed. Which of the following statements about the timing of the mutational event in this man is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It occurred after somatic and germline lineages had separated

choices.label: B
choices.text: It occurred before the inner cell mass had formed

choices.label: C
choices.text: It occurred in a somatic cell after birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurred in one of his parents' gametes before his conception

choices.label: E
choices.text: It occurred in the zygote before the first cleavage division

explanation.summary: Pure germline mosaicism must arise after somatic and germline cells have separated lineages.
explanation.whyCorrect: In pure germline mosaicism the mutation is restricted to the gamete lineage only and nowhere else. Such mosaicism must arise after somatic and germline cells have separated lineages, so that the mutation is confined to germ cells while somatic tissues such as blood, skin, and buccal cells remain unaffected.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A mutation before the inner cell mass formed would affect both somatic and germline descendants, not the germline alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A postnatal somatic mutation would not enter the gamete lineage and could not be transmitted to two children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mutation in a parental gamete would be constitutional, present in all of his cells, and would make him affected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A zygotic mutation would be present in every cell, including somatic tissues that tested negative.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has a patch of cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas limited to his left shoulder. Genetic testing detects an NF1 mutation at low levels in skin from the affected area and also in his blood. He later fathers a daughter who has generalized (nonsegmental) NF1 with the same mutation. Which of the following best explains why both his somatic tissues and his germline carry the mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mutation arose before somatic and germline lineages separated

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutation arose in a primordial germ cell after lineage separation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutation arose in a skin stem cell after birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutation arose in a trophoblast cell of the early conceptus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutation was inherited from a parent with germline mosaicism

explanation.summary: Combined somatic and germline mosaicism results when the mutation occurs before the separation of the inner cell mass, germline cells, and somatic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosaicism can involve both somatic lineages and the germline in the same person. Whether this combination occurs depends on whether the mutation occurred before or after the separation of the inner cell mass, the germline cells, and the somatic cells during embryogenesis; a mutation before that separation seeds both compartments, so the individual is affected and can produce fully affected offspring.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A mutation in a primordial germ cell after lineage separation would give pure germline mosaicism with no somatic involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A postnatal skin mutation would not reach the blood or the germline and could not be transmitted to a child.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A trophoblast mutation produces confined placental mosaicism and does not enter the embryo proper or germline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inheriting the mutation would make him constitutionally (fully) affected, not mosaic with a localized patch.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has hypopigmented streaks on the skin of her right leg and trunk. A somatic mutation is suspected, but sequencing of DNA from peripheral blood does not detect a pathogenic variant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to evaluate the presence and extent of somatic mosaicism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic testing of samples from multiple different tissue types

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotype analysis of both parents' peripheral blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat sequencing of peripheral blood leukocytes in one year

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequencing of DNA from the parents' buccal mucosal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequencing of DNA from the patient's own placenta stored at birth

explanation.summary: The presence and extent of somatic mosaicism is evaluated by genetic testing on samples of multiple different tissue types.
explanation.whyCorrect: Differentiating between the types of mosaicism can be tricky because a mosaic mutation may be present in some tissues and absent from others. The presence and extent of somatic mosaicism can be evaluated using genetic testing on samples of multiple different tissue types, such as affected skin, rather than relying on a single negative blood sample.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The parents are unaffected and the question concerns the child's own tissue distribution; parental karyotypes do not address it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mosaic mutation absent from blood will not appear on a repeat blood sample; the distribution across tissues is what matters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parental buccal cells do not evaluate the child's somatic tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Placental tissue reflects extraembryonic lineages and does not define which of the child's own tissues are affected.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor tells a medical student that the possibility of germline mosaicism in an unaffected parent must be especially considered when a child presents with an autosomal dominant or X-linked disorder. Which of the following best explains this emphasis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only one mutated allele is sufficient to cause these disorders

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recessive disorders cannot be produced by mosaic parents

choices.label: C
choices.text: These disorders have the highest germline mutation rates

choices.label: D
choices.text: These disorders never arise from new mutations in the child

choices.label: E
choices.text: These genes lie on chromosomes with more mitotic divisions

explanation.summary: Germline mosaicism matters most in autosomal dominant and X-linked disorders because a single mutated allele transmitted from a mosaic parent is enough to cause disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The possibility of germline mosaicism must especially be considered with autosomal dominant or X-linked disorders because only one mutated allele is sufficient to cause the disorder. A phenotypically normal parent whose gametes carry the mutation can therefore produce an affected child from a single transmitted allele.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mosaicism can involve any gene; the emphasis reflects that one transmitted allele is sufficient in dominant and X-linked conditions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rationale is about how many mutant alleles are needed for disease, not about differing mutation rates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: De novo mutations in the child are common in these disorders; the point is that mosaicism is an alternative explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The number of germline mitotic divisions depends on the sex of the parent, not on the chromosome carrying the gene.

questions.stem: Unaffected parents bring their 6-year-old son for evaluation of an autosomal dominant skin disorder that affects only patches of skin on his left arm and back; genetic testing shows the mutation in affected skin but not in blood. Which of the following conclusions about the parents is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Germline mosaicism in a parent would have produced a fully affected child

choices.label: B
choices.text: One parent inherited the mutation but shows complete non-penetrance

choices.label: C
choices.text: One parent must carry the same mutation in somatic mosaic form in the skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their risk of a second affected child is 25% in every pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their risk of a second affected child is 50% in every pregnancy

explanation.summary: A mosaic child cannot have received the mutation from a parent's germline, because a transmitted mutation produces a fully affected child; the parents' recurrence risk equals the population risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: With unaffected parents and a child with somatic mosaicism, neither parent inherited the mutation, and neither has germline mosaicism for it, because if they had, the child would be fully affected rather than mosaic. The mutation arose post-conception in the child, so the parents' risk of having a second affected child is the same as the population risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Both parents tested negative in blood and show no phenotype; a transmitted mutation would also have made the child fully affected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The child's patchy involvement indicates a post-conception event in the child; a parental mosaic mutation is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 25% risk applies to carrier parents of a recessive disorder, which is not the situation here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 50% recurrence risk applies to a constitutionally affected parent, not to unaffected parents of a mosaic child.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with no signs of disease has germline mosaicism for an autosomal dominant disorder; a fraction of his sperm carry the mutation. He fathers a daughter who inherits the mutation and is affected. When the daughter reaches reproductive age, what proportion of her gametes is expected to carry the mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A small fraction, as in her father's sperm

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 25%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 50%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 75%

choices.label: E
choices.text: None, as in her father's somatic tissues

explanation.summary: Offspring of a germline mosaic parent who inherit the mutation carry it constitutionally, so half of their gametes carry it.
explanation.whyCorrect: In germline mosaicism, the first-generation parent carries the mutation in only a fraction of germ cells. A child conceived from a mutant gamete carries the mutation in the entire organism, and in that second generation half of the gametes carry the mutation, as for any constitutional heterozygous mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fractional involvement applies only to the mosaic parent; the daughter's every cell, including germ cells, carries the mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A heterozygous individual transmits the mutant allele to half, not one quarter, of gametes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A heterozygous individual transmits the mutant allele to half, not three quarters, of gametes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The daughter inherited the mutation constitutionally, so her germline is fully involved, unlike a somatic-only mosaic.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait macules restricted to one region of the right thigh, consistent with segmental neurofibromatosis. Her parents are unaffected. Which of the following best describes the earliest point in development at which the causative mutation could have arisen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the two-cell stage of embryonic development or later

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a parental gamete before fertilization occurred

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the zygote before its first mitotic division

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only after birth, in a terminally differentiated skin cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only after the completion of organogenesis in utero

explanation.summary: Segmental disease reflects mosaicism, which can only arise from a mutation at the two-cell stage of embryonic development or later.
explanation.whyCorrect: Segmental neurofibromatosis is a result of mosaicism, and the mechanism confining the phenotype to one anatomic location is genetic mosaicism. Mosaicism can only arise from a mutation that occurs in a cell at the two-cell stage of embryonic development or later, because an event any earlier would be present in every descendant cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A gametic mutation would be constitutional and produce full, nonsegmental disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mutation in the single-cell zygote is inherited by all cells, producing full disease rather than a segmental pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Postnatal events are possible but far from the earliest point at which mosaicism can arise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A mutation after organogenesis is possible but is not the earliest point; the two-cell stage is the earliest.

questions.stem: A researcher compares expression levels of X-linked genes in fibroblasts from a 46,XX individual and a 46,XY individual and finds they are approximately equal, despite the 46,XX cells having two X chromosomes. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Female cells degrade half of their X-linked mRNA transcripts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Male cells duplicate their single X before transcription

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most genes on one X chromosome are silenced as dosage compensation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Y chromosome carries copies of most X-linked genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked genes in females are transcribed at half the rate per allele

explanation.summary: X inactivation is a dosage compensation mechanism that silences most genes on all but one X chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: X inactivation is a normal physiological process in which most of the genes on all but one X chromosome are inactivated (silenced) in somatic cells. Inactivation of extra X chromosomes is a form of dosage compensation that ensures X-chromosomal genes are not expressed at proportionally higher levels compared with XY males.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dosage compensation acts at the level of chromosome inactivation, not by degrading transcripts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Males do not duplicate their X; females silence one of theirs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Y chromosome does not duplicate the X gene content; equal expression comes from silencing one X in females.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Compensation is achieved by silencing one whole X, not by halving transcription from each allele.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated for tall stature and small testes. Karyotype analysis shows 47,XXY. Which of the following best describes X chromosome inactivation in his somatic cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both X chromosomes are inactivated

choices.label: B
choices.text: No X inactivation occurs because he is phenotypically male

choices.label: C
choices.text: One X chromosome is inactivated and appears as a Barr body

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Y chromosome is inactivated instead of an X chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: X inactivation occurs only in his germ cells

explanation.summary: X inactivation occurs in all individuals with more than one X chromosome, silencing all but one X.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inactivation process occurs in all individuals with greater than one X chromosome, silencing most genes on all but one X in somatic cells. A 47,XXY individual therefore inactivates one X, and the inactive X is cytologically visible as a heterochromatic Barr body in interphase cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One X always remains active; only the 'extra' X chromosomes are inactivated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inactivation depends on the number of X chromosomes, not on sexual phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dosage compensation silences extra X chromosomes; the Y is not the target of this process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X inactivation is described in somatic cells, not restricted to the germline.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a structurally abnormal X chromosome in which the region containing the X inactivation center has been deleted; her other X chromosome is normal. Which of the following best predicts the pattern of X-linked gene expression in her somatic cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both X chromosomes are inactivated in every somatic cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both X chromosomes remain active, giving biallelic gene expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inactivation is random, giving a mosaic ratio near 50:50

choices.label: D
choices.text: The abnormal X is preferentially inactivated in nearly all somatic cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The normal X is preferentially inactivated in nearly all cells

explanation.summary: The X inactivation center is required for X inactivation; an X lacking it cannot be silenced, so both X chromosomes stay active with biallelic expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: X inactivation is under control of the X inactivation center (XIC), which contains XIST; the XIC is required for normal X chromosome inactivation. When an abnormal X lacks the XIC, no X inactivation of that chromosome occurs, and instead of monoallelic expression there is biallelic gene expression from both X chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At least one X always remains active, and here the abnormal X cannot be inactivated at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random inactivation requires that either X be capable of inactivation, which the XIC-deleted X is not.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preferential inactivation of an abnormal X applies to unbalanced structural abnormalities that retain the XIC; without the XIC the chromosome cannot be inactivated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: One X must remain active; the normal X is not silenced simply because the other cannot be.

questions.stem: A cytogenetics laboratory examines interphase nuclei from a 46,XX patient and identifies a condensed heterochromatic mass at the nuclear periphery. Which of the following molecular features would most likely distinguish this chromosome from its active homolog?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of the XIST gene from its inactivation center

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletion of most of its protein-coding genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA methylation and modified histone proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased transcription of most of its genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of its centromeric DNA sequence

explanation.summary: The inactive X is distinguished from the active X by epigenetic marks, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and a specific histone variant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many epigenetic features distinguish the active and inactive X chromosomes, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and a specific histone variant. These marks underlie the epigenetic silencing of most genes on the inactive X, which is visible cytologically as the Barr body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: XIST is present and expressed from the inactive X; its absence would prevent inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genes on the inactive X are silenced, not deleted; the DNA sequence is the same as the active X.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The inactive X shows silencing of most genes, not increased transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The inactive X is a structurally intact chromosome; inactivation is epigenetic, not a loss of DNA sequence.

questions.stem: A study of gene expression in female fibroblasts finds that approximately 15% of X chromosome genes are expressed to some extent from both the active and the inactive X. Genes that escape inactivation in this way are preferentially located in which of the following regions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immediately adjacent to the XIST gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distal region of the long (q) arm

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distal region of the short (p) arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pericentromeric region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the X inactivation center

explanation.summary: About 15% of X-linked genes escape inactivation, and these are preferentially located near the distal Xp region.
explanation.whyCorrect: Not all genes on the inactivated X chromosome are silenced; approximately 15% of X chromosome genes are expressed from both active and inactive X chromosomes to some extent. These genes are preferentially located near the distal Xp region, the far end of the short p arm of the X chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escape genes are preferentially at distal Xp, not adjacent to XIST.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The distal long arm is not the described location; escape genes cluster on the distal short arm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Escape genes cluster at the distal short arm, not around the centromere.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The X inactivation center houses XIST, the master regulator of silencing, not the cluster of escaping genes.

questions.stem: A 46,XX woman who is a carrier for an X-linked disorder undergoes an X inactivation study on peripheral blood. The proportion of cells expressing the maternal versus the paternal X is 35:65. Which of the following best describes how this result compares with the general female population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is highly skewed; about 90% of females fall between 45:55 and 55:45

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is highly skewed; nearly all females are exactly 50:50

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is unusual; most females show complete inactivation of the paternal X

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is within the typical range; about 90% of females fall between 25:75 and 75:25

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is within the typical range; about 90% of females fall between 5:95 and 95:5

explanation.summary: Most females fall within an X inactivation ratio range of about 25:75 to 75:25, the expected spread for a random event.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most females have approximately equal proportions of cells expressing alleles from the maternal or paternal X and fall within a range that extends from about 25:75 to about 75:25, encompassing roughly 90% of females. Such a distribution reflects the expected range of outcomes for a random event, so a 35:65 ratio is typical.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The typical range is much wider than 45:55 to 55:45; 35:65 is not skewed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: X inactivation is a random event with a spread of outcomes; most females are not exactly 50:50.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In typical females the choice of inactivated X is random, not consistently paternal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ratios near 5:95 or 95:5 are the extreme tails, not the range containing 90% of females.

questions.stem: A geneticist notes that a small subset of X-linked genes is imprinted. Which of the following best describes the expression of such a gene across the somatic cells of a 46,XX individual?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is expressed from both X chromosomes in every cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is expressed from the paternal X in some cells and the maternal X in others

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is expressed only in cells where the Barr body is absent

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is silenced on both X chromosomes in every cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same parental copy is consistently silent or active in all cells

explanation.summary: Imprinted X-linked genes are not randomly inactivated; the same parental copy is consistently silent or active, so their expression is not mosaic.
explanation.whyCorrect: A small subset of X-linked genes is imprinted, meaning their expression depends on whether they are inherited from the mother or the father. These genes are not randomly inactivated; instead the same parental copy is consistently either silent or active, depending on the gene, due to epigenetic mechanisms, so their expression is not mosaic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biallelic expression describes genes that escape inactivation, not imprinted genes, which express one parental copy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cell-to-cell variation in which parental allele is expressed describes random X inactivation, which imprinted genes do not follow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imprinted expression is determined by parental origin, not by the presence or absence of a Barr body.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imprinting silences one parental copy, not both.

questions.stem: Unaffected parents have two children with Marfan syndrome who share the same FBN1 mutation, and germline mosaicism in one parent is suspected. The parents ask whether a test can determine their exact risk of having a third affected child. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A parental skin biopsy quantifies the fraction of mutant gametes

choices.label: B
choices.text: No test defines the extent of germline involvement; counsel increased risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sequencing parental blood quantifies the fraction of mutant gametes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their risk is exactly 50%, as for any autosomal dominant disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their risk is not increased because both parents tested negative

explanation.summary: There is no way to definitively test the extent of germline involvement, so unaffected parents with suspected germline mosaicism are counseled that future offspring have an increased risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: When one parent is suspected to have mosaicism for the FBN1 mutation that affects their germline, there is no way to definitively test for the extent of germline involvement. The parents are therefore counseled that, although they are unaffected, any future offspring do have an increased risk of inheriting the same mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Skin is a somatic tissue and cannot quantify germline involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blood is a somatic tissue; a negative or positive blood result does not measure the fraction of gametes carrying the mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 50% risk applies to a constitutionally affected heterozygous parent; the mosaic parent's risk depends on an unknown fraction of gametes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Negative somatic testing does not exclude germline mosaicism, which is precisely what two affected children suggest.

questions.stem: A researcher points out that all somatic cells in a 46,XX woman contain identical genetic information, yet she is described as a 'functional mosaic' with respect to the X chromosome. Which of the following best explains this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells differ in the DNA sequence of their X-linked genes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells differ in the number of Barr bodies they contain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cells differ in which parental X-linked alleles they express

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some cells inactivate both X chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some cells lose one X chromosome during development

explanation.summary: Monoallelic X-linked expression creates two functionally distinct cell populations, making females mosaic for X-linked gene expression rather than genotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Even though all somatic cells in females have the same genetic information, monoallelic expression from the X chromosome leads to two functionally distinct cell populations: one expressing alleles of X-linked genes from the paternal X and one expressing from the maternal X. Individuals with more than one X chromosome are therefore mosaic with respect to X-linked gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The DNA sequence is identical in all cells; the difference lies in which allele is expressed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Every 46,XX somatic cell has one inactive X; the cells differ in which X is inactive, not in Barr body number.
whyWrongByChoice.D: One X always remains active in every somatic cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of an X would be a genetic (chromosomal) mosaicism; functional mosaicism does not involve chromosome loss.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy is evaluated for poor feeding, failure to thrive, and developmental delay. Examination shows low-set ears, a small chin, and a heart murmur; echocardiography reveals a ventricular septal defect. Recurrent infections and low serum calcium are noted. The physician suspects a 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome. Which technique is the most appropriate to confirm this specific microdeletion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)

choices.label: B
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polymerase chain reaction of the FXN gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum electrolyte panel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Southern blot

explanation.summary: FISH is the targeted method of choice for confirming a clinically suspected microdeletion such as 22q11.2.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH uses fluorescently labeled probes complementary to a specific locus, so when a particular microdeletion is already suspected it can confirm the deletion (e.g., one red 22q11 signal alongside a normal control probe). It resolves submicroscopic changes invisible on a standard karyotype.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A standard G-banded karyotype only detects abnormalities of roughly 5-10 Mb or larger and cannot resolve a submicroscopic 22q11 microdeletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCR of FXN targets the Friedreich ataxia gene and is unrelated to a 22q11 microdeletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An electrolyte panel documents hypocalcemia but does not establish the underlying chromosomal diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Southern blot detects specific sequences and repeat expansions but is a low-throughput, radiolabel-dependent method not used to confirm this microdeletion.

questions.stem: A newborn has a flattened facial profile, a small nose with a flat bridge, a protruding tongue, and a single transverse palmar crease. Echocardiography demonstrates an atrioventricular septal defect. A cytogenetic study visualizes all chromosomes arranged in pairs and shows three copies of chromosome 21. Which technique produced this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: C
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Karyotyping visualizes all chromosomes as pairs and readily reveals aneuploidy such as trisomy 21.
explanation.whyCorrect: A G-banded karyotype arranges stained metaphase chromosomes into numbered pairs, allowing assessment of chromosome number and structure. Down syndrome appears as three copies of chromosome 21 (47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21), which was the finding that first linked Down syndrome to trisomy 21.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH detects copy number variation as a dosage ratio but does not display chromosomes as visible pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH highlights only a targeted locus rather than displaying the full set of paired chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Southern blot detects specific DNA sequences on a membrane, not whole-chromosome number.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins, not chromosomes.

questions.stem: In preparing a G-banded karyotype, cultured cells are treated with a chemical that halts cell division at the stage where chromosomes are most condensed and aligned at the cell's equator, maximizing their visibility. Which agent is used for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A restriction endonuclease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Colchicine

choices.label: C
choices.text: DAPI

choices.label: D
choices.text: Giemsa stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trypsin

explanation.summary: Colchicine arrests dividing cells at metaphase, when chromosomes are maximally condensed and best visualized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cultured cells are treated with colchicine to stop cell division at metaphase, the stage at which chromosomes are most condensed and aligned at the cell equator. This makes them highly defined and ideal for analysis before lysis and staining.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA for methods like Southern blot and are not used to arrest cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DAPI is a blue DNA counterstain used in FISH, not a metaphase-arresting agent in karyotyping.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giemsa is the dye mixture that produces the banding pattern after the cells are already arrested.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trypsin is a protease that partially digests histones and chromosomal proteins to help reveal banding; it does not arrest the cell cycle.

questions.stem: During interpretation of a G-banded chromosome, a technologist notes darkly stained bands (G-positive) with Giemsa. Compared with the lighter G-negative bands, which set of properties best characterizes these dark bands?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AT-rich, gene-poor, heterochromatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: AT-rich, gene-rich, euchromatin

choices.label: C
choices.text: GC-rich, gene-poor, heterochromatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: GC-rich, gene-rich, euchromatin with active transcription

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regions containing only telomeric repeats

explanation.summary: Dark G-positive bands are AT-rich, gene-poor heterochromatin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Giemsa binds more strongly to AT-rich DNA, producing dark bands that are gene-poor and generally associated with heterochromatin. Light G-negative bands are the opposite: GC-rich, gene-rich euchromatin with more active transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dark bands are gene-poor heterochromatin, not gene-rich euchromatin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dark bands are AT-rich, not GC-rich.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes the light G-negative bands, not the dark bands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dark bands reflect broad AT-rich, gene-poor regions, not exclusively telomeric repeats.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a male patient shows material exchanged between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22, with both chromosomes visibly altered. The two homologs of chromosomes 9 and 22 are each affected on one member. Which description best fits this abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 45,X monosomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: A submicroscopic microdeletion detectable only by FISH

choices.label: C
choices.text: del(22)(q11.2), a single-chromosome deletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: dup(22)(p23.3p23), a single-chromosome duplication

choices.label: E
choices.text: t(9;22), a translocation involving two chromosomes

explanation.summary: Involvement of two different chromosomes exchanging material indicates a translocation, t(9;22).
explanation.whyCorrect: Because two chromosomes (9 and 22) are both altered, the finding represents a translocation between them, t(9;22). A deletion or duplication would impact only a single chromosome, and the presence of a Y confirms the patient is male rather than having Turner syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 45,X (Turner) would show a single X and no Y; this patient is a male with a Y chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The exchange between two whole chromosomes is visible on the karyotype and is not a submicroscopic, FISH-only lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A deletion of 22q11.2 affects only one chromosome, but here two chromosomes are altered.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A duplication affects one chromosome and would not explain changes to both 9 and 22.

questions.stem: A geneticist wants an unbiased, genome-wide survey of chromosomal copy number variation in a child with developmental delay, intellectual disability, and dysmorphic features and a normal karyotype. Patient DNA is labeled with a red dye and reference DNA with a green dye, then co-hybridized to a microarray. In a well where the green signal exceeds the red, what has occurred in the patient's DNA at that locus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A deletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: A duplication

choices.label: D
choices.text: A point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: No copy number variation

explanation.summary: In array CGH, a green-dominant (weaker red) signal means the patient DNA failed to bind, indicating a deletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Array CGH compares red-labeled test DNA to green-labeled reference DNA and reads the red-to-green ratio. A stronger green than red signal means the patient (test) DNA did not bind the probe, implying the sequence is deleted at that locus. A red-dominant well indicates duplication, and a yellow well indicates no CNV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH cannot detect balanced translocations, which do not change copy number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A duplication would produce a red-dominant, not green-dominant, signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Array CGH measures copy number dosage and does not identify single-base point mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absence of copy number change gives a balanced yellow signal (equal red and green).

questions.stem: On an array CGH plot, a genomic region returns a DNA dosage score of -1. Which interpretation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duplication with four copies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duplication with three copies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygous deletion (one copy)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous deletion (zero copies)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal dosage (two copies)

explanation.summary: A dosage score of -1 on array CGH corresponds to a heterozygous deletion with one remaining copy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The array CGH dosage scale runs from -2 to +2: -2 is a homozygous deletion (0 copies), -1 is a heterozygous deletion (1 copy), 0 is normal (2 copies), +1 is a duplication with 3 copies, and +2 is a duplication with 4 copies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Four copies corresponds to a score of +2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Three copies corresponds to a score of +1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Zero copies corresponds to a score of -2, not -1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal two-copy dosage corresponds to a score of 0.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl has poor feeding, recurrent vomiting, and failure to thrive. She has microcephaly, epicanthal folds, and a ventricular septal defect. Initial testing shows a normal 46,XX karyotype, but a chromosomal microarray subsequently detects a 1.5 Mb deletion at 7q11.23. Which property of array CGH explains why it detected an abnormality that the karyotype missed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It amplifies the deleted region to make it visible

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can detect balanced translocations that karyotyping cannot

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has much higher resolution, detecting CNVs

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is more sensitive for low-level mosaicism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires prior knowledge of the exact deletion location

explanation.summary: Array CGH has far higher resolution than karyotyping, detecting CNVs down to ~50-200 kb.
explanation.whyCorrect: A standard karyotype only reliably detects abnormalities of about 5-10 Mb or larger, so a 1.5 Mb 7q11.23 deletion (Williams syndrome) can be missed. Array CGH detects copy number variants as small as approximately 50-200 kb, giving it the resolution to identify this microdeletion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH measures hybridization dosage; it does not amplify the deleted DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Array CGH actually cannot detect balanced translocations because they do not change copy number.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Array CGH has reduced, not increased, sensitivity for low-level mosaicism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Array CGH is an unbiased, untargeted method and does not require prior knowledge of the lesion.

questions.stem: A researcher must accurately size a very large trinucleotide GAA repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene in a patient with progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria, and cardiomyopathy. The expansion is too long for reliable amplification by conventional PCR. Which technique is best suited to size this expansion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: C
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Southern blot can accurately size large repeat expansions that are too long for conventional PCR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Southern blotting digests genomic DNA with a restriction enzyme, separates fragments by gel electrophoresis, and detects the target with a labeled probe. It can accurately size large repeat expansions, such as the FXN GAA expansion of Friedreich ataxia, that exceed the length reliably amplified by conventional PCR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH measures copy number dosage, not the length of a triplet repeat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH localizes a probe to a chromosomal region but does not size a triplet repeat expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A karyotype lacks the resolution to measure a repeat expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins, not the DNA repeat length.

questions.stem: A student is comparing molecular techniques by their principal target molecule. Which pairing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Northern blot detects proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Southern blot detects post-translational modifications

choices.label: C
choices.text: Southern blot detects RNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Western blot detects DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot detects proteins

explanation.summary: Western blot detects proteins; Southern detects DNA, Northern detects RNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The blot family is distinguished by target: Southern blot detects DNA, Northern blot detects RNA, Western blot detects proteins, and Eastern blot detects post-translational modifications. Western blot remains a very common laboratory technique for protein detection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Northern blot detects RNA, not proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Post-translational modifications are the Eastern blot target, not the Southern blot target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Southern blot detects DNA, not RNA (RNA is the Northern blot target).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Western blot detects proteins, not DNA.

questions.stem: A couple with three consecutive first-trimester pregnancy losses is referred for evaluation. Both partners are phenotypically normal. Karyotype testing of both partners is recommended because balanced reciprocal and Robertsonian translocations are the major abnormalities identified in this setting. What is the primary reason a balanced translocation carrier is typically phenotypically normal yet at risk for pregnancy loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It causes a triplet repeat expansion in the carrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: It produces a submicroscopic duplication detectable only by array CGH

choices.label: C
choices.text: No genetic material is gained or lost, but gametes may be unbalanced

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rearrangement adds a whole extra chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rearrangement deletes a large gene-rich region

explanation.summary: Balanced translocation carriers have no net loss or gain of material but can form unbalanced gametes, causing pregnancy loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a balanced translocation the total genetic material is preserved, so the carrier is usually phenotypically normal. However, during meiosis the carrier can produce unbalanced gametes with missing or extra segments, leading to recurrent pregnancy loss; this is why karyotyping both partners is part of the recurrent-loss evaluation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Triplet repeat expansions are a distinct mechanism unrelated to balanced translocations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A balanced translocation does not change copy number and is actually a lesion array CGH cannot detect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adding a whole chromosome is aneuploidy, not a balanced translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A balanced rearrangement by definition does not delete material, which is why the carrier is unaffected.

questions.stem: A clinician is choosing a diagnostic test but wants a method that does NOT require prior knowledge of the suspected abnormality. Which of the following best describes the key limitation that makes FISH unsuitable when the abnormality is unknown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FISH can only be performed on proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: FISH cannot use fluorescent probes

choices.label: C
choices.text: FISH has very low resolution and misses small changes

choices.label: D
choices.text: FISH is a targeted method

choices.label: E
choices.text: FISH requires digestion with a restriction enzyme

explanation.summary: FISH is a targeted method requiring prior knowledge, so it only detects what its probe is designed to find.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH is an 'a priori' targeted approach: a probe must be designed for a known sequence, so it only reveals suspected abnormalities. When the abnormality is unknown, an unbiased genome-wide method such as array CGH or karyotyping is needed instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH targets DNA sequences on chromosomes, not proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH depends on fluorescently labeled probes; using them is a defining feature, not a limitation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FISH is actually a high-resolution technique that detects small changes missed by karyotyping.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion is a step in Southern blot, not FISH.

questions.stem: A newborn boy has a flattened facial profile, a small nose with a flat bridge, a short neck, and a tongue that tends to protrude. Karyotype shows 47,XY,+21. Congenital heart defects occur in roughly 30-40% of patients with this condition. Which heart defect is the most common in these patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrioventricular septal defect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coarctation of the aorta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patent ductus arteriosus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tetralogy of Fallot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transposition of the great arteries

explanation.summary: Atrioventricular septal defect is the most common congenital heart defect in Down syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heart defects affect 30-40% of individuals with Down syndrome (trisomy 21), and atrioventricular septal defect is the most common of these. The craniofacial features described (flat facial profile, small nose with flat bridge, short neck, protruding tongue) are characteristic of the syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coarctation of the aorta is not the characteristic heart defect of Down syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patent ductus arteriosus is not the most common defect in this population; atrioventricular septal defect is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetralogy of Fallot is not the most common cardiac lesion associated with trisomy 21.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transposition of the great arteries is not the lesion most frequently seen in Down syndrome.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with Down syndrome is brought in by his group-home caregiver because of 2 years of progressive memory loss and decline in his ability to perform daily tasks he previously managed independently. Thyroid function tests are normal, and he has no snoring or daytime somnolence. Which condition, known to occur with increased frequency in Down syndrome, best explains his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Childhood-type acute leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early-onset Alzheimer disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hirschsprung disease of infancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstructive sleep apnea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sensorineural hearing loss

explanation.summary: Down syndrome is associated with early-onset Alzheimer disease, which presents as progressive cognitive decline in mid-adulthood.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to congenital malformations, individuals with Down syndrome have an increased risk of thyroid disorders, sleep apnea, leukemia in early childhood, immunodeficiency, and early-onset Alzheimer disease. Progressive memory loss and functional decline in a middle-aged adult with Down syndrome, with thyroid disease and sleep apnea excluded, points to early-onset Alzheimer disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The increased leukemia risk in Down syndrome is in early childhood and would not present as adult-onset memory loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hirschsprung disease is a gastrointestinal anomaly of infancy, not a cause of cognitive decline in adulthood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sleep apnea is associated with Down syndrome but the absence of snoring and daytime somnolence argues against it as the cause of progressive dementia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hearing loss affects about 90% of individuals with Down syndrome but does not explain progressive memory loss and loss of daily function.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman at 16 weeks of gestation has abnormal serum marker screening and a cell-free DNA result suggesting trisomy 21. A diagnostic fetal karyotype is planned, which requires culturing cells before colchicine treatment and Giemsa staining. Which sample provides the cells for this culture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell-free DNA in maternal plasma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal cells from amniotic fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal buccal epithelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal peripheral blood lymphocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maternal skin fibroblasts

explanation.summary: Prenatal karyotyping cultures fetal cells obtained from amniotic fluid by amniocentesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Karyotyping begins with cultured cells, which are often obtained from blood or amniotic fluid. For prenatal diagnosis of Down syndrome, amniocentesis provides fetal cells from the amniotic fluid that are cultured, arrested at metaphase with colchicine, and stained with Giemsa to visualize the chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cell-free DNA is used for a blood-based screening test; it is not cultured cells and cannot be karyotyped.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal buccal cells carry the maternal genome, not the fetal chromosomes being assessed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal lymphocytes would give the mother's karyotype, not the fetus's.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maternal fibroblasts would not reveal the fetal chromosome complement.

questions.stem: During preparation of a G-banded karyotype, cells that have been arrested at metaphase are lysed and the released chromosomes are positioned on a slide. Before Giemsa stain is applied, the chromosomes are briefly exposed to a protease. Which effect of this treatment is intended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arrest of the cell cycle at metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of DNA at specific recognition sequences

choices.label: C
choices.text: Denaturation of DNA into single strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intercalation into DNA to produce fluorescence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Partial digestion of histones that compact the DNA

explanation.summary: Trypsin partially digests histones and other DNA-compacting proteins before Giemsa staining.
explanation.whyCorrect: After lysis, proteins that compact DNA such as histones are partially digested using the protease trypsin. This step precedes Giemsa staining, which then reveals the banding pattern specific to each chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metaphase arrest is achieved earlier by colchicine, not by a protease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sequence-specific DNA cleavage is the role of restriction enzymes in Southern blotting, not of trypsin in karyotyping.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Denaturation of DNA to single strands is a step in FISH sample preparation, not part of protease treatment for banding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DNA intercalation with fluorescence describes DAPI counterstaining in FISH, not protease action.

questions.stem: A laboratory director explains to trainees why Southern blotting, once a mainstay of molecular diagnostics, is now rarely performed in the clinical laboratory even though it can still analyze genomic DNA directly. Which statement best summarizes the reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot analyze genomic DNA without prior amplification

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cannot size repeat expansions beyond the PCR limit

choices.label: C
choices.text: It detects RNA transcripts rather than genomic DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires colchicine-arrested metaphase chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Newer methods offer higher resolution and throughput

explanation.summary: Southern blotting has been largely replaced because newer methods provide higher resolution, automation, and greater throughput.
explanation.whyCorrect: Southern blotting, developed by Edwin Southern in 1975, is not often used today because methods such as PCR-based approaches and array CGH offer higher resolution, automation, and greater throughput, making them more suitable for modern clinical and research applications. It remains a historic method worth knowing because related blots share its principles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Southern blot analyzes genomic DNA directly; its ability to do so without amplification was one of its strengths before PCR was widespread.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Southern blot is actually valued for sizing large repeat expansions that are too long for conventional PCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Southern blot detects DNA sequences; RNA is the target of the Northern blot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Southern blot uses digested genomic DNA on a gel, not metaphase chromosome preparations.

questions.stem: A student is asked to rank cytogenetic techniques by their sensitivity for detecting small copy number changes. One technique is rated as having only moderate sensitivity: it can detect small CNVs but requires a larger amount of input DNA than the high-sensitivity methods. Which technique is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array CGH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: C
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polymerase chain reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Southern blot

explanation.summary: Southern blot has moderate sensitivity: it can detect small CNVs but requires more DNA than array CGH or FISH.
explanation.whyCorrect: When cytogenetic techniques are matched to their degree of sensitivity, array CGH and FISH are high sensitivity, Southern blot is moderate sensitivity, and karyotype is low sensitivity. Southern blot can also detect small CNVs, but it requires more DNA than the high-sensitivity methods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH is a high-sensitivity technique that detects CNVs down to about 50-200 kb.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH is a high-sensitivity, high-resolution technique that detects small changes missed by karyotyping.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotype has low sensitivity because it detects only large abnormalities of about 5-10 Mb.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PCR is a DNA amplification step used in genotyping approaches, not the moderate-sensitivity CNV detection method described.

questions.stem: The name of the technique fluorescence in situ hybridization includes a Latin phrase meaning 'in place.' Which feature of the method does this phrase describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The chromosomes are cultured and arrested at metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: The DNA is first extracted and cut with restriction enzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The probe binds its target directly on the chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: The probe is labeled with a radioactive isotope before use

choices.label: E
choices.text: The signal is read by a scanner on a microarray grid

explanation.summary: 'In situ' refers to the probe hybridizing to its target directly on the chromosome, in place.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH uses fluorescently labeled, short single-stranded DNA probes complementary to a specific genomic target. They hybridize, or bind, to their matching sequence directly on the chromosome, which is why the technique is called 'in situ' (Latin for 'in place').

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metaphase arrest is a karyotyping step and does not explain the meaning of 'in situ.'
whyWrongByChoice.B: Extraction and restriction digestion of DNA describe Southern blotting, in which the DNA is removed from its chromosomal context.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FISH probes are fluorescently labeled; radioactive probes belong to the 1960s precursor methods and Southern blot.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reading signals from a microarray grid is how array CGH works, not how FISH is visualized.

questions.stem: During a FISH procedure, a slide of metaphase chromosomes is treated before the fluorescently labeled probes are added and allowed to bind. What is the purpose of this pre-treatment of the sample DNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To amplify the target sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: To arrest the cells at metaphase

choices.label: C
choices.text: To denature the DNA into single strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: To digest histones and expose banding

choices.label: E
choices.text: To transfer the DNA onto a membrane

explanation.summary: FISH sample preparation denatures the target DNA into single strands so the single-stranded probe can hybridize.
explanation.whyCorrect: In FISH sample preparation, DNA from metaphase chromosomes or interphase nuclei is denatured to become single-stranded. The fluorescent probes, which are themselves short single-stranded DNA sequences, are then added and allowed to hybridize to their complementary target sequences.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH does not amplify the target; it detects the sequence in place with a labeled probe.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metaphase arrest with colchicine occurs during cell culture for karyotyping and is not the purpose of this FISH step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease digestion of histones to reveal banding is a G-banding step, not a FISH hybridization step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfer to a membrane is part of Southern blotting; FISH keeps the DNA on the chromosome.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a leukemia is evaluated in a cancer genetics laboratory. The team wants to determine whether a specific gene segment has moved from its normal chromosome to a different chromosome, and uses fluorescently labeled probes on the patient's cells viewed under a fluorescence microscope. Which capability of FISH is being used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Determining the chromosomal location of a sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measuring copy number ratios across the genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quantifying the amount of a protein in tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sizing a trinucleotide repeat expansion in a gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Visualizing all 23 chromosome pairs at once

explanation.summary: FISH detection reveals not only the presence or absence of a sequence but also its location, such as translocation to another chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Using a fluorescence microscope, FISH shows the presence or absence of a sequence (deleted or duplicated) and its location (for example, whether it is translocated to another chromosome). This makes FISH a standard tool in cancer genetics for detecting translocations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Genome-wide copy number ratios are measured by array CGH, not FISH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein quantification is done by Western blot, not by FISH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sizing repeat expansions is a Southern blot application.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Visualizing all chromosome pairs is the function of a karyotype; FISH highlights only targeted loci.

questions.stem: A FISH assay for 22q11 deletion syndrome uses two probes: a red TUPLE1 probe located at 22q11 and a green ARSA probe on chromosome 22. In a patient's metaphase spread, both chromosome 22 homologs show a green signal, but only one shows a red signal. What is the purpose of including the green ARSA probe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds within 22q11 to amplify the deletion signal

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects a duplication of the 22q11 region

choices.label: C
