choices.text: It labels the reference genome for a ratio calculation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It marks both chromosome 22s from outside the deleted region

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stains total chromosomal DNA to orient the spread

explanation.summary: The ARSA probe lies outside the deleted region and serves as a control identifying both copies of chromosome 22.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH detects the 22q11 deletion with two probes: the ARSA probe (green) is located outside the deleted region and acts as a control, whereas the TUPLE1 probe (red) sits at the 22q11 location. Because both chromosome 22s carry the green control signal but only one carries the red signal, the deletion is present in the heterozygous state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ARSA probe is located outside the deleted region, not within 22q11.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The assay is designed to detect a deletion; the control probe does not test for duplication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Labeling a reference genome for a red-to-green ratio describes array CGH, not a FISH control probe.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staining of all chromosomal DNA is done by DAPI (blue), not by the ARSA probe.

questions.stem: In a FISH image from a patient evaluated for a microdeletion, every chromosome appears blue, with small red and green dots marking the probe sites on chromosome 22. Which agent produces the blue appearance of the chromosomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cy3, a green fluorescent label

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cy5, a red fluorescent label

choices.label: C
choices.text: DAPI, a DNA-intercalating dye

choices.label: D
choices.text: Giemsa, a DNA-binding dye mixture

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trypsin, a protein-digesting enzyme

explanation.summary: In FISH, chromosomes are counterstained blue with DAPI, a DNA-intercalating molecule.
explanation.whyCorrect: In FISH, chromosomes are stained with DAPI (blue), a DNA-intercalating molecule, so that all chromosomes are visible in blue while the fluorescently labeled probes appear as colored signals at their target loci.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cy3 is the green fluorescent label used for the reference DNA in array CGH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cy5 is the red fluorescent label used for the test DNA in array CGH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giemsa is the dye mixture used for G-banding in karyotypes, producing dark and light bands rather than blue fluorescence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trypsin is the protease used to partially digest histones during karyotype preparation; it is not a stain.

questions.stem: A cytogenetics laboratory compares the sample requirements of G-banded karyotyping and fluorescence in situ hybridization. Which of the following is required for karyotyping but is NOT required for FISH?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A microarray grid of DNA probes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells arrested in metaphase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fluorescently labeled DNA probes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior knowledge of the target sequence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion of DNA

explanation.summary: Karyotyping requires metaphase chromosomes, whereas FISH can be performed on metaphase chromosomes or interphase nuclei.
explanation.whyCorrect: Karyotyping depends on colchicine arrest at metaphase, when chromosomes are most condensed and aligned at the cell's equator, so that they can be photographed and arranged into pairs. FISH, by contrast, denatures DNA from metaphase chromosomes or interphase nuclei, so dividing cells arrested at metaphase are not a requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A microarray grid is used in array CGH, not in either karyotyping or FISH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluorescent probes are used by FISH, not by karyotyping, which uses Giemsa stain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prior knowledge of the sequence is a requirement of FISH (a targeted method), not of karyotyping, which is unbiased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion is a Southern blot step and is used by neither technique.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old boy with a cleft palate, hooded eyes, and a heart defect that gives his skin a bluish tint develops muscle cramps followed by a brief seizure. Serum calcium is low. FISH later confirms a 22q11 deletion. Underdevelopment of which structure best explains the seizure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal glands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidneys

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parathyroid glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid gland

explanation.summary: In DiGeorge syndrome, underdeveloped parathyroid glands cause low calcium, leading to muscle cramps or seizures.
explanation.whyCorrect: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) is a multisystem disease. Low calcium levels due to underdeveloped parathyroid glands can lead to muscle cramps or seizures. Other features include heart defects causing a bluish skin tint, cleft palate, hooded eyes, a small chin or enlarged nose tip, and developmental delays.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal underdevelopment is not a feature of 22q11 deletion and does not cause hypocalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kidney abnormalities can occur in DiGeorge syndrome but the low calcium and seizure are attributed to parathyroid underdevelopment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymic underdevelopment accounts for the T-cell defects and frequent infections in DiGeorge syndrome, not for hypocalcemic seizures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid disorders are associated with Down syndrome; they do not explain the low calcium in this patient.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman presents with metastatic adenocarcinoma whose primary site cannot be identified by imaging. Her oncologist orders a commercial test that isolates circulating tumor cells from a blood sample and analyzes them by comparative genomic hybridization. Which information is this test designed to provide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serum concentrations of proteins secreted by the tumor

choices.label: B
choices.text: The exact nucleotide sequence of point mutations in driver genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The presence of a balanced translocation within tumor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The size of a trinucleotide repeat within tumor DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor's primary origin and genetic risk factors guiding therapy

explanation.summary: CGH on circulating tumor cells reveals genomic instability and can identify the tumor's primary origin and guide personalized treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: By revealing genomic instability, array CGH has become a valuable tool in precision oncology for identifying biomarkers that predict tumor progression and guide personalized treatment. Several companies offer CGH testing on circulating tumor cells isolated from blood, which allows determination of the primary origin of the tumor, identification of genetic risk factors, and guidance of personalized treatment strategies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CGH analyzes DNA copy number, not protein levels in serum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Array CGH measures copy number dosage; it does not read nucleotide sequences or identify point mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Balanced translocations do not change copy number and cannot be detected by array CGH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sizing trinucleotide repeats is a Southern blot application, not the purpose of CGH.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy with a ventricular septal defect, recurrent infections, low serum calcium, and a small chin undergoes FISH with a TUPLE1 probe for 22q11 deletion. Both chromosome 22 homologs show a normal red signal. The physician's clinical suspicion of DiGeorge syndrome remains high. Which test is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array CGH

choices.label: B
choices.text: G-banded karyotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat the same FISH assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: When a targeted FISH result is negative but clinical suspicion stays high, array CGH provides broader unbiased genomic screening.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH is the appropriate confirmatory test for suspected DiGeorge syndrome, but array CGH can be used if the FISH result is negative while clinical suspicion remains high, or if broader genomic screening is needed. Because FISH detects only what its probe is designed to find, an unbiased genome-wide method is the logical next step.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A standard karyotype is not sensitive enough to detect microdeletions and would not resolve the question.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeating the same targeted assay would only re-examine the single probe locus and would not broaden the search.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Southern blot is a low-throughput, targeted method that is not the best tool for detecting a microdeletion syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins and does not assess chromosomal deletions.

questions.stem: During an array CGH run, test DNA labeled with a red dye and reference DNA labeled with a green dye are co-hybridized to a microarray. The scanner reports that the large majority of wells fluoresce yellow. What is the correct interpretation of these wells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hybridization failed and the run must be repeated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Test and reference DNA bound equally; no copy number variation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patient carries a balanced translocation at those loci

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient has a duplication with three copies at those loci

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient has a heterozygous deletion at those loci

explanation.summary: A yellow signal means red and green signals are equal, indicating no CNV, which is what most wells show.
explanation.whyCorrect: The scanner calculates the red-to-green fluorescence ratio in each well. A yellow signal, where red and green are equal, indicates no copy number variation at that locus. This is what is observed in most wells because most of the genome has normal dosage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Yellow wells reflect successful, balanced hybridization of both samples, not a failed run.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Balanced translocations do not alter copy number and are not detected by array CGH at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A three-copy duplication would appear as a red-dominant well (dosage +1), not yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A heterozygous deletion would appear as a green-dominant well (dosage -1), not yellow.

questions.stem: A geneticist suspects that a child's phenotype results from a chromosomal abnormality present in only a small percentage of the child's cells, with the remaining cells being chromosomally normal. Array CGH on a blood sample is reported as normal. Which limitation of array CGH best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot distinguish test DNA from reference DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cannot measure copy number of whole chromosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has reduced sensitivity for low-level mosaicism

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires prior knowledge of the abnormality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its resolution is limited to abnormalities of 5-10 Mb

explanation.summary: Array CGH has reduced sensitivity for detecting mosaicism, especially when the abnormal cell population is low.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the limitations of array CGH is reduced sensitivity for detecting mosaicism, particularly when the abnormal cell population is small. Because the array measures the pooled red-to-green ratio of all cells in the sample, a small abnormal fraction may not shift the ratio enough to be called.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Test and reference DNA are distinguished by their red and green labels, so this is not a limitation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Array CGH detects copy number variation across the entire genome; whole-chromosome dosage is not beyond its scope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Array CGH is an unbiased method that does not require prior assumptions; that limitation belongs to FISH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 5-10 Mb detection limit describes the karyotype; array CGH resolves CNVs of about 50-200 kb.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with intellectual disability has a normal array CGH result. A later targeted test identifies a small deletion in a region of her genome. Review of the microarray design shows that this region was not represented by any probes on the array. Which limitation of array CGH accounts for the missed deletion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dependence on radioactive probe labeling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inability to detect balanced rearrangements

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete genome coverage where probes are absent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced sensitivity for mosaic abnormalities

choices.label: E
choices.text: Requirement for metaphase chromosome preparations

explanation.summary: Some genomic regions are underrepresented on the array because of absent probes, leading to incomplete genome coverage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Array CGH resolution depends on probe coverage. Some genomic regions are underrepresented due to the absence of probes, leading to incomplete genome coverage, so a deletion in an unprobed region produces no signal change and is missed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH uses fluorescent dyes, not radioactive labels; radiolabeling belongs to Southern blot.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A deletion is an unbalanced change, so the balanced-rearrangement limitation is not relevant here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing in the scenario indicates mosaicism; the deletion was missed because the region lacked probes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Array CGH uses extracted DNA and does not require metaphase chromosomes.

questions.stem: A couple has had three consecutive first-trimester pregnancy losses. Both partners are phenotypically normal, and array CGH performed on each partner returned normal results. The physician still suspects an inherited chromosomal cause. Which test is the most appropriate next step, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FISH, because it surveys the whole genome without prior knowledge

choices.label: B
choices.text: G-banded karyotype, because array CGH cannot detect balanced translocations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat array CGH, because the first result was likely a hybridization failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot, because it sizes triplet repeat expansions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot, because it detects abnormal protein products

explanation.summary: Balanced translocations do not alter copy number, so a karyotype rather than array CGH is needed to detect them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Karyotype testing of couples is part of the evaluation of recurrent pregnancy loss because balanced reciprocal and Robertsonian translocations are the major abnormalities identified. Array CGH cannot detect balanced chromosomal rearrangements because no genetic material is gained or lost, so a normal array does not exclude a balanced translocation; a karyotype, which visualizes chromosome structure directly, is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH is a targeted method requiring prior knowledge; it does not survey the whole genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The normal array is expected with a balanced translocation, so repeating it would not help.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Triplet repeat expansions are not the suspected cause of recurrent pregnancy loss in this couple.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins and has no role in identifying chromosomal rearrangements.

questions.stem: In a Southern blot, genomic DNA is first digested with a restriction enzyme and the resulting fragments are separated by size on a gel. Which step occurs immediately next, before the labeled probe can bind to the sequence of interest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amplifying the fragments by PCR

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arresting the cells at metaphase with colchicine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hybridizing the fragments to a microarray

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staining the fragments with Giemsa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferring the DNA onto a membrane

explanation.summary: After gel electrophoresis, the DNA is transferred onto a membrane, where the radiolabeled probe then binds.
explanation.whyCorrect: Southern blotting proceeds in order: DNA is digested with a restriction enzyme, fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis, the DNA is transferred onto a membrane, and a radioactive-labeled DNA probe binds to the sequence of interest on that membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Southern blot analyzes genomic DNA directly without PCR amplification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colchicine metaphase arrest is a karyotyping step; Southern blot starts from extracted DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hybridization to a microarray is the array CGH approach; Southern blot uses a membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giemsa staining is used for chromosome banding in karyotypes, not in Southern blotting.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to measure the amount of a specific messenger RNA transcript in tissue samples using a membrane-based blotting technique that shares its principles with Southern blotting. Which technique should be used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eastern blot

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Northern blot

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southern blot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot

explanation.summary: Northern blot detects RNA using the same blotting principles as Southern blot.
explanation.whyCorrect: Techniques similar to Southern blot use the same principles for other targets: Northern blot detects RNAs (though it is not very used anymore), Western blot detects proteins, and Eastern blot detects post-translational modifications. Measuring a specific mRNA therefore calls for a Northern blot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eastern blot detects post-translational modifications of proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH hybridizes probes to chromosomal DNA in place; it is not a membrane blot for RNA quantity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Southern blot detects DNA sequences, not RNA transcripts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot detects proteins, not mRNA.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy has 2 years of progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and pyramidal weakness of the lower limbs; echocardiography shows cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing reveals a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene on both alleles. Which mechanism best explains his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced translocation disrupting the FXN locus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletion of the entire FXN gene on one chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gain of function from an abnormally long frataxin protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overproduction of frataxin that overloads mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcriptional silencing of FXN with reduced frataxin levels

explanation.summary: In Friedreich ataxia, the intronic GAA expansion silences FXN transcription, reducing the mitochondrial protein frataxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Friedreich ataxia is caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of FXN, which encodes the mitochondrial protein frataxin. When the repeats exceed a critical threshold, FXN is transcriptionally silenced and frataxin levels fall significantly, disrupting mitochondrial function in high-energy tissues such as the nervous system, heart, and skeletal muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced translocation is not the lesion in Friedreich ataxia, which is a repeat-expansion disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The disease is caused by repeat expansion within the gene, not by deletion of the whole gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The expansion is intronic and silences transcription; it does not lengthen the frataxin protein or confer a gain of function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect is a deficiency of frataxin, not an excess.

questions.stem: Two unrelated patients are diagnosed with Friedreich ataxia, each carrying GAA repeat expansions in intron 1 of FXN on both alleles. Patient 1 developed gait ataxia at age 9 and has severe cardiomyopathy. Patient 2 first noticed symptoms at age 24 and has a milder course. Which difference between the patients most likely explains the discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patient 1 has a larger GAA repeat expansion than Patient 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patient 1 has a smaller GAA repeat expansion than Patient 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patient 1 inherited the disorder in an autosomal dominant pattern

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patient 2 has a point mutation rather than a repeat expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patient 2's expansion lies in the coding region of FXN

explanation.summary: Larger GAA expansions correlate with earlier onset and more severe Friedreich ataxia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The severity and progression of Friedreich ataxia are closely linked to the size of the GAA repeat expansion, with larger expansions generally correlating with earlier onset and more severe clinical outcomes. The disease typically begins before age 25, with first signs often between ages 10 and 15, so the patient with onset at 9 and severe cardiomyopathy most likely carries the larger expansion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A smaller expansion would predict later onset and milder disease, the opposite of Patient 1's course.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Friedreich ataxia has autosomal recessive transmission in both patients; inheritance pattern does not differ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem states both patients carry GAA repeat expansions, so a point mutation is not the difference.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The FXN expansion is located in intron 1, not the coding region, in both patients.

questions.stem: A Southern blot sizing the FXN GAA repeat is performed on a family. The proband, a boy with ataxia, shows two bands: one corresponding to a large expansion of about 800 GAA repeats and one corresponding to about 300 GAA repeats, with no normal-size allele. His mother, who is unaffected, carries the 800-repeat allele together with a normal allele. His father is also unaffected. Which statement best explains the pattern of inheritance in this family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A de novo expansion arising in the proband

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance in the parents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance from two carrier parents

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial inheritance because frataxin is a mitochondrial protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive inheritance from a carrier mother

explanation.summary: Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive; the affected proband inherited one expanded FXN allele from each unaffected carrier parent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Friedreich ataxia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with autosomal recessive transmission. Southern blot analysis of the family shows the proband carries a large maternally inherited expansion (about 800 GAA) plus a second expanded allele of about 300 GAA, with no normal allele. Each unaffected parent carries one expanded and one normal allele, consistent with recessive inheritance where both alleles must be expanded to cause disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 800-repeat allele is demonstrably maternally inherited, so this is not a de novo event.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mother carries the large expansion yet is unaffected because she also has a normal allele, which fits recessive rather than dominant inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frataxin is a mitochondrial protein, but FXN is a nuclear gene inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, not through mitochondrial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FXN is not X-linked, and the proband received one expanded allele from each parent, which X-linked inheritance cannot explain.
